title: Mathematical Foundations of LLM Training and Inference
text:
Contents
A language model’s behavior depends on calculations you can inspect: how text becomes numbers, how errors change weights, and how a trained model produces an answer. This book develops the mathematical foundations of large language models through small examples and computational labs. It helps you connect those calculations to practical decisions about model quality, adaptation, memory, and inference.

title: Roadmap
text:
Starting knowledge
A useful model must produce the right kind of output, learn from appropriate data, and behave reliably on new examples. This book develops the calculations behind those requirements. It connects text representations and prediction errors to model training, generated answers, and resource costs.
Artificial intelligence, or AI, is the broad field of systems that perform tasks associated with perception, reasoning, prediction, or generation. Machine learning, or ML, develops their behavior from data. Deep learning uses multilayer neural networks to learn intermediate representations.
A language model assigns probabilities to token sequences or missing tokens in context. A large language model, or LLM, uses a large neural network for this purpose. Generative AI produces content such as text, images, or audio. Language generation is one application within that broader group.
The book separates four decisions: what the task requires, how the model combines information, what training measures, and how an output is selected. A model family does not uniquely determine its task. The same transformer architecture can support different outputs when its inputs, objective, and prediction interface change.
The guide assumes elementary algebra, functions, sums, and basic probability. Python examples use lists, indexing, functions, and imports. Derivatives and PyTorch’s automatic differentiation are taught within the book.
A tensor is an array with explicit axes and a numerical type. Shape \([B,T,D]\) describes \(B\) examples, \(T\) positions per example, and \(D\) coordinates per position. Thus shape \([2,3,4]\) contains 24 logical values. Its device identifies where the values reside, such as CPU memory or a GPU.
Integer token IDs select vocabulary entries. Floating-point arrays hold numerical features, and Boolean arrays can indicate valid positions. 2  Token IDs and batches introduces these objects in batches. 23  Tensor storage and execution later explains their storage and execution costs.
Matrix multiplication combines values along a shared axis. If \(X\) has shape \([B,D_{in}]\) and \(W\) has shape \([D_{in},D_{out}]\), then \(XW\) has shape \([B,D_{out}]\). Scoring a batch develops the calculation and PyTorch’s stored weight orientation. ?sec-ch-m2-notation provides a reference while reading.

Adapting and running LLMs, Chapters 20–21 | Adaptation choices and state reused during generation | Practical execution also depends on input modality and tensor storage | | VI. Implementation and extensions, Chapters 22–24 | Multimodal inputs, tensor memory, and complete experiments | Component measurements and failures support a judgment about the full system |






Figure 1: The six parts connect model inputs to tested implementations through a cumulative reading progression.



Two representation routes share the initial task definition. Count-based document features can feed a classifier, while token IDs select learned vectors for a sequence model. Neither route requires passing through the other.
Similarly, probabilities support two branches. 7  Decoding strategies follows output selection with fixed parameters. 8  Cross-entropy and perplexity compares outputs with targets, and 9  Validation and testing evaluates new examples. The gradient chapter, 10  Backpropagation, precedes the optimizer comparison in 11  Momentum and AdamW.
For text classification, continue through nonlinear models, embedding lookup, and Word2Vec in Chapters 12–14, then use Text classification with learned embeddings. For sequence modeling, compare the count baseline in Fixed histories with recurrence before attention and transformers. The corresponding experiments follow the same order in 24  Experiments and system integration.
For adaptation and serving, complete Chapters 17–21 before the two-model experiment in Adapting answers to the reader. The multimodal experiment in Multimodal components and combined answers combines reference retrieval with a separate answer component. Its error records connect the final system back to the original task definition.
This is a mathematics companion to the performance engineering course. It explains the objects and calculations needed to inspect model quality, training, and inference. Kernel programming, Tensor Core scheduling, memory coalescing, and complete distributed deployment configurations belong to the performance guide.
Mixed precision, serving engines, and timing appear here where they affect a numerical assumption, memory estimate, or experimental choice. The book does not provide a full production deployment recipe for each library it mentions.

Model objects and families
Following an example through a model is easier when its data objects remain distinct. The table below is an orientation reference. Each linked chapter develops the calculation rather than assuming the summary is sufficient preparation.
Object or decision | Meaning | Full explanation | |—|—|—| | Examples and targets | Observed inputs and the outputs the task requires | 1  Prediction targets | | Task | Numeric prediction, class selection, sequence prediction, or a useful learned representation | 1  Prediction targets and 18  Transformer architectures | | Representation | Token IDs, masks, feature vectors, and batches supplied to a model | Chapters 2–4 and 13  Embedding tables | | Parameters | Weights, biases, embedding tables, and projections changed by training | 5  Linear scores and 10  Backpropagation | | Activations and logits | Intermediate values and unnormalized output scores | 12  Activation functions and 6  Sigmoid and softmax | | Loss and gradient | An objective value and its sensitivity to parameter changes | 8  Cross-entropy and perplexity and 10  Backpropagation | | Optimizer state | Persistent information used by an update rule, such as momentum | 11  Momentum and AdamW | | Inference state | Request-specific values, including selected tokens and cached attention keys and values | 7  Decoding strategies and 21  KV cache and serving |
Regression returns a numerical estimate. Classification selects labels, including multiple independent labels when the task requires them. Sequence objectives can predict the next token, reconstruct hidden positions, or generate a target sequence from an input. Representation learning instead develops vectors for downstream use. These objectives are distinguished in 1  Prediction targets, 14  Word2Vec, and 18  Transformer architectures.
A model family controls how available input information can influence a prediction. Recurrent neural networks, or RNNs, carry state through positions. Long short-term memory networks, or LSTMs, add gates to that state. Transformers use attention over permitted positions. The following comparison identifies their teaching locations.

Family

Training and inference also have different purposes. Training changes parameters using a loss and an update rule. Inference applies the current parameters to an input. Evaluation uses held-out examples to assess the result without treating their target labels as another training batch.

title: Notation
text:
Symbols and dimensions
The symbols below recur in data, model, training, and inference equations. Each chapter adds local indices or dimensions when a computation needs them.
A corpus \(C\) contains documents \(d_1,\ldots,d_N\):
\[
C = \{d_1,\ldots,d_N\}
\tag{1}\]
A tokenization map \(\tau\) converts text into a sequence of \(T\) tokens:
\[
\tau(\text{text}) = (t_1,\ldots,t_T)
\tag{2}\]
Each token \(t_i\) receives an integer ID from vocabulary \(\mathcal V\), whose size is \(V\):
\[
x_i=\operatorname{id}(t_i),\quad x\in\{0,\ldots,V-1\}^{T},\quad V=|\mathcal V|
\tag{3}\]
A batch containing \(B\) token sequences of padded length \(T\) forms an integer array:
\[
X \in \mathbb{Z}^{B\times T}
\tag{4}\]
The same letter can have a local meaning in different equations. Read the dimensions beside the equation first. This table collects the recurring conventions rather than changing symbols used by an original source.
Return to the corresponding explanations: Token batches, Batch scores, Embedding lookup, Linear models, Probability outputs, Loss reduction, Sigmoid, activations, Gradients, updates, Attention, Multiple heads, Adam, LoRA.
In a vocabulary discussion, \(V\) is a size. In attention, \(V\) is an array of value vectors. Likewise, \(L\) can mean scalar loss or a layer count in a cache estimate. The local definitions resolve these uses. Natural logarithms give losses in nats, with perplexity computed by exponentiating the average negative log probability. Base-two logs give bits and require base-two exponentiation.

text:
Masks and matrix orientation
Masks exclude contributions at different stages. A padding token value by itself is insufficient when the tokenizer also uses that value for a real end-of-sequence token.



Table 2: Masks affect different consumers and reductions.










Object
Values and dimensions
Consumer and effect




Tokenizer attention_mask
Usually \(1\) for a real token and \(0\) for inserted padding, \([B,T]\)
Supplies padding visibility to the model


Additive attention mask
\(0\) for permitted and \(-\infty\) for blocked scores, with shape required by the receiving API
Added before softmax, making blocked attention weights zero


Loss labels with ignore_index
Target IDs with a sentinel such as \(-100\), \([B,T]\)
Excludes positions from both summed loss and the supervised-position count


Pooling mask
\(1\) for included vectors and \(0\) otherwise, \([B,T]\)
Excludes padding vectors and sets the mean’s denominator






Boolean mask conventions depend on the receiving API. Check whether True means permitted or blocked before converting a tokenizer mask. Chapter 2 establishes token validity, Pooling sequences applies masked pooling, and §16.3 constructs attention visibility.
For a row-vector batch, mathematical weights have dimensions \([D_{in},D_{out}]\). A stored PyTorch linear weight has dimensions \([D_{out},D_{in}]\). Denote the stored tensor by \(A\) and write \(X A^{\mathsf T}+b\), with \(W=A^{\mathsf T}\). Neither transposition nor broadcasting changes the number of output examples.

title: Part I: From text to mathematical objects
text:
Chapters in this part
A language model cannot calculate directly from a sentence. It needs examples with targets and a stable numerical representation for every token, document, and batch.
Chapter 1 defines inputs, targets, and example losses. Chapters 2 and 3 prepare token batches and subword vocabularies. Chapter 4 develops a separate count-feature route for documents.
The resulting matrices are inputs to a model, but they are not yet decisions. Part II converts them into scores, probabilities, losses, and evaluation results.

title: 1  Prediction targets
text:
1.1 Defining the task
A model is useful when its outputs help answer the question posed by an application. Before choosing its architecture, we need to specify that question and the evidence available to answer it. An article classifier needs a topic for each article. A text generator needs a continuation for the text already supplied.
Both tasks begin with examples, but they obtain their targets differently. This chapter defines those objects and shows how text supplies its own targets. It then combines individual errors into a training objective.
Suppose an application sorts news articles into business and sport. To judge a proposed classifier, we need an article and the topic it should receive. The input is the article, the target is its recorded topic, and the prediction is the model’s proposed topic. An example is one observation used in learning or evaluation. For this prediction task, its training record pairs an input with a target.
These roles describe the task before they describe a model. A long article and a short headline can both be inputs. The target still has to express the decision the application needs. If the application requires several topics per article, a single topic label cannot represent a correct answer.
A classification target selects a category. Binary classification has two possible categories, while multiclass classification selects one from several categories. Multilabel classification allows several categories to apply together. A regression target is a numerical quantity, such as a delivery time. A sequence target contains an ordered series of outputs, as in translation or text continuation. The form of the target determines what an error means.
The target’s source is a separate choice. In supervised learning, a dataset supplies target values, often through annotation or recorded outcomes. A label is a supplied target, such as the topic attached to an article. In self-supervised learning, the training procedure constructs targets from the observed data. Hiding part of a sentence, for example, leaves a visible input and a hidden target. The procedure still needs an explicit rule for deciding which information the model may see.
In unsupervised learning, no separate task label is supplied for each example. Clustering groups observations by a chosen similarity, while dimensionality reduction represents them with fewer coordinates. Their usefulness still requires a criterion, such as preserved relationships or performance in a later task.
Reinforcement learning uses feedback from actions rather than a correct output label for every input. A policy specifies how actions are chosen, and a reward assigns a numerical outcome to their consequences. The learner observes a state, chooses an action, and receives a new state and reward from its environment. Feedback can arrive after several actions, complicating the assignment of credit. Section 20.3 connects preference-based rewards to language-model adaptation.
Returning to prediction with a target for each input, the dataset notation records these pairs without committing to an architecture:
\[
D = \{(x_i,y_i)\}_{i=1}^{n}
\tag{1.1}\]
Here \(D\) is a dataset of \(n\geq1\) examples. The index \(i\) selects an example, \(x_i\) is its complete input, and \(y_i\) is its target. The braces collect the pairs. They do not imply that the input is already a numerical vector.
For instance, \(D\) can contain ("markets rise", business) and ("team wins", sport). Later, a feature gives the model a numerical description of an input. If those descriptions are \([1,0]\) and \([0,1]\), and the class labels are 1 and 0, the numerical dataset is \(\{([1,0],1),([0,1],0)\}\). The representation has changed, while the pairing between an input and its target remains intact.
There is another distinction concerning what probability a model describes. A conditional probability, written \(P(y\mid x)\), describes possible outputs when an input is supplied. A discriminative model learns that relationship directly, as a topic classifier does. A generative model describes how observations, or structured outputs, can be generated. A language model describes probabilities of token sequences. It can also generate a continuation conditioned on an existing prefix. These are modeling choices, rather than additional target types alongside classification and regression.
The task also leaves room for different architectures. A classifier can use a linear model, a recurrent network, or a transformer. Each must produce an output that can be compared with the same topic target. The later architecture chapters explain how these models combine information. Choosing an architecture does not repair a target that fails to represent the application’s decision.
To estimate behavior on new examples, we separate the data before fitting the model. The training split supplies examples used to adjust model parameters. Parameters are the model’s adjustable numerical values. The validation split guides choices such as model size and training settings. The test split is reserved for the final evaluation. Repeatedly choosing a model from its test results makes those results part of the selection process and weakens their value as an independent estimate.
The following runnable pandas example creates four labeled rows. It places three in training and one in validation, retaining the same columns in both. This deliberately tiny split illustrates data organization. It cannot provide a reliable estimate of prediction quality, and it omits the separate test split required by a real experiment.
The first table contains “markets rise,” “team wins,” and “shares fall.” The validation table contains “player scores.” Their row indices are disjoint, and each text retains its label. In a real dataset, related or duplicated examples may also need to stay in the same split. Evaluation develops that requirement.
Article labels must be supplied with the data. A text continuation can obtain its target from the next observed part of the text itself.

Code example: A small labeled dataset with explicit train and validation splits

import pandas as pd

# Each row is one example; label is the supervised target.
examples = pd.DataFrame({
    "text": ["markets rise", "team wins", "shares fall", "player scores"],
    "label": [0, 1, 0, 1],
})

train = examples.iloc[:3]
validation = examples.iloc[3:]
print(train[["text", "label"]])
print(validation[["text", "label"]])

title: 1  Prediction targets
text:
1.2 Preparing next-token targets
Consider a sequence with three symbols: cat, sat, and a marker for the end of the sequence. After seeing cat, a model should predict sat. After seeing cat sat, it should predict the end marker. Each training input contains only information available before its target.
A token is a unit into which a tokenizer divides text. Tokens may be words, word pieces, characters, or special markers. For this example, suppose the three tokens have integer IDs \([4,8,9]\). Chapter 2 explains the vocabulary mapping. The integers here identify symbols, and their numerical distances carry no meaning.
A prefix is the sequence available before predicting the next token. In autoregressive generation, the model extends that prefix one token at a time. A context window limits how many token positions the model can use when making a prediction.
For a sequence of \(T\) tokens, a next-token target is defined by shifting the sequence one position:
\[
\operatorname{target}_t=x_{t+1},\quad t=1,\ldots,T-1
\tag{1.2}\]
The symbol \(x_t\) now denotes the token at position \(t\), rather than the whole example \(x_i\) used above. The position index runs from 1 to \(T-1\). For \([4,8,9]\), the visible positions are \([4,8]\) and their aligned targets are \([8,9]\). At the second position, the input prefix is \([4,8]\) and the required target is 9. The final token has no following target inside this sequence.
Training can evaluate several positions together if the computation prevents an earlier position from reading its future target. This restriction is causal: a prediction depends only on permitted earlier information. The attention chapter explains how a model enforces it. At this stage, the essential rule is that the input must not reveal the answer it is being evaluated on.
A probability is a number between 0 and 1 describing how likely an outcome is under a model. Probabilities over all possible next tokens sum to 1. For a particular sequence, the probability chain rule combines successive conditional probabilities:
\[
P(x_{1:T}) = \prod_{t=1}^{T} P(x_t\mid x_{<t})
\tag{1.3}\]
Here \(x_{1:T}\) means the entire sequence, and \(x_{<t}\) means the tokens before position \(t\). The product symbol multiplies one factor for each position. The first factor describes the first token, with an empty prefix or a specified beginning marker. Later factors describe a token given the preceding tokens.
If the three factors are \(0.5\), \(0.4\), and \(0.25\), their product is \(0.5\times0.4\times0.25=0.05\). This does not assume the tokens are independent. The second and third probabilities already depend on the earlier tokens. A finite context window may approximate that dependence by retaining only a recent prefix.
The chain rule includes a first-token factor, while the within-sequence shift above supplies \(T-1\) targets. To train the first-token prediction as well, the data preparation must supply an initial context, such as a beginning marker. Keeping these conventions explicit prevents a silent mismatch between a probability formula and its training examples.
Some stored positions do not supply training targets. Padding may be inserted to form a rectangular batch, or an application may deliberately exclude part of an example from supervision. Such positions must be distinguished from genuine next-token targets. Preparing batches records their validity, and loss calculation uses it when combining errors.

title: 1  Prediction targets
text:
1.3 Combining example losses
A dataset usually contains many predictions to judge. One model may improve on one example while becoming worse on another. We therefore need a stated rule for combining individual errors into a quantity that can guide training.
A loss assigns a numerical penalty to a prediction and its target. Its formula depends on the task. For now, assume the penalties have already been calculated. A model produces losses of 0.341, 0.598, and 0.437 on three examples. Their sum is 1.376, and their mean is \(1.376/3\approx0.459\). The mean gives each example equal weight.
The empirical risk is the average loss on the observed dataset:
\[
\widehat{R}(\theta)=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{loss}(f_\theta(x_i),y_i)
\tag{1.4}\]
The model \(f_\theta\) uses parameters \(\theta\) to predict an output for \(x_i\). The function \(\operatorname{loss}\) compares that output with \(y_i\). The summation adds the \(n\) penalties, and division by \(n\) forms their mean. The expression is undefined for an empty dataset.
This average is one possible training objective, the quantity a training procedure seeks to reduce. It is a scalar, meaning one number, even when the predictions contain many values. Scores, probabilities, and loss functions will explain where the three example penalties come from. Backpropagation will then show how the objective guides a parameter update.
An average must match the unit being judged. Averaging one loss per document gives documents equal weight. Averaging one loss per valid token gives longer documents more influence because they supply more targets. Padding supplies no observed target and must not enlarge the denominator. Chapter 8 develops the full token-loss calculation, including explicit masks and excluded positions.
The training objective measures fit to the available training data. It does not establish that the model helps on new examples. That is why the dataset split and the later evaluation procedure remain necessary even when the average training loss becomes small.
We now have inputs, targets, and a rule for combining errors. The next step is to turn the text inputs into numerical objects without losing which token occupies each position.

Chapter checkpoint
A next-token example stores IDs \([4,8,9]\). A colleague uses \([4,8]\) as both the input positions and their targets. What has changed about the task? Separately, three valid predictions have total loss 1.8, and two padding positions occupy storage. What denominator gives the mean loss per valid prediction?
Feedback: The copied targets ask the model to reproduce the currently visible token. Next-token targets should be \([8,9]\), with future information excluded from each prediction. The valid-prediction denominator is 3, giving \(1.8/3=0.6\). Padding does not create two additional observed targets.

title: 2  Token IDs and batches
text:
2.1 Preparing token IDs
The prediction task now specifies which text is available and which token should come next. A numerical model still cannot use a character string directly. It needs a stable address for each token and a way to keep several sequences together without confusing added storage with observed text.
Token IDs provide those addresses. Batches organize them into arrays, while validity information records which positions belong to each original sequence.
Suppose a tokenizer divides cat sat into two tokens. The model needs to refer to the same cat whenever that token appears. A vocabulary is a finite collection of tokens with fixed integer IDs. A token ID identifies an entry in that collection.
\[
V = \{v_0,\ldots,v_{\lvert V\rvert-1}\}
\tag{2.1}\]
The vocabulary \(V\) contains \(|V|\) token types, written \(v_0\) through \(v_{|V|-1}\). The legal IDs therefore run from 0 to \(|V|-1\). The vertical bars denote the number of entries. They do not describe the length of a tokenized sentence.
For a four-token vocabulary [<pad>, cat, sat, dog], cat has ID 1 and sat has ID 2. The text cat sat becomes \([1,2]\). In the vocabulary used for Chapter 1’s example, the same words had IDs 4 and 8. Both assignments are valid, but a particular trained model requires its own exact mapping.
The conversion applies a lookup function at every position:
\[
x_t = \operatorname{id}(t_t)
\tag{2.2}\]
Here \(t_t\) is the token string at position \(t\), \(\operatorname{id}\) is the vocabulary lookup, and \(x_t\) is the resulting integer. The lookup preserves order and length. It changes the representation of each token, rather than measuring its meaning. ID 8 is not twice as meaningful as ID 4, and adjacent IDs need not describe related words.
A model can later use an ID to select a parameter row or to identify the expected output token. If the vocabulary has 50,000 entries, a model that scores every possible next token needs 50,000 output coordinates. A larger vocabulary can reduce sequence length, but it also enlarges these vocabulary-dependent objects. Subword tokenization explains that trade-off.
Not every possible string needs its own vocabulary entry. The tokenizer may split an unfamiliar word into known pieces. Some vocabularies also supply an unknown token, usually written <unk>, as a fallback when an item cannot be represented. Recovering token strings from IDs is possible through the vocabulary. Recovering the exact original text additionally depends on whether preprocessing discarded information, such as capitalization or repeated spaces.
For a vocabulary with an unknown-token fallback, lookup has two cases:
\[
\mathrm{ids}[t]=\begin{cases}\mathrm{vocab}[\mathrm{token}_t],&\text{if }\mathrm{token}_t\text{ is represented in the vocabulary},\\ \mathrm{vocab}[\mathrm{UNK}],&\text{otherwise}\end{cases}
\tag{2.3}\]
The array entry ids[t] receives the token’s vocabulary ID when it exists. Otherwise it receives the vocabulary’s unknown-token ID. For a toy mapping with cat at 1 and <unk> at 0, cat maps to 1 and an unrepresented item maps to 0. A tokenizer that can decompose that item into known pieces should apply that decomposition before resorting to a fallback.
Other special tokens represent structure. A beginning-of-sequence marker identifies a starting boundary, an end-of-sequence marker identifies an ending boundary, and a padding token fills reserved positions. The abbreviations BOS, EOS, and PAD refer to those roles. A mask token and chat-role markers serve other input formats, introduced in Section 3.3.
A sequence of IDs is an ordered one-dimensional array. Several sequences introduce another axis, which is where the storage problem begins.

title: 2  Token IDs and batches
text:
2.2 Preparing batches
An operation can process several examples together, but sentences rarely contain the same number of tokens. A batch is a collection of examples processed together. To store it as one rectangular array, shorter sequences need additional positions. Padding supplies those positions while retaining which entries belong to the original text.
A tensor is an array described by its axes, shape, and element type. A scalar has no axes, a vector has one, and a matrix has two. The shape lists the length of each axis. A token-ID batch with shape \([B,T]\) contains \(B\) rows and \(T\) reserved positions per row. Its rank, or number of axes, is two.
For \(B=2\) and \(T=4\), there are eight stored IDs. The entry \(X_{b,t}\) selects one row and one position. Mathematical examples here count positions from 1, while Python indices start at 0. Thus X[1, 2] selects the third position of the second row. A tensor’s element type also matters: token IDs are integers, rather than continuous measurements.
Consider [BOS, cat, sat, EOS] and [BOS, dog, EOS]. Right padding to four positions gives [BOS, dog, EOS, PAD] for the second row. The rows now share a shape, but the last entry in the second row is still artificial.
A validity mask records that distinction. Let \(L_b\) be the original length of row \(b\) before right padding. For one-based positions, define:
\[
M_{b,t}=\begin{cases}1,&1\le t\le L_b,\\0,&L_b<t\le T\end{cases}
\tag{2.4}\]
The mask \(M\) has shape \([B,T]\), matching the ID array. In this example it is [[1,1,1,1], [1,1,1,0]]. This length-based formula assumes right padding without truncation. With left padding or truncation, use the actual position metadata produced during preparation.
The distinction must come from preparation metadata when a tokenizer uses the same ID for EOS and PAD. In that case, a test such as input_ids != pad_id would incorrectly remove a real end marker. Equal integer values do not imply equal roles.
The next runnable PyTorch example isolates that case without downloading a tokenizer. Its IDs are supplied by a fixed toy vocabulary. BOS is 1, cat is 4, dog is 6, sat is 8, and EOS is 9. The padding configuration reuses ID 9. The integer tensors remain on the CPU, the processor used by default in this example.
The slice :len(sequence) selects the occupied positions in one row. The loop fills those positions and marks them valid. A separate clone() supplies labels so replacing ignored targets cannot change the input IDs. The operator ~ reverses a Boolean mask, selecting the positions that are not valid.

Code example: A real end marker and inserted padding can share an ID

import torch

sequences = [[1, 4, 8, 9], [1, 6, 9]]
lengths = torch.tensor([len(row) for row in sequences])
width = int(lengths.max())
input_ids = torch.full((len(sequences), width), 9, dtype=torch.long)
valid = torch.zeros_like(input_ids, dtype=torch.bool)
for row_index, sequence in enumerate(sequences):
    input_ids[row_index, :len(sequence)] = torch.tensor(sequence)
    valid[row_index, :len(sequence)] = True
labels = input_ids.clone()
labels[~valid] = -100

assert input_ids.tolist() == [[1, 4, 8, 9], [1, 6, 9, 9]]
assert valid.tolist() == [[True, True, True, True], [True, True, True, False]]
assert labels[1, 2].item() == 9
assert labels[1, 3].item() == -100
print(input_ids.tolist(), valid.int().tolist(), labels.tolist())
The second row contains two occurrences of ID 9. Its third position is a genuine EOS, so its mask value remains 1. Its fourth position was inserted, so its mask value is 0. The assertions make this difference observable.
A model may consume validity information in several places. An attention operation uses it to exclude padded source positions. A loss calculation uses it to exclude artificial targets. Pooling uses it to avoid treating padding as part of a document representation. These consumers need related information, but their exact mask shapes and conventions can differ.
In a tokenizer result, the field attention_mask commonly supplies this initial valid-position information, with 1 for valid and 0 for padding. It is separate from the causal restriction that stops an earlier token from reading a later token. Attention combines those restrictions explicitly.
For loss implementations that accept an ignore index, excluded targets receive a value such as \(-100\):
\[
\mathrm{label}_{b,t}=-100\quad\text{when }M_{b,t}=0
\tag{2.5}\]
Here \(M_{b,t}=0\) identifies an inserted position. The ignore index lies outside the vocabulary and is interpreted by the loss function. It must never be passed as an ordinary token ID to a vocabulary lookup. A real EOS target remains eligible for training.
The following transformers example performs the text preparation with the GPT-2 tokenizer. It requires that package and the tokenizer files, obtained from the model repository or a local cache. It prints the tensor shapes and verifies that unequal-length inputs actually produce padding.

Code example: Tokenizer batch with padding and mask

from transformers import AutoTokenizer

texts = ["cat", "the dog ran across the garden and stopped"]
tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("gpt2")
tokenizer.pad_token = tokenizer.eos_token
batch = tokenizer(texts, padding=True, return_tensors="pt")
input_ids = batch["input_ids"]
attention_mask = batch["attention_mask"]
labels = input_ids.clone()
labels[attention_mask == 0] = -100

assert input_ids.shape == attention_mask.shape == labels.shape
assert (attention_mask == 0).any()
assert (labels[attention_mask == 0] == -100).all()
print(input_ids.shape, attention_mask.tolist())

# GPT-2 causal LM classes shift these labels internally.
# A direct loss calculation must perform its own next-token alignment.
The tokenizer returns integer input_ids and the aligned attention_mask. Copying the IDs preserves real target values, and the mask selects only inserted positions for replacement with \(-100\). The code follows the GPT-2 causal language-model interface, which performs the next-token shift internally. An implementation that calculates the loss directly must align predictions and next-token targets itself. Loss reduction shows both arrangements and prevents a double shift.
The diagram below places an ID batch beside its mask. Read corresponding positions together: one supplies a vocabulary address, and the other records whether that address came from the original sequence.






Figure 2.2: A validity mask distinguishes a real end marker from padding that reuses the same token ID.



The common rectangular shape allows batch computation. It does not make every stored entry a valid token or supervised target. Truncation creates a different trade-off: it removes actual context to meet a length limit, so its policy must be considered when evaluating predictions.
We now have a numerical interface for text: IDs of shape \([B,T]\) and aligned validity information. The next chapter explains how a tokenizer chooses reusable pieces for the vocabulary, affecting both its size and the lengths of these sequences.

Chapter checkpoint
A row is [BOS, dog, EOS, EOS] because EOS also serves as right padding. Its original length is three. Which positions are valid, and why is comparing token values with the EOS ID insufficient?
Feedback: The validity row is [1,1,1,0]. The third position is the observed end marker, while the fourth is inserted padding. Their identical IDs require separate preparation metadata. The real end marker remains a target when the training task supervises it.

title: 3  Subword tokenization
text:
3.1 Byte pair encoding
A word vocabulary gives common words short representations, but new names, spellings, and technical terms are difficult to cover. A character vocabulary can spell them, but it often produces much longer sequences. Subword tokenization uses reusable pieces between those extremes.
The vocabulary must be learned before a trained model can rely on its IDs. This chapter follows that construction, compares alternative selection rules, and explains the structural tokens that accompany ordinary text.
Suppose many words share the characters u followed by g. Storing ug as one vocabulary entry can shorten those words without adding an entry for every complete word. Byte Pair Encoding, or BPE, repeatedly adds entries by merging frequent adjacent symbols. It adapts an earlier compression method to vocabulary construction.
There are two distinct operations. Training a tokenizer determines its vocabulary and merge rules from a corpus. Applying the tokenizer uses those fixed rules on new text. Recounting pairs in each new sentence would create a changing representation that no fixed model could reliably interpret.
Start with a base set of symbols, such as characters or bytes. Count adjacent pairs in the training corpus, including the number of times each training word occurs. The merge rule selects a pair with the largest count:
\[
(a^\star,b^\star)=\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{a,b}\operatorname{count}(a,b)
\tag{3.1}\]
The symbols \(a\) and \(b\) identify candidate adjacent pieces. The function \(\operatorname{count}(a,b)\) adds their occurrences across the corpus. The operator \(\operatorname*{arg\,max}\) returns the pair attaining the largest value. A deterministic tie rule is needed when several pairs have that value.
The selected pair becomes a single new symbol:
\[
V_{k+1}=V_k\cup\{a^\star b^\star\}
\tag{3.2}\]
Here \(V_k\) is the vocabulary after \(k\) merges, and \(a^\star b^\star\) is the concatenation of the selected pieces. If that symbol is new, the vocabulary grows by one entry. Each word representation is then updated by replacing matching, nonoverlapping pairs. Counts must be recomputed on the updated representation before selecting another merge.
For example, counts 30 for (l,o) and 12 for (o,w) favor the first pair. If a new merged symbol is added to a vocabulary of size 100, its size becomes 101. These small calculations describe one decision. The following corpus shows why the recount is essential.
Use word counts hug:10, pug:5, pun:12, bun:4, and hugs:5. Initially, each word is split into characters followed by a separate </w> boundary marker. Thus hug begins as [h,u,g,</w>]. Boundary markers are eligible for merging in this example.
In round 1, (u,g) occurs \(10+5+5=20\) times, (p,u) occurs \(5+12=17\) times, and (u,n) occurs \(12+4=16\) times. The most frequent pair is (u,g), so the first new symbol is ug.
In round 2, the new representations include [h,ug,</w>] and [p,ug,</w>]. The counts of (h,ug) and (ug,</w>) are each 15. Both (u,n) and (n,</w>) occur 16 times. Using the first pair encountered in the fixed corpus order breaks the tie in favor of (u,n), creating un.
In round 3, the two words ending in un now contribute \(12+4=16\) occurrences of (un,</w>). That pair exceeds the counts of 15 for (h,ug) and (ug,</w>). The third merge therefore creates un</w>. Omitting the boundary pairs from the recount would incorrectly select hug at this step.
In round 4, (h,ug) and (ug,</w>) each occur 15 times. The same tie rule selects (h,ug), creating hug. The word hug is now represented by [hug,</w>], and pun by [p,un</w>]. Both use two symbols instead of four. The original eight-symbol vocabulary has gained ug, un, un</w>, and hug.
The source’s variant omits the boundary marker and starts with seven characters. Its first three merges are ug, un, and hug, reaching the stated vocabulary size ten. Adding a mergeable boundary symbol changes the candidate counts, which explains the extra round in the trace above. Both variants need their boundary policy stated explicitly.
The runnable example below calculates those four rounds. Each tuple stores one word’s current symbols, while its integer weight records the word count. The scan replaces nonoverlapping occurrences from left to right. Python’s insertion order supplies the stated tie rule for this fixed corpus.
The printed merge sequence is ('u','g'), ('u','n'), ('un','</w>'), and ('h','ug'). A production tokenizer also needs a normalization policy, stopping criterion, and treatment of special symbols. This example isolates merge selection and replacement so their effect is visible.
The figure follows the same distinction between selecting a pair and applying its replacement. Each later decision reads the representation produced by the earlier one.
At application time, the tokenizer uses the learned merge order on the new input. The model’s input and output tables still assume the resulting vocabulary IDs. Changing the tokenizer underneath a trained model can change both the meaning of an ID and the number of positions the model receives.

title: 3  Subword tokenization
text:
Code example: Four BPE merges with weighted recounts and explicit boundaries

from collections import Counter

corpus = [(tuple(word) + ("</w>",), count) for word, count in
          [("hug", 10), ("pug", 5), ("pun", 12), ("bun", 4), ("hugs", 5)]]
merges = []
for _ in range(4):
    pairs = Counter()
    for symbols, weight in corpus:
        for pair in zip(symbols, symbols[1:]):
            pairs[pair] += weight
    best = max(pairs, key=pairs.get)
    merges.append(best)
    updated = []
    for symbols, weight in corpus:
        merged, position = [], 0
        while position < len(symbols):
            if tuple(symbols[position:position + 2]) == best:
                merged.append("".join(best))
                position += 2
            else:
                merged.append(symbols[position])
                position += 1
        updated.append((tuple(merged), weight))
    corpus = updated
    print(best, pairs[best])

assert merges == [("u", "g"), ("u", "n"), ("un", "</w>"), ("h", "ug")]
assert corpus[0][0] == ("hug", "</w>")
assert corpus[2][0] == ("p", "un</w>")








Figure 3.2: Each BPE merge changes the symbols counted in the next round.

title: 3  Subword tokenization
text:
3.2 WordPiece and SentencePiece
Raw frequency is one way to choose reusable pieces. Another is to ask whether two pieces occur together more strongly than their separate frequencies suggest. WordPiece uses subword units and often marks a continuation piece with ##. The course illustrates its selection idea with this relative pair score:
\[
score(a,b)=\frac{\operatorname{count}(a,b)}{\operatorname{count}(a)\,\operatorname{count}(b)}
\tag{3.3}\]
The numerator counts adjacent occurrences of \(a\) and \(b\). The denominator multiplies their separate counts. A pair can therefore have a lower raw count and a higher relative score. This simplified score explains the comparison. It is not a complete specification of every WordPiece trainer.
Suppose u occurs 40 times, n occurs 20 times, and g occurs 15 times. If (u,n) occurs 16 times, its score is \(16/(40\times20)=0.02\). If (n,g) occurs 12 times, its score is \(12/(20\times15)=0.04\). The second pair wins despite having fewer occurrences.
The runnable code starts from those counts and reports the pair with the largest score. The dictionaries preserve the pieces and pair frequencies so the denominator can be checked directly.

Code example: WordPiece pair scores from corpus counts

from collections import Counter

piece_counts = Counter({"u": 40, "n": 20, "g": 15})
pair_counts = Counter({("u", "n"): 16, ("n", "g"): 12})

scores = {
    pair: count / (piece_counts[pair[0]] * piece_counts[pair[1]])
    for pair, count in pair_counts.items()
}
print(max(scores, key=scores.get), scores)
The result selects ('n','g'). At application time, a typical WordPiece tokenizer finds vocabulary pieces within a word, using continuation markers for pieces after its beginning. The vocabulary and segmentation policy remain fixed. Rare text is represented by available pieces, or by an unknown-token policy when segmentation fails.
SentencePiece addresses a different part of the interface. It trains from raw sentences without requiring whitespace to be a hard word boundary. Spaces can be represented explicitly, which is useful for multilingual text. SentencePiece is a framework that supports both BPE and a unigram tokenizer. It is therefore not simply a third merge rule alongside BPE and WordPiece.
The unigram tokenizer starts with more candidate pieces than it intends to retain. It assigns probabilities to pieces and considers possible segmentations of the training text. A segmentation’s probability multiplies the probabilities of its pieces. Summing across valid segmentations gives the probability assigned to the text under that vocabulary.
The teaching objective selects a vocabulary subject to a target size:
\[
V^\star=\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{V:\,|V|=K}\left[-\sum_{s\in C}\log P(s\mid V)\right]
\tag{3.4}\]
Here \(C\) is the training corpus, \(s\) is one text, \(K\) is the vocabulary budget, and \(P(s\mid V)\) includes the available segmentations and their estimated piece probabilities. The negative natural logarithm gives likely text a smaller penalty. For example, probability 1 contributes 0, while probability 0.1 contributes about 2.303. The sum combines those penalties across the corpus.
Without a vocabulary-size constraint or another penalty, the expression does not explain why a trainer should remove pieces. Practical unigram training estimates probabilities and prunes candidates toward the required size, retaining the symbols needed by its coverage policy. This is an iterative approximation, rather than an exhaustive search over every possible vocabulary.
Suppose removing pu changes corpus loss from 10.00 to 10.01, while removing hug changes it to 10.80. The first removal causes less damage under that comparison. Repeating such decisions reduces vocabulary size while monitoring how well the remaining pieces represent the corpus.
The comparison figure separates pair-based construction from vocabulary pruning. Both produce integer token sequences, although their treatment of whitespace and rare words may produce different sequence lengths.






Figure 3.3: Relative pair scores guide the WordPiece example, while Unigram pruning compares the cost of removing pieces.



Domain text makes these choices tangible. Code identifiers, biomedical terms, and Hebrew words may be split into many pieces by an unsuitable vocabulary. Longer sequences require more stored positions and more subsequent computation. A domain token is a piece added or retained for such text. Adding it to an existing model also requires compatible model parameters and training, so it is not merely a spelling change.
The text-classification experiment compares BPE and WordPiece on the same sentences before measuring a downstream model. That separates an observed segmentation difference from an unsupported claim that one tokenizer must be better overall.

title: 3  Subword tokenization
text:
3.3 Structural tokens
Ordinary subwords describe text content, but a model also needs to distinguish sequence boundaries and input roles. A special token reserves a vocabulary entry for such structure. Its role comes from the data format and training convention.
Beginning and end markers delimit a sequence. Padding fills unused batch positions, with validity recorded separately as Chapter 2 explains. Separators can distinguish segments within one input. These roles may use different IDs, or share an ID under a specific interface convention.
BERT reserves [CLS], a classification token, at the start of an input for predictions about that input as a whole. Its [SEP] token separates text segments and marks their end. A pair of segments can therefore have the format [CLS] A [SEP] B [SEP]. These markers identify structure, rather than words supplied by the user. Chapter 18 explains how the model uses this format for a prediction about the relationship between two segments.
A mask token marks missing content in a masked-language-model input. Let \(M\) be a set of selected positions. A simple corruption rule replaces the original token at each selected position:
\[
x'_t=\begin{cases}\mathrm{MASK},&t\in M,\\x_t,&\text{otherwise}\end{cases}
\tag{3.5}\]
The original ID is \(x_t\), and the presented input ID is \(x'_t\). If \(t\in M\), the input contains the mask token. Otherwise it retains \(x_t\). The symbol \(M\) here denotes a set of positions, rather than Chapter 2’s array of validity indicators.
For \(x=[5,6,7]\) and \(M=\{2\}\), the presented sequence is [5,MASK,7]. The target at the selected position remains 6. The model must infer that token from permitted surrounding information. A mask token is consequently different from padding: its position carries an intentional prediction problem.
Chat formats use role markers or separators to identify system, user, assistant, and tool spans. A role token is a token used for one of those structural roles. The marker remains an integer ID to the model. It gains its learned function through the training examples and the input format used at inference time.
Tokenization now supplies a vocabulary, segmentation rules, and explicit sequence structure. One modeling route retains the ordered IDs for learned representations. Another counts selected pieces into document features, which the next chapter develops.

Chapter checkpoint
After merging u and n, a corpus contains 16 occurrences of [un,</w>] and 15 of [h,ug]. Boundary markers are eligible for merging. Which pair should BPE select next? Why should applying the trained tokenizer to one new sentence avoid recomputing a new merge ranking?
Feedback: It selects (un,</w>) because 16 exceeds 15. The counts must describe the updated symbols. Applying a fixed merge policy keeps the vocabulary interface compatible with the trained model. Learning a fresh ranking from the new sentence would change that interface.

title: 4  Count vectors and TF-IDF
text:
4.1 Counting text
A topic classifier can often learn useful distinctions from the words an article contains. Before building a model that follows every token position, we can test a simpler representation: count selected words or phrases and give every document the same feature coordinates.
Count vectors and TF-IDF provide this representation. They make the connection between a document and its numerical features visible, while exposing what is lost when most word order is discarded.
Suppose two articles contain cat, sat, and dog in different amounts. Assigning one coordinate to each of these terms lets us compare the articles using the same measurements. A bag-of-words representation records term counts while discarding their order. A count vector stores those counts in a fixed vocabulary order.
For vocabulary [cat, sat, dog], the text cat sat cat becomes \([2,1,0]\). The first coordinate counts cat, the second counts sat, and the third counts dog. Swapping the vocabulary order without rearranging the vector would change its meaning.
The count at one coordinate is:
\[
\operatorname{BoW}(d)_j=\operatorname{count}(t_j\in d)
\tag{4.1}\]
Here \(d\) is the document, \(t_j\) is the term assigned to coordinate \(j\), and \(\operatorname{BoW}(d)_j\) is its count. Scanning the document increments the selected coordinate whenever the term occurs. The vector width depends on the vocabulary, rather than the document’s length.
We can count longer local patterns as well. An n-gram is a contiguous sequence of \(n\) tokens. A unigram contains one token, a bigram contains two, and a trigram contains three. Sliding a two-token window over new york new york produces new york, york new, and new york. The first bigram therefore has count 2.
\[
\phi_{\mathrm{ngram}}(d)_g=\operatorname{count}(g\in d)
\tag{4.2}\]
The symbol \(g\) identifies one n-gram, and \(\phi_{\mathrm{ngram}}(d)_g\) gives its feature count. Each retained n-gram has its own coordinate. Bigrams preserve evidence of adjacent order, although they do not retain the full sequence. An n-gram feature counts a pattern within a document. An n-gram language model uses context counts to predict a next token, which is a different operation.
The unit being counted must be fixed before interpreting a coordinate. Word, character, and subword features create different vocabularies. The figure compares those choices at the feature-construction stage.
A character feature can remain useful inside an unfamiliar word. A word feature is easier to interpret directly but treats different spellings as distinct terms. Combining unigrams and bigrams expands the feature space, so the choice affects storage as well as the evidence a model can use.
To process several documents, stack their feature vectors into a document-term matrix. Each row represents a document, and each column represents the same vocabulary feature in every row:
\[
X\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times\lvert V\rvert}
\tag{4.3}\]
The matrix \(X\) has \(N\) document rows and \(|V|\) feature columns. For 10 documents and 500 retained features, its shape is \([10,500]\). A batch of \(B\) selected documents uses the same feature columns, giving shape \([B,|V|]\).
Most documents contain only a small fraction of a large vocabulary. A sparse matrix stores the nonzero values and information identifying their positions, rather than storing every zero explicitly. The vocabulary axis still contains every retained feature, including those absent from a particular document.
A feature vector can also combine measurements chosen for a task. The course’s sentiment example uses six coordinates: positive-word count, negative-word count, presence of no, pronoun count, presence of !, and log word count.
For a concrete version, lowercase the text and separate punctuation from words. Let the positive lexicon contain good, the negative lexicon contain bad, and the pronoun list contain i and you. The text I feel good, no bad news! has six words and gives \((1,1,1,1,1,\log 6)\). Its last coordinate is approximately \(1.792\).
The presence indicators are 1 when their condition holds and 0 otherwise. The logarithm compresses differences in document length, so a tenfold length increase adds \(\log 10\) to this feature. An empty document needs a separate rule because \(\log 0\) is undefined. Using \(\log(1+\text{word count})\) is one possible change, which must be applied consistently.
These measurements encode the designer’s assumptions about sentiment. Counting no does not identify which phrase it negates, and a small lexicon can miss domain-specific meanings. Learned features in Chapter 12 address a different question: which transformations of the supplied measurements should training adjust?
Counts expose which terms occur, but a common term may contribute little to distinguishing documents. Weighting addresses that limitation.

title: 4  Count vectors and TF-IDF
text: Figure 4.2: Character, word, and subword pieces divide the same complete text at different boundaries.
crumbs: Part I: From text to mathematical objects

title: 4  Count vectors and TF-IDF
text:
4.2 Weighting terms with TF-IDF
A word repeated within one article may be informative. A word appearing in almost every article may be less useful for distinguishing topics. Term frequency-inverse document frequency, or TF-IDF, combines these two observations.
The term frequency \(\mathrm{tf}_{d,j}\) measures how often term \(j\) appears in document \(d\). Here it is the raw count. The document frequency \(\mathrm{df}_j\) counts how many fitted documents contain that term at least once. Repeating a word ten times within one document increases its term frequency, but adds only one to its document frequency.
The following unsmoothed teaching formula combines the two:
\[
\mathrm{tfidf}_{d,j}=\mathrm{tf}_{d,j}\log\left(\frac{N}{\mathrm{df}_j}\right)
\tag{4.4}\]
There are \(N\geq1\) fitted documents, and a retained term has \(1\leq\mathrm{df}_j\leq N\). The inverse-document-frequency factor is \(\log(N/\mathrm{df}_j)\), using the natural logarithm. A term present in every fitted document gives ratio 1 and logarithm 0. A rarer term gives a larger positive factor.
If a term appears three times in one document and in 10 of 100 fitted documents, its weight is \(3\log(100/10)=3\log(10)\approx6.91\). Its within-document repetition increases the weight. Its occurrence in only one tenth of the corpus keeps the inverse-document-frequency factor substantial.
This weighting changes the values of the feature coordinates, while retaining their vocabulary meanings. It does not create a learned semantic relationship between different words. It also depends on the fitted corpus, so the same count can receive a different weight when the corpus changes.
Library defaults can use a different formula. Scikit-learn’s default smoothed factor is \(1+\log((1+N)/(1+\mathrm{df}_j))\). It then normalizes each nonzero document row by its Euclidean length. That length is the square root of the sum of squared row entries. The resulting row has length 1, so a longer document is not larger merely because all its counts are larger.
For \(N=3\) and \(\mathrm{df}_j=2\), the smoothed factor is \(1+\log(4/3)\approx1.288\) before row normalization. This differs from the unsmoothed factor \(\log(3/2)\approx0.405\). A comparison with the unsmoothed formula must therefore state both smoothing and normalization settings.
The vocabulary and document frequencies must now be fitted without allowing held-out data to influence the representation.
crumbs: Part I: From text to mathematical objects

title: 4  Count vectors and TF-IDF
text:
4.3 Fitting the representation
A model evaluated on new documents needs the same feature coordinates that it received during training. Fitting a vectorizer establishes its vocabulary and, for TF-IDF, its document-frequency statistics. Transforming text applies those established objects to another document collection.
Fit on the training split, then transform the validation and test splits. Fitting again on validation text could add columns, change their order, and alter the weights. Even when the final matrix shape stays the same, using held-out text to choose the representation changes the experiment’s information boundary.
The runnable scikit-learn example below fits unigrams and bigrams on three training documents. A count vectorizer supplies the vocabulary. A TF-IDF vectorizer then uses that same vocabulary and learns its document frequencies from the same training documents. The final transformation processes one new document without refitting.

Code example: Count and TF-IDF matrices with a fixed training vocabulary

from sklearn.feature_extraction.text import CountVectorizer, TfidfVectorizer

train_documents = ["cat sat", "dog sat", "cat chased dog"]
new_documents = ["dog chased cat"]

counts = CountVectorizer(ngram_range=(1, 2))
X_count = counts.fit_transform(train_documents)

tfidf = TfidfVectorizer(vocabulary=counts.vocabulary_, ngram_range=(1, 2))
X_tfidf = tfidf.fit_transform(train_documents)
X_new_tfidf = tfidf.transform(new_documents)

print(counts.get_feature_names_out())
print(X_count.shape, X_tfidf.shape, X_new_tfidf.shape)
print(X_count.toarray())
The feature list is cat, cat chased, cat sat, chased, chased dog, dog, dog sat, and sat. Both training matrices have shape \([3,8]\), and the new TF-IDF matrix has shape \([1,8]\). Their rows differ in value, while the columns retain the same meanings.
For cat sat, the count row is \([1,0,1,0,0,0,0,1]\). For dog sat, it is \([0,0,0,0,0,1,1,1]\). For cat chased dog, it is \([1,1,0,1,1,1,0,0]\). These values account separately for individual words and retained adjacent pairs.
The new document dog chased cat contains known unigrams, but its bigrams dog chased and chased cat are absent from the fitted vocabulary. They do not create new columns. A document containing no retained feature can produce a zero row, which requires a deliberate downstream policy.
The matrices remain sparse. Calling toarray() in the example makes the small counts visible, but allocating a dense copy of a large document-term matrix can consume substantial memory. Libraries such as scipy.sparse store these matrices, and a compatible classifier can operate on their sparse representation.
The corpus is deliberately small so each column can be checked. It supports an implementation demonstration, rather than a meaningful comparison of classifier quality.

title: 4  Count vectors and TF-IDF
text:
4.4 Limits of count features
Two inputs can have identical count vectors while expressing different meanings. The phrases good not bad and bad not good have the same unigram counts. A classifier using those counts receives the same representation for both. No choice of classifier weights can recover the discarded order from that identical input.
Bigrams distinguish some such cases, but a fixed local window cannot represent every long-distance relationship. Vocabulary identity creates another limitation: car and automobile occupy different coordinates, so the representation itself supplies no evidence of their similarity. Training a classifier may still learn similar weights for them when the data supports that association.
Count features remain useful when transparency, limited training data, or a simple baseline matters. A coordinate can be traced directly to a word or phrase. Dense representations use many nonzero values in a smaller coordinate space. Learned embeddings are one such representation, developed in Chapter 13. Their coordinates are adjusted during training and need not correspond to individual words.
Sparse document features and token embeddings are alternative starting representations. A sequence model can look up embeddings directly from token IDs. It does not need to turn a document into bag-of-words counts first. Conversely, a sparse classifier can use count or TF-IDF features without an embedding table.
We have now constructed numerical inputs with fixed, interpretable axes. The next chapter introduces the model coefficients that act on those inputs, then calculates one score for each possible class. That multiplication will consume the feature axis and produce a distinct class axis.

Chapter checkpoint
A vectorizer fitted on training data has 500 columns. A colleague fits another vectorizer on validation data and also obtains 500 columns. Is the validation matrix necessarily compatible with the trained classifier? What would preserve compatibility?
Feedback: Equal widths do not establish equal meanings. Column 12 might refer to a different term, and TF-IDF weights might come from different document frequencies. Transform validation text with the vectorizer fitted on training data, keeping both its vocabulary and weighting statistics fixed.

title: Part II: From scores to loss
text:
Chapters in this part
Numerical inputs alone do not tell a model whether a prediction is useful. A model needs a score, a way to interpret the score, and a loss that measures disagreement with observed targets.
Chapter 5 introduces linear scores, and Chapter 6 converts them into probabilities. Chapter 7 follows fixed-model output selection. Chapter 8 measures training loss, while Chapter 9 evaluates generalization. These are related branches from probability outputs.
Loss and evaluation reveal what needs improvement. Part III shows how derivatives assign that error to parameters and change them.

title: 5  Linear scores
text:
5.1 Linear prediction
The document features now have numerical values and consistent coordinates. A model needs a rule that turns those values into a prediction. The simplest useful rule attaches a coefficient to each feature, adds the contributions, and includes an offset.
That calculation can estimate a numerical target or produce evidence for a class. Following it from one example to a batch establishes the matrix operations used throughout the later models.
Suppose two measured features help predict a numerical target. Their contributions need not have the same sign or importance. A weight is a coefficient that scales one feature’s contribution. A bias is an offset added independently of the feature values.
Collect the \(D\) features in a vector \(x\) and their weights in a vector \(w\) of the same length. A dot product multiplies matching coordinates and adds the products. The expression \(w^\top x\) means \(w_1x_1+\cdots+w_Dx_D\). The superscript \(\top\) indicates transposition, turning a column into a row for the multiplication.
The prediction is:
\[
\hat{y}=w^\top x+b
\tag{5.1}\]
The symbol \(\hat y\) denotes the model’s predicted value, while \(b\) is the scalar bias. The full expression is an affine map, a linear map plus an offset. The term “linear model” commonly includes that offset.
For \(x=(2,-1)\), \(w=(0.5,3)\), and \(b=1\), the contributions are \(0.5\times2=1\) and \(3\times(-1)=-3\). Adding them and the bias gives \(\hat y=1-3+1=-1\). Each weight has a direct role in this calculation. Its interpretation still depends on the feature’s units and the other features present.
The bias can also be included as a constant feature. For \(x=(2,-1)\), use \(x'=(1,2,-1)\) and \(w'=(1,0.5,3)\). Then \(w'^T x'=1+1-3=-1\), exactly the same prediction. The leading constant changes notation, not the model’s behavior.
Across inputs, each coefficient describes how its feature changes the score when other features remain fixed. For one input, the products \(w_jx_j\) describe its individual score contributions. These global coefficients and local contributions are different explanations, and neither establishes a causal effect of changing the real-world feature.
We can judge the prediction only after supplying a target. The residual is the target minus the prediction:
\[
r_i=y_i-\hat{y}_i
\tag{5.2}\]
The subscript \(i\) selects an example. A positive residual means the target is above the prediction. For target \(y=3\) and prediction \(-1\), the residual is \(3-(-1)=4\). This sign convention must remain explicit because some implementations define the difference in the opposite order.
Squaring residuals prevents positive and negative errors from canceling. The mean squared error, abbreviated MSE, averages those squared values:
\[
L_{\mathrm{MSE}}=\frac{1}{n}\sum_i(y_i-\hat{y}_i)^2
\tag{5.3}\]
There are \(n\geq1\) examples. Each term \((y_i-\hat y_i)^2\) is nonnegative, and division by \(n\) gives equal weight to the examples. For the one-example calculation above, the squared error and the mean squared error are both \(4^2=16\). An error twice as large contributes four times as much squared error.
This objective measures discrepancy in squared target units. It can emphasize large misses, which matters when some observations contain extreme errors. We have evaluated a model with supplied parameters. The learning chapters will derive how parameters change during training.
Classification uses the same affine calculation, but interprets its result as a score rather than a numerical target estimate.
crumbs: Part II: From scores to loss

title: 5  Linear scores
text:
5.2 Decision boundaries
For a binary classification task, we can use a positive score to favor one class and a negative score to favor the other. A score, also called a logit in this classification setting, is the unnormalized model output before a probability transformation:
\[
z=w^\top x+b
\tag{5.4}\]
The feature and weight vectors again have length \(D\), and the bias is scalar. A logit can be any real number. It does not become a probability merely because a class decision uses its sign. Sigmoid will give that score a binary probability interpretation.
The decision boundary contains the inputs at which the chosen decision rule changes class. For the zero-score threshold, it is the set:
\[
\{x\mid w^\top x+b=0\}
\tag{5.5}\]
The notation collects all feature vectors \(x\) whose affine score is zero. With nonzero \(w\), the boundary is a line in two dimensions, a plane in three, and a hyperplane in higher dimensions. The weight vector determines its orientation, while the bias shifts its position. A different decision threshold shifts the boundary as well.
Take \(w=(1,-1)\) and \(b=-1\), giving score \(z=x_1-x_2-1\). For \(x_A=(3,1)\), the score is \(3-1-1=1\). For \(x_B=(1,2)\), it is \(1-2-1=-2\). The points lie on opposite sides. For \(x_C=(2,1)\), the score is \(2-1-1=0\), placing it on the boundary itself.
The figure connects those signed scores to regions of feature space. Crossing the boundary changes the decision under this threshold rule.






Figure 5.2: The sign of an affine score places a point on either side of its decision boundary.



A score grows along the weight direction, but it is not generally a geometric distance. Multiplying both weights and bias by a positive constant preserves the zero boundary while changing score magnitudes. Those magnitudes matter once the scores become probabilities.
Logistic regression combines an affine score with the sigmoid probability function. The probability varies nonlinearly with the score, while the zero-score boundary remains linear in the supplied features. A single boundary cannot separate every pattern. Nonlinear representations will construct an example where changing the feature representation is necessary.
For more than two mutually exclusive classes, the model needs a score for each candidate. Matrix multiplication computes those scores for many examples at once.
crumbs: Part II: From scores to loss

title: 5  Linear scores
text:
5.3 Scoring a batch
Processing one row at a time repeats the same weighted sum. Stacking rows into a matrix exposes the shared operation. Let \(X\) have shape \([B,D]\), with \(B\) examples and \(D\) features. A weight vector of shape \([D]\) produces one score per example:
\[
z=Xw+b
\tag{5.6}\]
The multiplication consumes the feature axis and leaves a result \(z\) of shape \([B]\). The same scalar bias is added to every row’s score. A feature-width mismatch is a mathematical error before it is a library error: a row with three features cannot form this dot product with two weights.
Use the three-example batch \(X=[[1,0],[0,1],[1,1]]\), targets \(y=[1,0,1]\), weights \(w=[0.8,-0.3]\), and bias \(b=0.1\). The scores are:

First row: \(1(0.8)+0(-0.3)+0.1=0.9\).
Second row: \(0(0.8)+1(-0.3)+0.1=-0.2\).
Third row: \(1(0.8)+1(-0.3)+0.1=0.6\).

Thus \(z=[0.9,-0.2,0.6]\). The targets remain separate and do not enter the score calculation. They will be used to judge the predictions. These same rows and scores continue through the probability, loss, and gradient calculations.
The runnable PyTorch example creates the small tensors explicitly. The @ operator performs matrix multiplication, and adding the scalar bias applies the same offset to all three results.

Code example: The running batch from features to logits

import torch

X = torch.tensor([[1.0, 0.0], [0.0, 1.0], [1.0, 1.0]])
y = torch.tensor([1.0, 0.0, 1.0])
w = torch.tensor([0.8, -0.3])
b = torch.tensor(0.1)

logits = X @ w + b
print(logits)  # tensor([ 0.9000, -0.2000,  0.6000])
The printed vector contains 0.9000, -0.2000, and 0.6000. No parameter update has occurred. One scalar score per row is sufficient for the binary probability representation introduced next.
For a multiclass model, each feature needs a separate coefficient for each output class. A weight matrix places those coefficients in columns. The complete vocabulary-feature calculation is:
\[
Z=XW+b,\quad X\in\mathbb{R}^{B\times\lvert V\rvert},\quad W\in\mathbb{R}^{\lvert V\rvert\times K},\quad b\in\mathbb{R}^{K},\quad Z\in\mathbb{R}^{B\times K}
\tag{5.7}\]
Here \(B\) is the number of documents, \(|V|\) is the number of input features, and \(K\) is the number of output classes. The matrix \(W\) has shape \([|V|,K]\), and the bias vector has shape \([K]\). Entry \(Z_{b,k}\) adds the products of document row \(b\) and weight column \(k\), then adds the class bias \(b_k\). In this formula, the subscript \(b\) indexes a document, while the vector symbol \(b\) denotes biases.
The output has shape \([B,K]\). The vocabulary axis is consumed by the multiplication, leaving a batch axis and a class axis. Class scores therefore do not share a vocabulary axis with the input matrix.
For two documents and three features, use:
\[X=\begin{bmatrix}2&1&0\\0&1&3\end{bmatrix},\qquad W=\begin{bmatrix}0.5&-0.2\\1.0&0.4\\-0.5&0.8\end{bmatrix},\qquad b=[0.1,-0.1].\]
The first document’s scores are \(2(0.5)+1(1.0)+0(-0.5)+0.1=2.1\) and \(2(-0.2)+1(0.4)+0(0.8)-0.1=-0.1\). The second document’s scores are \(0(0.5)+1(1.0)+3(-0.5)+0.1=-0.4\) and \(0(-0.2)+1(0.4)+3(0.8)-0.1=2.7\).
The result is \(Z=[[2.1,-0.1],[-0.4,2.7]]\). Each row contains two competing scores for one document. The matrix figure shows how the matching feature dimensions align in those dot products.






Figure 5.3: A batch of two three-feature inputs produces two class scores per input.



Adding the bias vector uses broadcasting. An elementwise operation can expand an axis of length 1 across the matching axis of another input. Here the library treats shape \([K]\) as \([1,K]\) and applies that same bias row to all \(B\) rows. It does not add together the documents or create new learned bias values.
More generally, elementwise broadcasting compares axes from the right. Corresponding lengths must be equal, or one must be 1. This rule differs from matrix multiplication. For example, adding shapes \([B,1]\) and \([B]\) can unexpectedly produce \([B,B]\), so dimensions alone must be checked against their intended roles.
The next runnable example performs the two-document calculation and checks every result. It uses a dense tensor for inspection. A large count matrix would usually remain sparse and require a compatible multiplication.

Code example: Vocabulary-feature batches mapped to class logits

import torch

# Rows are documents; columns are vocabulary features.
X = torch.tensor([[2.0, 1.0, 0.0], [0.0, 1.0, 3.0]])
W = torch.tensor([[0.5, -0.2], [1.0, 0.4], [-0.5, 0.8]])
b = torch.tensor([0.1, -0.1])

# Matrix multiplication computes every document-class dot product.
Z = X @ W + b
expected = torch.tensor([[2.1, -0.1], [-0.4, 2.7]])
assert Z.shape == (2, 2)
assert torch.allclose(Z, expected)
PyTorch’s nn.Linear(D,K) stores its weight array in the transposed orientation, shape \([K,D]\). If that stored array is \(A\), the same calculation is \(XA^\top+b\). This storage convention changes how we read a parameter array, rather than changing the affine model. Tensor layout later examines storage and operation costs in more detail.
We now have scores with defined meanings and dimensions. The next chapter converts one binary score or a row of competing scores into probabilities.

Chapter checkpoint
A batch has shape \([8,500]\), and its classifier weights have shape \([500,3]\). What does each axis of the result represent? If every weight and bias in a binary model is doubled, what happens to its zero-score boundary and its score magnitudes?
Feedback: The result has shape \([8,3]\): eight documents and three class scores per document. The input feature axis is consumed. Positive scaling preserves the binary zero-score boundary, but doubles all scores. The probability transformation can therefore change confidence even when the boundary stays fixed.

title: 6  Sigmoid and softmax
text:
6.1 Binary probabilities
The three-example classifier produced scores \([0.9,-0.2,0.6]\). Their signs support a binary decision, but a score of 0.9 does not mean a probability of 90 percent. We need a probability rule that gives the scores a consistent interpretation.
Sigmoid handles one binary outcome. Softmax compares several competing outcomes. Both rely on exponentials, whose mathematical properties also explain how to calculate them safely.
For a binary task, let \(p\) be the model’s probability of the positive outcome. The other outcome has probability \(1-p\). The odds compare those two probabilities:
\[
\mathrm{odds}=\frac{p}{1-p}
\tag{6.1}\]
For \(p=0.8\), the odds are \(0.8/0.2=4\). The event has four times the probability of its complement. For \(p=0.5\), the odds are 1. Odds are ratios, so they are not restricted to the interval from 0 to 1.
The log-odds, or logit link, take the natural logarithm of that ratio:
\[
\operatorname{logit}(p)=\log\left(\frac{p}{1-p}\right)
\tag{6.2}\]
This expression is defined for \(0<p<1\). Probability 0.5 gives log-odds 0. Larger probabilities give positive log-odds, and smaller probabilities give negative values. A Bernoulli distribution describes one binary outcome with probabilities \(p\) and \(1-p\).
Logistic regression models the log-odds as the affine score \(z=w^\top x+b\). To obtain the probability from the score, solve \(z=\log(p/(1-p))\). Exponentiating gives \(e^z=p/(1-p)\). Multiplying by \(1-p\) and collecting terms gives \(p=e^z/(1+e^z)\). Dividing numerator and denominator by \(e^z\) yields the sigmoid function:
\[
\sigma(z)=\frac{1}{1+\exp(-z)}
\tag{6.3}\]
The symbol \(\exp(a)\) means \(e^a\), where \(e\approx2.718\). For finite real \(z\), sigmoid returns a value strictly between 0 and 1. At \(z=0\), it returns \(1/(1+1)=0.5\). Positive scores favor the positive outcome, while negative scores favor its complement.
For \(z=2\), the probability is \(1/(1+e^{-2})\approx0.8808\). Using the unrounded probability gives odds \(e^2\approx7.389\) and log-odds 2. Rounding \(p\) to 0.881 before dividing gives odds about 7.40, so small discrepancies in displayed values come from rounding. Adding one unit to a score multiplies its odds by \(e\).
Return to the three-example batch from Chapter 5. Applying sigmoid separately gives:
These are probabilities for three different examples. They need not sum to 1. Each has its own complementary probability, such as \(1-0.711=0.289\) for the first example’s negative outcome.
The sigmoid curve flattens near its extremes. A fixed change in a very large score causes only a small change in the displayed probability. That describes the probability function’s local sensitivity. It does not by itself establish that a confidently wrong model learns slowly. The gradient derivation includes the loss function when answering that question.
A binary probability needs only one score because the other probability is its complement. Several mutually exclusive classes require a joint normalization across their competing scores.
