title: 6  Sigmoid and softmax
crumbs: Part II: From scores to loss

title: 6  Sigmoid and softmax
text:
6.2 Competing outcomes
Suppose one document can receive exactly one of three topics. Its model produces a logit vector, one score per topic. A categorical distribution assigns a probability to each of these mutually exclusive outcomes. All probabilities must be nonnegative and sum to 1.
Softmax obtains that distribution by exponentiating the scores and dividing by their total:
\[
p_i=\frac{\exp(z_i)}{\sum_j\exp(z_j)}
\tag{6.4}\]
Here \(z_i\) is the score for candidate \(i\), and \(p_i\) is its probability. The sum includes all candidates for this one example. Exponentiation makes finite scores positive. Division by their sum normalizes the vector, so adding the resulting probabilities returns 1.
For scores \(z=(2,1,0)\), the exponentials are approximately \((7.389,2.718,1)\). Their sum is 11.107, giving probabilities \((0.665,0.245,0.090)\). The highest score remains the most likely candidate, but every probability depends on the competitors as well.
The probability ratio for two candidates is \(p_i/p_j=\exp(z_i-z_j)\) because the common denominator cancels. Only score differences matter. Adding the same constant to every score preserves those differences and the full distribution. Increasing just one score increases its probability and decreases the probabilities assigned to the other candidates.
The axis of normalization is therefore part of the model’s meaning. For scores of shape \([B,K]\), each of the \(B\) examples needs its own distribution over \(K\) classes. Normalizing the last axis produces that result. Normalizing the batch axis would make unrelated documents compete with each other.
This also distinguishes multiclass from multilabel prediction. If several labels may apply together, independent sigmoid outputs can describe their individual probabilities. They are not required to sum to 1. A softmax distribution instead encodes a choice of one candidate among the supplied alternatives.
The figure compares the scalar binary map with the normalization of competing scores. Read its output axes according to those different probability meanings.






Figure 6.2: Sigmoid supplies one binary probability. Softmax normalizes competing scores into one categorical distribution.



The following runnable PyTorch example preserves both cases. It applies sigmoid to the three binary logits and softmax to two rows of three class logits. The second class row contains equal scores, so its probabilities are all one third.

Code example: Sigmoid for binary logits and softmax for multiclass logits

import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F

binary_logits = torch.tensor([0.9, -0.2, 0.6])
binary_probabilities = torch.sigmoid(binary_logits)

class_logits = torch.tensor([[2.0, 1.0, 0.0], [0.2, 0.2, 0.2]])
class_probabilities = F.softmax(class_logits, dim=-1)

print(binary_probabilities)
print(class_probabilities)
print(class_probabilities.sum(dim=-1))
The binary output has shape \([3]\). The categorical output has shape \([2,3]\), and each row sums to 1. A normalized model output is not automatically a reliable estimate of real-world frequencies. Evaluation will compare confidence with observed correctness.
A categorical distribution can also supply a sample, one outcome drawn according to its probabilities:
\[
y\sim\operatorname{Categorical}(p_1,\ldots,p_K)
\tag{6.5}\]
The symbol \(y\) here is a sampled output, rather than a supplied training target. The notation \(\sim\) means “drawn from.” For probabilities \((0.7,0.2,0.1)\), the cumulative intervals are \([0,0.7)\), \([0.7,0.9)\), and \([0.9,1)\). A uniform random draw of 0.75 lies in the second interval and selects class index 1 under zero-based indexing.
The distribution is now suitable for selection or comparison with a target. Before using it, we must ensure its implementation preserves the mathematics when scores are large.
crumbs: Part II: From scores to loss

title: 6  Sigmoid and softmax
text:
6.3 Stable normalization
For logits \([1000,1001]\), the relative difference is only 1. The probabilities should be ordinary finite numbers. Directly computing \(e^{1000}\) on a computer can nevertheless overflow before division has a chance to cancel the large scale.
Floating-point arithmetic represents numbers with finite precision and a finite range. Overflow occurs when a result exceeds that range. Numerical stability concerns whether an implementation obtains useful results despite those finite representations.
Softmax’s invariance to a common shift provides the remedy. Let \(m\) be the largest logit in a row. Subtract it before exponentiation:
\[
\operatorname{softmax}(z)_i=\frac{\exp(z_i-\max(z))}{\sum_j\exp(z_j-\max(z))}
\tag{6.6}\]
Every numerator is multiplied by \(e^{-m}\), and so is the denominator. The factor cancels, leaving the same distribution. The largest shifted score is zero, whose exponential is 1. All other shifted scores are nonpositive, so their exponentials are at most 1.
For \([1000,1001]\), subtracting 1001 gives \([-1,0]\). Exponentiation gives approximately \([0.3679,1]\). Dividing by 1.3679 yields \([0.2689,0.7311]\). The large common scale has disappeared without changing the intended probabilities.
Sometimes we need log probabilities directly. The log-sum-exp operation calculates the logarithm of the sum of exponentials:
\[
\operatorname{logsumexp}(z)=m+\log\left(\sum_j\exp(z_j-m)\right),\quad m=\max_j z_j
\tag{6.7}\]
To obtain the stable form, factor \(e^m\) out of the sum. The logarithm of that factor contributes \(m\), and the remaining sum contains the shifted exponentials. For \([1,2]\), the result is \(2+\log(e^{-1}+1)\approx2.313\). For \([1000,1001]\), it is approximately 1001.313.
The log probability of candidate \(i\) is \(z_i-\operatorname{logsumexp}(z)\). Libraries can calculate this directly with log_softmax, avoiding an intermediate probability that might round to zero before a later logarithm. The loss chapter uses these log probabilities to score observed targets.
The stable formula assumes a nonempty row of finite logits. Extremely small probabilities can still underflow to zero, and nonfinite input values need a separate policy. In particular, excluding every candidate does not leave a distribution to normalize. The later masking examples will state what should happen in that case.
Scores can now support two different uses. With a fixed model, a selection rule produces an output. During training, the probability assigned to an observed target supplies a loss. We first follow the output-selection branch.

Chapter checkpoint
Three independent binary examples have logits \([0.9,-0.2,0.6]\). Why is applying softmax across these three values a different model from applying sigmoid to each? What happens to a categorical distribution when 1000 is added to every logit?
Feedback: Softmax would make the examples compete for one total probability mass. Sigmoid gives each example its own positive-outcome probability and complement. Adding a common constant to categorical logits leaves their softmax probabilities unchanged, although a direct exponential implementation may overflow. Subtracting the row maximum avoids that intermediate overflow.

title: 7  Decoding strategies
text:
7.1 Greedy selection
A next-token distribution describes several possible continuations. An application still needs one visible output. Decoding selects a token, appends it to the available context, and repeats the process when more text is required.
This chapter follows inference with a fixed model. Changing a decoding rule changes how its scores are used, while its trained parameters remain fixed. After exploring that branch, we return to the probability assigned to an observed training target.
Suppose the model assigns probabilities \((0.6,0.3,0.1)\) to three candidate tokens. The most direct rule chooses the first candidate. Greedy decoding always selects the highest-probability outcome at the current step:
\[
\mathrm{next}=\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{i}p_i
\tag{7.1}\]
The index \(i\) identifies a candidate, and \(p_i\) is its probability. The operator \(\operatorname*{arg\,max}\) returns an index attaining the largest value. With zero-based token indices, \((0.1,0.7,0.2)\) selects index 1. Equal maximum values require a tie policy if the result must be deterministic.
A decoder step computes next-token scores for the current context. Their vocabulary distribution is:
\[
P(\mathrm{next}=i\mid\mathrm{context})=\operatorname{softmax}(\mathrm{logits})_i
\tag{7.2}\]
The softmax calculation is the one established in Chapter 6. Greedy selection can operate directly on logits because softmax preserves their ordering. It does not need to materialize every probability merely to find the largest score.
A classifier may make one such choice and stop. An autoregressive language model appends the selected token, computes scores for the extended context, and selects again. The selected token is therefore an input to later decisions. Generation ends when the stopping rule is met, for example after an end marker or a maximum output length.
Greedy decoding solves the current one-step choice. It does not guarantee the most probable complete continuation, because a slightly less likely first token can lead to much more likely later tokens. It also repeats the same choices under the same scores and tie rules, which may be unsuitable when the application needs several alternatives.
Selection should be distinguished from the computation producing the scores. The serving chapter reuses model state to avoid repeated work. Such reuse aims to preserve the same model computation. A decoding rule deliberately changes how candidate outputs are chosen.
crumbs: Part II: From scores to loss

title: 7  Decoding strategies
text:
7.2 Sampling controls
Sampling can produce several continuations from the same prompt, but very low-probability choices may be unhelpful. We can adjust the distribution before drawing a token. Temperature changes its concentration, while top-k and top-p restrict which candidates remain eligible.
For positive temperature \(T\), divide every logit by \(T\) before normalization:
\[
p_i^{(T)}=\frac{e^{z_i/T}}{\sum_j e^{z_j/T}}
\tag{7.3}\]
Here \(T\) is temperature, rather than the sequence length used in other chapters. At \(T=1\), the original softmax is recovered. A value above 1 reduces score differences and makes the distribution flatter. A value between 0 and 1 increases those differences and makes it sharper. The formula is undefined at zero. Interfaces that offer zero-temperature generation typically select greedily through a separate rule.
Start with logits \([2,1,0]\), whose probabilities are approximately \([0.665,0.245,0.090]\). At temperature 2, the logits become \([1,0.5,0]\), giving approximately \([0.506,0.307,0.186]\). The largest candidate is still largest, but the alternatives receive more probability. For the two-logit case \((2,1)\), temperature 2 likewise changes the score gap from 1 to 0.5.
Top-k sampling retains exactly the \(k\) largest candidates before drawing a token. Let \((i_1,\ldots,i_V)\) order the vocabulary indices from highest to lowest probability, breaking ties consistently. The retained set is:
\[
S_k=\{i_1,\ldots,i_k\},\quad p_{i_1}\ge p_{i_2}\ge\ldots\ge p_{i_V},\quad 1\le k\le V
\tag{7.4}\]
The vocabulary contains \(V\) candidates, and \(1\leq k\leq V\). The retained support is the set of outcomes allowed to receive nonzero probability. For probabilities \((0.5,0.3,0.2)\) and \(k=2\), only the first two indices remain.
Top-p sampling, also called nucleus sampling, retains the smallest leading set whose total probability reaches a threshold. Write that threshold as \(\tau\) to distinguish it from the individual probabilities \(p_i\):
\[
S_\tau=\{i_1,\ldots,i_m\},\quad m=\min\left\{r:\sum_{j=1}^{r}p_{i_j}\ge\tau\right\},\quad 0<\tau\le1
\tag{7.5}\]
The candidates use the same decreasing order, and \(0<\tau\leq1\). For \((0.5,0.3,0.2)\) and \(\tau=0.8\), the first two probabilities reach the threshold exactly. A sharply concentrated distribution may need only one candidate. A flatter distribution may need many.
After either filter selects a nonempty set \(S\), the remaining mass must be normalized again. For \(i\in S\), use \(q_i=p_i/\sum_{j\in S}p_j\), and set \(q_i=0\) outside it. Sampling then draws from \(q\), so excluded candidates cannot be selected.
Keep the starting point explicit when comparing settings. Filtering the original \([0.665,0.245,0.090]\) with \(k=2\) gives approximately \([0.731,0.269,0]\). Top-p with threshold 0.8 retains the same two candidates because their original combined mass is about 0.910. It therefore gives the same renormalized result in this case.
Combining temperature 2 with top-k is a different experiment. First obtain \([0.506,0.307,0.186]\), then retain the largest two values and renormalize. The result is approximately \([0.622,0.378,0]\). Top-p at 0.8 also keeps those two under this distribution, whose combined mass is about 0.814. Applying top-k to the original probabilities while describing temperature-adjusted sampling would mix two different computations.
The figure shows where these controls act between model scores and the sampled token. Filtering precedes the random draw.






Figure 7.2: Temperature changes the distribution before filtering and sampling.



The following runnable PyTorch example uses four scores, temperature 0.8, and top-k 2. torch.topk returns the retained values and indices. The code places negative infinity at excluded positions, so their exponentials become zero during softmax.

Code example: Temperature and top-k filtering for one next-token decision

import torch

logits = torch.tensor([2.0, 1.0, 0.5, -1.0])
temperature = 0.8
top_k = 2

scaled = logits / temperature
values, indices = torch.topk(scaled, top_k)
filtered = torch.full_like(scaled, float("-inf"))
filtered[indices] = values
probabilities = torch.softmax(filtered, dim=-1)

print(probabilities)
print(torch.multinomial(probabilities, num_samples=1))
The resulting probabilities are approximately \([0.777,0.223,0,0]\). The final call draws one retained index and returns an integer tensor with one element. That sampled result is random. A specified generator seed helps make an experiment repeatable, although exact reproducibility also depends on the implementation and execution environment.
Generation interfaces such as GenerationConfig and generate expose these choices through settings including do_sample, temperature, top_k, and top_p. Their supported combinations and defaults must be checked for the selected implementation. The library map connects those interfaces to their practical use.
Lower temperature and narrower support do not establish factual correctness. They concentrate choices according to the model’s existing scores. The application must evaluate whether the resulting diversity, repetition, and errors meet its needs.

title: 7  Decoding strategies
text:
7.3 Beam search
Greedy decoding discards every alternative to the best current token. Beam search instead retains several partial continuations. Its beam width is the number kept after each expansion. This trades additional computation and state for a broader search over sequences.
Suppose the first-token probabilities are \(P(A)=0.6\) and \(P(B)=0.4\). After \(A\), the next-token probabilities are \(P(X\mid A)=0.51\) and \(P(Y\mid A)=0.49\). After \(B\), they are \(P(X\mid B)=0.9\) and \(P(Y\mid B)=0.1\). Compare continuations of exactly two tokens.
Greedy decoding chooses \(A\), then \(X\), giving sequence probability \(0.6\times0.51=0.306\). A beam of width 2 retains both \(A\) and \(B\) after the first step. Expanding them produces \(AX:0.306\), \(AY:0.294\), \(BX:0.36\), and \(BY:0.04\). Keeping the best two gives \(BX\) and \(AX\). The most probable complete sequence here starts with the locally less likely first token.
Rather than multiplying many small probabilities, beam search usually adds their logarithms. A sequence score for a candidate prefix is:
\[
score(y_{1:t})=\sum_{i=1}^{t}\log P(y_i\mid y_{<i},x)
\tag{7.6}\]
The sequence \(y_{1:t}\) contains \(t\) generated tokens, and \(x\) is the supplied prompt or input. Each factor conditions on that input and the earlier generated tokens. The logarithm converts the probability product into a sum. A larger log score represents a more probable sequence under this criterion.
For a two-token candidate with probabilities 0.5 and 0.4, the score is \(\log(0.5)+\log(0.4)=\log(0.2)\approx-1.609\). Every added probability factor is at most 1, so additional tokens cannot increase the raw log score. Comparing different lengths therefore requires care.
A length normalization modifies that comparison. One simple choice divides the accumulated log score by \(t^\alpha\), with a specified exponent \(\alpha\). This is a new search criterion, rather than the raw sequence probability. For a two-token sequence with probability 0.2 and a three-token sequence with probability 0.18, the raw scores favor the first. With \(\alpha=1\), their normalized scores are about \(-0.805\) and \(-0.572\), favoring the second. Different libraries may use different length formulas.
An implementation must also state how completed sequences and unfinished beams compete, when an end marker stops expansion, and what happens at the output-length limit. Those choices can change the result even at a fixed beam width.
Beam search remains approximate because discarded prefixes are not reconsidered. A wider beam searches more alternatives, but the model’s preferred sequence need not be the most useful response. With deterministic model outputs and tie handling, beam search is a deterministic search procedure. It is distinct from drawing random candidates from a distribution.
The output branch has now converted probabilities into visible tokens. We next return to an observed target and ask how much penalty its assigned probability should contribute during training.

Chapter checkpoint
Why does width-2 beam search retain a useful alternative in the \(A/B\) example that greedy decoding loses? If top-k follows temperature scaling, which distribution must be renormalized after filtering?
Feedback: Keeping \(B\) allows the search to discover \(BX\) with probability 0.36, above greedy \(AX\) at 0.306. Filtering must act on the temperature-adjusted distribution when that is the specified sequence of operations. Using the original distribution would implement a different sampling policy.

title: 8  Cross-entropy and perplexity
text:
8.1 Loss from a target probability
Decoding selected an output from a fixed model’s distribution. Training asks a different question: how much probability did that model assign to the observed target? A model that gives the correct answer probability 0.01 should incur a greater penalty than one that gives it probability 0.8.
Negative log likelihood turns that comparison into a loss. Combining the losses gives a training objective, while perplexity expresses average token loss on a different scale. The same mathematics also separates uncertainty in the data from disagreement with a model.
A correct-or-incorrect decision gives zero-one loss: zero for a correct predicted class and one for an error. With a positive target and threshold 0.5, probabilities 0.1 and 0.4 both incur loss one. That score hides the improvement in target probability.
As a function of the underlying score, zero-one loss is flat away from its decision boundary and discontinuous at the boundary. It provides no useful local direction for the gradient updates developed later. A probability-sensitive loss preserves information that the hard decision discards.
Suppose the observed target has probability 0.25 under a model. The negative log likelihood, or NLL, assigns the penalty \(-\log(0.25)\approx1.386\). A probability of 1 gives zero penalty, and probabilities approaching zero give increasingly large penalties.
\[
\mathrm{NLL}=-\log P_\theta(y\mid x)
\tag{8.1}\]
The input is \(x\), the observed target is \(y\), and \(\theta\) denotes the model parameters. The expression \(P_\theta(y\mid x)\) is the probability assigned to that target. A likelihood regards the observed data as fixed and asks how well the model parameters explain it. Taking a negative logarithm converts maximizing that probability into minimizing a penalty.
Natural logarithms measure this loss in nats. A nat is an information unit using base \(e\). Dividing a value in nats by \(\log 2\) converts it to bits. Thus one nat is approximately 1.443 bits. The negative logarithm is also called surprisal: an event assigned a small probability carries a large value.
For a binary outcome, sigmoid supplies probability \(p\) for target 1 and \(1-p\) for target 0. The observed-label likelihood is \(p^y(1-p)^{1-y}\). Taking its negative logarithm gives binary cross-entropy, or BCE:
\[
L_{\mathrm{BCE}}=-y\log p-(1-y)\log(1-p)
\tag{8.2}\]
Here \(y\in\{0,1\}\). When \(y=1\), the second term vanishes and the loss is \(-\log p\). When \(y=0\), the first term vanishes and the loss is \(-\log(1-p)\). For a positive target, \(p=0.8\) gives about 0.223 nats, while \(p=0.1\) gives about 2.303 nats. The latter prediction assigns much less probability to what actually occurred.
For a categorical outcome, a one-hot target is a vector with 1 at the observed class and 0 elsewhere. If there are three classes and the observed class index is 1, its one-hot vector is \([0,1,0]\). Categorical cross-entropy compares that target with the predicted probability vector:
\[
L_{\mathrm{CE}}=-\sum_i y_i\log p_i
\tag{8.3}\]
The index \(i\) runs over classes, \(y_i\) is the target indicator, and \(p_i\) is the corresponding model probability. Only the observed class contributes to the sum. If its class index is \(c\), this simplifies to:
\[
H(\mathbf y,p)=-\sum_i y_i\log p_i=-\log p_c,\quad y_c=1
\tag{8.4}\]
For model probabilities \([0.2,0.7,0.1]\) and target index 1, the loss is \(-\log(0.7)\approx0.357\). A target receiving probability 0.25 gives 1.386 nats, matching the NLL example. The vector formula and the observed-class formula therefore describe the same calculation for a one-hot target.
The figure connects a target’s probability to its penalty. High confidence is useful only when it favors the observed outcome.
A large loss identifies a poorly predicted target. It does not alone determine how much every parameter will change. That also depends on the derivatives through the model and the update rule, introduced in backpropagation.
Implementations should preserve the numerical stability established in Section 6.3. BCEWithLogitsLoss receives raw binary logits and targets of matching shape. CrossEntropyLoss can receive categorical logits and integer class indices, avoiding an explicit one-hot array. It combines the stable log-probability calculation with target selection. Passing sigmoid or softmax probabilities into an interface expecting logits would apply the wrong transformation.

title: 8  Cross-entropy and perplexity
text: Figure 8.2: Cross-entropy for a single observed class penalizes the negative logarithm of its probability.
crumbs: Part II: From scores to loss

title: 8  Cross-entropy and perplexity
text:
8.2 Combining valid losses
We can now calculate the three penalties that Chapter 1 supplied without derivation. The running batch has targets \([1,0,1]\) and sigmoid probabilities approximately \([0.711,0.450,0.646]\). Their losses are \(-\log(0.711)\approx0.341\), \(-\log(1-0.450)\approx0.598\), and \(-\log(0.646)\approx0.437\).
The mean is \((0.341+0.598+0.437)/3\approx0.459\). This is the empirical-risk average, now applied to a specified loss. The separate example with supplied penalties 0.2 and 0.5 gives \((0.2+0.5)/2=0.35\) by the same rule.
A reduction combines several loss values through a sum, mean, or another stated rule. A sum gives a larger objective when more equally difficult examples contribute. A mean divides by their count. That scaling later affects the gradient as well, so a change of reduction is part of the training configuration.
The runnable PyTorch example below starts from the running batch’s fixed logits. It returns each binary loss before taking the mean, then compares that mean with the library’s default reduction. It separately checks a categorical target using log probabilities supplied as valid logits.

Code example: Separate binary losses and a categorical target

import math
import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F

logits = torch.tensor([0.9, -0.2, 0.6])
targets = torch.tensor([1.0, 0.0, 1.0])
per_example = F.binary_cross_entropy_with_logits(logits, targets, reduction="none")
mean_loss = per_example.mean()
assert torch.allclose(mean_loss, F.binary_cross_entropy_with_logits(logits, targets))

# These supplied positive probabilities have logarithms that are valid logits.
class_probabilities = torch.tensor([[0.2, 0.7, 0.1]])
class_target = torch.tensor([1])
categorical_loss = F.cross_entropy(class_probabilities.log(), class_target)
assert math.isclose(categorical_loss.item(), -math.log(0.7), rel_tol=1e-6)
print(per_example.tolist(), mean_loss.item(), categorical_loss.item())
The binary mean is approximately 0.45893. The categorical loss is approximately 0.35667. These checks measure probability-to-loss arithmetic and make no parameter update.
Language modeling applies the same observed-target rule at sequence positions. For token \(x_t\) and its permitted prefix, the local loss is:
\[
L=-\log P_\theta(x_t\mid x_{<t})
\tag{8.5}\]
Chapter 1’s within-sequence alignment uses a sequence of \(T\) tokens to supply \(T-1\) next-token targets. With no excluded targets, their average is:
\[
L_{\mathrm{LM}}(\theta)=-\frac{1}{T-1}\sum_{t=1}^{T-1}\log P_\theta(x_{t+1}\mid x_{\le t})
\tag{8.6}\]
The prediction at position \(t\) uses \(x_{\leq t}\) and is judged against \(x_{t+1}\). The condition \(T\geq2\) ensures at least one such pair. Additional beginning-token conventions must be stated separately.
Real batches can include padding and deliberately unsupervised positions. A loss mask identifies which target positions contribute to the objective. If \(M>0\) positions are supervised, the mean uses exactly those positions:
\[
\mathrm{CE}=-\frac{1}{M}\sum_{t\in\mathrm{unmasked}}\log P_\theta(x_t\mid x_{<t})
\tag{8.7}\]
Here \(M\) is a count, rather than a mask tensor. The index set in the sum identifies the valid targets. Both the numerator and denominator exclude padding and other ignored targets. If no target is valid, the training procedure must skip or reject that batch rather than divide by zero.
For correct-token probabilities 0.7 and 0.5, the mean loss is \(-(\log0.7+\log0.5)/2\approx0.525\). If a third stored position is padding, it neither adds a loss nor changes the divisor to 3. Dividing by storage length would make examples look artificially easier when more padding is added.
There are two common alignment interfaces. A direct loss calculation pairs logits[:, :-1, :] with next-token labels input_ids[:, 1:]. A causal language-model class such as GPT-2 can instead receive labels aligned with input_ids and perform that shift internally. Shifting both in preparation and inside the model would skip a target position and change the task.
The next runnable example uses the two padded ID rows from Chapter 2 and fixed, zero logits over a ten-token vocabulary. The predictions have shape \([2,4,10]\). Shifting leaves three possible target positions per row, of which five are valid. Flattening only the batch and sequence axes produces the \([N,V]\) logits expected by this direct cross-entropy call.

Code example: Next-token alignment with five valid targets

import math
import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F

input_ids = torch.tensor([[1, 4, 8, 9], [1, 6, 9, 9]])
valid = torch.tensor([[True, True, True, True], [True, True, True, False]])
vocabulary_size = 10
logits = torch.zeros(2, 4, vocabulary_size)

targets = input_ids[:, 1:].clone()
targets[~valid[:, 1:]] = -100
predictions = logits[:, :-1, :].reshape(-1, vocabulary_size)
flat_targets = targets.reshape(-1)
per_target = F.cross_entropy(predictions, flat_targets, ignore_index=-100, reduction="none")
active = flat_targets != -100
count = int(active.sum())
assert count == 5
assert targets[1, 1].item() == 9
assert targets[1, 2].item() == -100
mean_loss = per_target[active].sum() / count
library_mean = F.cross_entropy(predictions, flat_targets, ignore_index=-100)
assert torch.allclose(mean_loss, library_mean)
assert math.isclose(mean_loss.item(), math.log(vocabulary_size), rel_tol=1e-6)
print(count, mean_loss.item(), mean_loss.exp().item())
The real EOS in the shorter row remains a target, while its inserted padding is ignored. Every zero-logit row is uniform over ten tokens, so each valid loss is \(\log10\approx2.303\). The total and count produce that same mean across the five valid positions.
A mean over tokens gives each supervised token equal influence. A mean of per-document means gives documents equal influence instead. Those objectives can differ when document lengths differ. State the intended unit before comparing losses across datasets or batches.

title: 8  Cross-entropy and perplexity
text:
8.3 Perplexity
An average token loss is additive in logarithms. Perplexity puts it back on a multiplicative scale by exponentiating the mean:
\[
\mathrm{PPL}=\exp(\mathrm{CE})
\tag{8.8}\]
The expression assumes natural-log cross-entropy. If base-2 logarithms were used, the corresponding inverse would be \(2^{\mathrm{CE}}\). A loss of 1.2 nats gives \(e^{1.2}\approx3.32\), and a loss of 2.0 gives approximately 7.39.
Perplexity is the inverse geometric mean of the probabilities assigned to observed targets. It can be understood through a uniform distribution: if every one of \(V\) tokens receives probability \(1/V\), the token loss is \(\log V\) and perplexity is exactly \(V\). This is an effective-choice interpretation, rather than a literal count of plausible outputs at every position.
Consider The cat sat on, with toy IDs \([1,2,3,4]\) and a vocabulary of 5,000 tokens. Input positions \([1,2,3]\) have targets \([2,3,4]\), and their logits have shape \([1,3,5000]\). The model width can be 64 without changing that vocabulary-output shape.
With uniform output probabilities, each target has probability \(1/5000=0.0002\). Its loss is \(\log5000\approx8.517\) nats, and perplexity is exactly 5,000 before rounding. If each observed target instead receives probability 0.3, the mean loss is \(-\log0.3\approx1.204\) and perplexity is \(1/0.3\approx3.333\). Neither value by itself establishes how the model obtained those predictions.
The inverse relation also clarifies what \(e^{-L}\) measures when \(L\) is mean negative log probability. It is the geometric mean of the observed-target probabilities, obtained by multiplying them and taking the appropriate root. For probabilities 0.9 and 0.1, it equals \(\sqrt{0.09}=0.3\), while their arithmetic mean is 0.5. Exponentiating negative average loss does not generally recover arithmetic mean confidence.
Lower perplexity means higher geometric-mean probability for the observed targets under the stated evaluation conditions.
Compare perplexities only when the evaluated text, tokenizer, target selection, and aggregation convention are compatible. Changing the tokenizer changes the unit called a token. A model can also lower next-token perplexity without improving an application’s desired output format or factual reliability.

title: 8  Cross-entropy and perplexity
text:
8.4 Entropy and distribution mismatch
Even an accurate probability model can remain uncertain about an outcome. To separate that inherent uncertainty from model disagreement, consider a target distribution \(p\) and a model distribution \(q\). In this section, \(p\) describes how outcomes occur, rather than the predicted distribution used earlier.
Entropy is the average surprisal when a distribution predicts outcomes drawn from itself:
\[
H(p)=-\sum_i p_i\log p_i
\tag{8.9}\]
Each outcome’s \(-\log p_i\) is weighted by the probability \(p_i\) of observing it. For \(p=(0.5,0.5)\), entropy is \(-0.5\log0.5-0.5\log0.5\approx0.693\) nats. A certain outcome has entropy zero. A uniform distribution over \(K\) outcomes has entropy \(\log K\).
General cross-entropy uses the model probabilities to score those same target outcomes: \(H(p,q)=-\sum_i p_i\log q_i\). Earlier, the observed categorical label supplied a one-hot target distribution. This broader expression also allows a target with probability spread across outcomes.
For target \(p=(0.5,0.5)\) and model \(q=(0.75,0.25)\), cross-entropy is \(-0.5\log0.75-0.5\log0.25\approx0.837\). The target’s entropy was about 0.693, so using the mismatched model adds about 0.144 nats of average loss.
That excess is the Kullback-Leibler divergence, abbreviated KL divergence:
\[
\operatorname{KL}(p\mathbin\Vert q)=\sum_i p_i\log\left(\frac{p_i}{q_i}\right)
\tag{8.10}\]
Subtracting entropy from cross-entropy gives \(\sum_i p_i(\log p_i-\log q_i)\), which is the displayed log-ratio expression. Therefore \(H(p,q)=H(p)+\operatorname{KL}(p\Vert q)\). The divergence is nonnegative for probability distributions and is zero when they agree.
KL divergence is not a symmetric distance: exchanging \(p\) and \(q\) generally changes it. Terms with \(p_i=0\) contribute zero by the limiting convention. If \(p_i>0\) while \(q_i=0\), the divergence and cross-entropy are infinite. These conditions matter when a model rules out an outcome that can actually occur.
The loss now measures both prediction fit and, when distributions are compared, the cost of mismatch. An application’s task metric can ask a different question, such as how many decisions were correct. The next chapter keeps those measurements distinct when judging behavior on held-out data.

Chapter checkpoint
Two valid targets have probabilities 0.7 and 0.5, followed by three padding positions. What count belongs in the mean loss? If one tokenizer splits each word into more pieces, can its token perplexity be compared directly with another tokenizer’s result?
Feedback: Divide the two valid loss terms by 2, giving approximately 0.525 nats. Padding changes storage, not the number of observed targets. Different tokenization changes the unit of the average, so raw token perplexities require a common or explicitly adjusted evaluation basis.

title: 9  Validation and testing
text:
9.1 Generalization
A small training loss shows that a model fits the examples used to adjust it. It does not establish that the same rule will help on new inputs. Evaluation needs separate data, a task-appropriate measurement, and an account of which errors matter.
This chapter turns those requirements into a comparison procedure. It distinguishes errors in class decisions, the ordering of model scores, and the reliability of reported probabilities.
Suppose an article classifier performs well on the articles used during training but fails on new reports. Its fitted parameters may capture recurring topic evidence, details peculiar to those articles, or both. Generalization is useful prediction on new examples from the intended task distribution.
The data-split roles separate fitting from this evaluation. Training examples adjust the model. Validation examples guide model choices. Test examples estimate performance after those choices are fixed. A hyperparameter is a setting chosen outside the parameter-fitting calculation, such as model width or learning rate.
Held-out loss uses the same loss and reduction as training, applied to different examples with fixed parameters. Two held-out losses of 0.2 and 0.5 have mean 0.35. Their arithmetic matches the empirical-risk average. Their experimental role differs because held-out losses do not supply a parameter update.
Data leakage occurs when information meant to be held out influences fitting or selection. It can enter through vocabulary fitting, feature selection, duplicated documents, or repeated use of test scores. The fixed-vocabulary example in Chapter 4 prevents one such route.
The split must match the kind of new input expected. Near-duplicate articles should not appear on both sides of a supposedly independent comparison. Records from the same person or event may require grouping. If the application predicts future outcomes, a random split can expose later information during fitting, so a time-based split may be appropriate. Benchmark material appearing in pretraining data creates a related concern for language-model evaluation.
Learning curves compare training and validation measurements as training progresses or data increases. Low training loss with much higher validation loss suggests that the fitted rule transfers poorly. Overfitting describes fitting details of the training sample that do not support the intended new-data behavior. A model that cannot fit important patterns even in training may be underfitting.
The terms bias and variance help describe possible causes. A restrictive representation can impose systematic errors across samples, contributing to bias. A fitted model that changes substantially with the training sample can contribute high variance. A gap in two curves alone does not prove either cause, and high training loss may also indicate a training failure.
These distinctions guide experiments. A poor fit on both splits can motivate checking features, model capacity, and the training procedure. A good training fit with a large validation gap can motivate more representative data, regularization, or a simpler model. Regularization constrains fitting to discourage solutions that depend too strongly on sample-specific details. Early stopping chooses a training checkpoint using validation behavior. Both must be selected without repeatedly consulting the final test set.
Training loss need not fall at every update. The important evaluation question is whether a chosen procedure improves the held-out measurements that matter, under a fixed comparison protocol.
crumbs: Part II: From scores to loss

title: 9  Validation and testing
text:
9.2 Classification errors
An overall correctness rate can hide the kind of mistakes an application cannot tolerate. For binary classification, choose which outcome counts as positive, then record both the actual and predicted class. A confusion matrix retains the resulting four counts.
A true positive is an actual positive predicted positive. A false negative is an actual positive predicted negative. A false positive is an actual negative predicted positive, and a true negative is an actual negative predicted negative. Their abbreviations are TP, FN, FP, and TN.
The figure arranges these outcomes by actual and predicted class. Check the axis labels before reading a library’s matrix, because a transpose exchanges the roles of rows and columns.






Figure 9.2: A confusion matrix keeps the actual class and predicted class distinct.



Use a test set with TP=30, FN=10, FP=10, and TN=50. It contains 40 actual positives, 60 actual negatives, and 100 examples in total. Several metrics answer different questions about those same outcomes.
Accuracy measures the fraction of all examples predicted correctly:
\[
\mathrm{accuracy}=\frac{TP+TN}{TP+TN+FP+FN}
\tag{9.1}\]
Here it is \((30+50)/100=0.80\). Accuracy can conceal imbalance. If almost every example is negative, always predicting negative can score highly while finding no positive cases.
Precision asks how many positive predictions are correct:
\[
\mathrm{precision}=\frac{TP}{TP+FP}
\tag{9.2}\]
Its denominator is the number predicted positive. The example gives \(30/(30+10)=0.75\). Recall, also called sensitivity, asks how many actual positives were found:
\[
\mathrm{recall}=\frac{TP}{TP+FN}
\tag{9.3}\]
Its denominator is the number actually positive. Here recall is also \(30/(30+10)=0.75\), though these metrics need not be equal. F1 combines precision \(P\) and recall \(R\) through their harmonic mean:
\[
F_1=\frac{2PR}{P+R}
\tag{9.4}\]
For \(P=R=0.75\), F1 is 0.75. The harmonic mean penalizes a large imbalance between precision and recall. It still omits true negatives, so it cannot replace every application-specific measurement.
Specificity asks how many actual negatives were correctly rejected: \(\mathrm{TN}/(\mathrm{TN}+\mathrm{FP})\). The example gives \(50/60\approx0.833\). Negative predictive value, or NPV, asks how many negative predictions are correct: \(\mathrm{TN}/(\mathrm{TN}+\mathrm{FN})\). It also gives \(50/60\approx0.833\) here, with a different denominator meaning.
These ratios need valid denominators. Precision is undefined when no example is predicted positive, and recall is undefined when the evaluated set has no actual positives. Report such cases and the library’s handling policy. Silently substituting a favorable value can conceal the missing evidence.
For multiclass prediction, inspect the full matrix before reducing it to one score. Per-class precision and recall can treat each class as positive against the rest. A macro average gives each class equal weight. A micro average combines the relevant counts before computing the metric. Multilabel tasks additionally allow several labels per example, so their decision thresholds and averaging convention must be stated.
The preferred balance depends on the consequences of false positives and false negatives. A threshold makes that balance an explicit decision.
crumbs: Part II: From scores to loss

title: 9  Validation and testing
text:
9.3 Thresholds, ranking, and confidence
A decision threshold converts a score or probability into an action. Under the rule “predict positive when \(p\geq\tau\),” lowering \(\tau\) can only add positive predictions on a fixed dataset. It cannot reduce either the number of true positives or false positives. Raising it can only remove such predictions. Precision, as a ratio of two changing counts, need not move monotonically.
If false positives and false negatives have different costs, compare them directly on validation data. For calibrated probabilities and fixed error costs, a positive decision has expected error cost \(C_{\mathrm{FP}}(1-p)\). A negative decision has expected error cost \(C_{\mathrm{FN}}p\). Choosing the smaller gives threshold \(C_{\mathrm{FP}}/(C_{\mathrm{FP}}+C_{\mathrm{FN}})\), assuming correct decisions have zero cost. Different costs or unreliable probabilities require a different analysis.
A receiver operating characteristic, or ROC, curve records the outcomes of sweeping the threshold. Its vertical coordinate is the true-positive rate, which equals recall. Its horizontal coordinate is the false-positive rate:
\[
\mathrm{TPR}=\frac{TP}{TP+FN},\quad\mathrm{FPR}=\frac{FP}{FP+TN}
\tag{9.5}\]
Both actual classes must be present for these rates to be defined. With TP=40, FN=10, FP=20, and TN=30, the coordinates are TPR=\(40/50=0.8\) and FPR=\(20/50=0.4\). Each threshold supplies another point.
The area under the ROC curve, or ROC AUC, summarizes the resulting ranking behavior:
\[
\mathrm{AUC}=\int_{0}^{1}\mathrm{TPR}(\mathrm{FPR})\,d\mathrm{FPR}
\tag{9.6}\]
The integral accumulates area as the false-positive rate moves from 0 to 1. For the piecewise-linear curve through \((0,0)\), \((0.5,0.8)\), and \((1,1)\), the two trapezoids have areas \(0.5(0+0.8)/2=0.2\) and \(0.5(0.8+1)/2=0.45\). Their total is 0.65.
Calibration concerns a different property: whether predicted probabilities match observed frequencies. Among many comparable predictions near 0.8, a calibrated model should be correct about 80 percent of the time. Grouping predictions into probability ranges and comparing confidence with observed outcomes gives a reliability check. Small groups provide uncertain estimates, so counts belong beside those comparisons.
A strictly increasing transformation of scores preserves their ordering and ROC curve, while it can change their probability interpretation. Good ranking therefore does not establish good calibration or select the right operating threshold.
The runnable scikit-learn example uses six fixed labels and scores. It applies threshold 0.5 for the confusion-matrix metrics and retains the original scores for ROC AUC.

Code example: Confusion-matrix metrics and ROC AUC from fixed predictions

from sklearn.metrics import (
    confusion_matrix,
    precision_recall_fscore_support,
    roc_auc_score,
)

y_true = [1, 1, 0, 0, 1, 0]
scores = [0.9, 0.4, 0.8, 0.2, 0.7, 0.1]
y_pred = [int(score >= 0.5) for score in scores]

print(confusion_matrix(y_true, y_pred))
print(precision_recall_fscore_support(y_true, y_pred, average="binary"))
print(roc_auc_score(y_true, scores))
The matrix is [[2,1],[1,2]] when rows are actual classes and columns are predicted classes in order 0,1. Precision, recall, and F1 are each \(2/3\). ROC AUC is \(7/9\approx0.778\), reflecting seven correctly ordered positive-negative pairs out of nine.
Raising this example’s threshold from 0.5 to 0.8 retains the positive example scored 0.9 and the negative example scored 0.8. Precision falls from \(2/3\) to \(1/2\), demonstrating why a higher threshold does not guarantee higher precision. The six observations make the arithmetic inspectable, but do not support a stable estimate of application performance.

title: 9  Validation and testing
text:
9.4 Comparing experiments
Model scores can mislead when the experiments use different data splits or preprocessing. A fair comparison fixes the data split, preprocessing, target rule, metric, and evaluation procedure while varying a stated setting. It records enough detail to explain why one result differs from another.
Grid search evaluates every combination in a specified set of hyperparameter values. Random search samples combinations from stated ranges or distributions under a fixed budget. Bayesian optimization uses previous evaluations to model promising settings and choose further trials. These methods differ in how trials are chosen. None removes the need for an untouched test set.
For example, comparing five learning rates with three batch sizes requires 15 grid trials. Keep the dataset and evaluation rule fixed, record the training budget for each trial, and compare learning curves as well as the final metric. If training randomness affects the conclusion, repeat representative settings with several seeds and report their variation. The classifier and optimizer experiments provide the course’s concrete protocols.
A benchmark packages a task with data and a scoring procedure. Results are comparable only when their conditions match, including model version, prompt format, allowed tools, decoding policy, and answer extraction. Each score measures performance under its particular protocol. It cannot establish overall model quality by itself.
Massive Multitask Language Understanding, or MMLU, evaluates answers across many academic and professional subjects. Its paper describes the tasks and scoring setup. TruthfulQA tests whether answers reproduce common human falsehoods. HellaSwag tests plausible continuations of described situations. These distinct targets help explain why the three scores cannot substitute for one another.
A language model may answer a classification prompt by generating a label string. Its output is still generated token by token, but the application may score one final class decision. Evaluation must therefore check both whether the output is in the required format and whether its content is correct. Architecture and objective choices connect those task interfaces to the model computation.
Select the model and threshold using validation evidence, then report the final test result without further tuning to it. Retain examples of each important error type. An aggregate score locates a problem only when it can be connected back to the inputs and decisions that produced it.
We can now construct inputs, calculate scores and losses, and judge predictions on separate data. The next part derives how the training objective supplies information for changing parameters.

Chapter checkpoint
A model has strong ROC AUC but its 0.9-confidence predictions are correct only 60 percent of the time. Which property is failing? Why should choosing a threshold from the final test set change how its result is reported?
Feedback: Its probability calibration is poor even if its ranking is useful. Choosing the threshold from test results uses that set for selection, so it no longer provides an untouched final evaluation of that choice. Threshold selection belongs with validation evidence.

title: 10  Backpropagation
text:
10.1 Local change and gradients
The running classifier has a mean loss of about 0.459. That number evaluates its current predictions, but does not yet say which parameter should change. To improve the model, we need to trace how a small parameter change affects the loss through the score and probability calculations.
Derivatives describe those local changes. The chain rule connects them through a computation graph, and backpropagation applies that rule to all relevant parameters. We then use the resulting gradients for one complete training step.
Consider \(f(x)=3x^2+1\). Near \(x=2\), increasing \(x\) slightly increases \(f(x)\) by about twelve times as much. The derivative is this local rate of change. Formally, it is the limit of \((f(x+h)-f(x))/h\) as the increment \(h\) approaches zero.
Expanding the difference gives \(3((x+h)^2-x^2)/h=6x+3h\). As \(h\) approaches zero, the derivative becomes \(f'(x)=6x\). At \(x=2\), it is 12. This derivative describes local behavior, rather than a fixed slope for every value of \(x\).
If a loss depends on several parameters, a partial derivative changes one parameter while holding the others fixed. The gradient collects all those partial derivatives. For parameter vector \(\theta\), the gradient \(\nabla_\theta L\) has one component for each parameter. A matrix parameter has a gradient with matching matrix dimensions.
For a small displacement \(\Delta\theta\), the first-order change in loss is approximately \(\nabla_\theta L^\top\Delta\theta\). A positive derivative means increasing that coordinate increases the loss locally. Moving against the gradient therefore provides a local direction of decrease when the gradient is nonzero and the step is sufficiently small.
The magnitude depends on the current parameters, the example, and the parameter’s scale. A large derivative is not a universal measure of that parameter’s importance. We need the derivative of the complete loss, rather than the sensitivity of an isolated intermediate value.

title: 10  Backpropagation
section: 10.2 The chain rule and computation graphs
text:
10.2 The chain rule and computation graphs
A parameter usually affects the loss indirectly. It changes a score, which changes a probability, which changes the penalty. The chain rule multiplies the local rates along that dependency:
\[
\frac{dL}{dx} = \frac{dL}{dy}\,\frac{dy}{dx}
\tag{10.1}\]
Here \(x\) is an earlier value, \(y\) is an intermediate value depending on \(x\), and \(L\) depends on \(y\). If \(dL/dy=5\) and \(dy/dx=3\), then \(dL/dx=15\). The two rates answer different questions, and their product describes the complete effect.
A computation graph records the values and operations producing a result. Its nodes represent values or operations, and its directed edges record dependencies. A forward pass evaluates those operations from inputs to outputs. The reverse calculation starts from the output sensitivity and returns derivatives to the earlier values.
Use the scalar classifier with input \(x=2\), weight \(w=0.5\), bias \(b=0.1\), and positive target 1:
\[
z = wx+b,\quad p=\sigma(z),\quad L=-\log(p)
\tag{10.2}\]
The multiplication gives \(wx=1.0\), the addition gives \(z=1.1\), sigmoid gives \(p\approx0.7503\), and the loss is \(L=-\log p\approx0.2873\). These are distinct nodes in one dependency chain.
We first need the local derivative of sigmoid. Differentiating \((1+e^{-z})^{-1}\) gives \(e^{-z}/(1+e^{-z})^2\), which can be written using the sigmoid value itself:
\[
\sigma'(z)=\sigma(z)\bigl(1-\sigma(z)\bigr)
\tag{10.3}\]
Thus \(dp/dz=p(1-p)\). At the example’s probability, this is approximately \(0.7503\times0.2497=0.1874\). At the earlier sigmoid example \(z=2\), it is approximately \(0.8808\times0.1192=0.1050\). This is the local sensitivity that becomes small near probabilities 0 and 1.
For the positive-target loss, \(dL/dp=-1/p\approx-1.3329\). Multiplying the local derivatives gives \(dL/dz\approx-1.3329\times0.1874\approx-0.2497\). It would be incorrect to infer the loss derivative from the sigmoid derivative alone.
The affine operation supplies the next local derivative:
\[
\frac{dz}{dw}=x
\tag{10.4}\]
Here \(dz/dw=x=2\) and \(dz/db=1\). The weight derivative follows the same chain rule:
\[
\frac{dL}{dw}=\frac{dL}{dz}\,\frac{dz}{dw}
\tag{10.5}\]
The results are \(dL/dw\approx-0.2497\times2=-0.4995\) and \(dL/db\approx-0.2497\). The graph figure places each multiplication beside the path that requires it.






Figure 10.2: Local derivatives connect the classifier loss to its weight and bias.



For a general binary target, differentiate the full BCE expression from Chapter 8. Its probability derivative is \(-y/p+(1-y)/(1-p)\). Multiplying by \(p(1-p)\) gives \(-y(1-p)+(1-y)p\), which simplifies to:
\[
\frac{dL}{dz}=p-y
\tag{10.6}\]
This explains the result \(p-y\) rather than assuming it. With \(p=0.8\), a positive target gives \(-0.2\) and a negative target gives \(0.8\). A confidently wrong probability of 0.95 for target 0 gives derivative 0.95, despite sigmoid’s small local slope there. The isolated probability function did not determine the complete learning signal.
A value can affect several later operations. The complete derivative then adds the contributions of all paths:
\[
\operatorname{grad}_{x}=\sum_{\text{paths }p}\operatorname{contribution}_{p}
\tag{10.7}\]
For example, contributions 2 and 5 sum to 7. This mathematical path sum is one meaning of gradient accumulation. Adding gradients from separate backward calls is a related storage behavior, discussed after the vector form of the chain rule.
crumbs: Part III: From error to learning

title: 10  Backpropagation
text:
10.3 Vector-Jacobian products
A layer can produce many output coordinates from many inputs. Differentiating each output independently would describe their relationships, but a scalar loss needs a particular weighted combination of them. A Jacobian arranges all local output-input derivatives into a matrix:
\[
J_{i,j}=\frac{\partial y_{i}}{\partial x_{j}}
\tag{10.8}\]
For \(x\in\mathbb R^n\) and \(y=f(x)\in\mathbb R^m\), the Jacobian \(J\) has shape \([m,n]\). Row \(i\) describes output \(y_i\), and column \(j\) describes input \(x_j\).
Take \(y=(x_1+2x_2,3x_1-x_2)\). Its Jacobian is \(J=[[1,2],[3,-1]]\). Suppose the loss sensitivities to the two outputs are \((2,3)\). These are the upstream gradient, the rates already calculated for the outputs of this operation.
A vector-Jacobian product combines those sensitivities with the operation’s Jacobian:
\[
\frac{dL}{dx}=\frac{dL}{dy}\,J
\tag{10.9}\]
This equation uses row-vector gradients. Shapes \([1,m]\) and \([m,n]\) produce \([1,n]\). For the example, \((2,3)J=(2\times1+3\times3,2\times2+3\times(-1))=(11,1)\). The first input receives contributions 2 and 9 from the two output paths.
Writing that multiplication for one coordinate makes the path sum explicit:
\[
\frac{\partial L}{\partial x_{j}}=\sum_{i}\frac{\partial L}{\partial y_{i}}\,\frac{\partial y_{i}}{\partial x_{j}}
\tag{10.10}\]
The input coordinate \(j\) is fixed, while \(i\) ranges over output coordinates. For a diagonal Jacobian with diagonal \((1,4)\) and the same upstream gradient \((2,3)\), the result is \((2,12)\). These examples retain both cross-coordinate and independent-coordinate cases.
Reverse-mode differentiation begins with output sensitivities and applies these products toward the inputs. A local backward operation can often compute the product directly, without materializing every entry of the full Jacobian. This is particularly useful when one scalar loss depends on many parameters.
The categorical loss provides another example. For softmax, \(\partial p_i/\partial z_j=p_i(\delta_{ij}-p_j)\), where \(\delta_{ij}\) is 1 when the indices are equal and 0 otherwise. Differentiating the observed-target cross-entropy gives \(-\sum_i y_i(\delta_{ij}-p_j)\). Because the target indicators sum to 1, the result is \(p_j-y_j\).
For probabilities \((0.7,0.2,0.1)\) and target class 0, the logit gradient is \((-0.3,0.2,0.1)\). Its dimensions match the three logits. Treating logits as independently adjustable values, gradient descent would raise the target logit and lower its competitors. A real parameter update combines shared paths and examples, so it need not move every logit exactly as an independent update would.
The mathematics now specifies what each reverse operation must return. Automatic differentiation manages that computation and its stored values.

title: 10  Backpropagation
text:
10.4 Automatic differentiation
Writing a derivative for every parameter by hand becomes impractical as the graph grows. Automatic differentiation evaluates the chain rule through the actual sequence of differentiable operations. Backpropagation is this reverse calculation applied to a model’s computation graph. It computes gradients, while an optimizer later uses them to change parameters.
PyTorch’s autograd system records relevant operations when gradient tracking is enabled. A leaf tensor is a tensor that begins a tracked computation rather than resulting from another tracked operation. Parameters are usually leaves with requires_grad=True. A non-leaf result can carry a grad_fn referring to the operation needed for its backward calculation.
For an input batch \(X\) of shape \([B,D]\) and parameter \(w\) of shape \([D,H]\), an intermediate result can have shape \([B,H]\). Such an intermediate output is also called an activation. A reduced loss is scalar, and the gradient computed for \(w\) has shape \([D,H]\).
The backward pass traverses the dependencies in reverse and sums contributions before continuing to earlier values. This differs from computing another forward prediction.
The common scalar call loss.backward() begins with sensitivity 1 for the loss itself. If the output contains several values, a caller must supply an upstream tensor specifying their weighted combination. That is a vector-Jacobian product, rather than an unexplained requirement that every differentiable output be scalar.
By default, leaf parameters receive accumulated derivatives in their .grad buffers. Intermediate derivatives are used during computation, but their .grad fields are not necessarily retained. The graph and the gradient buffer are separate objects with different lifetimes.
The runnable example below differentiates \(3x^2+1\) at \(x=2\). The first backward pass yields 12. A second backward pass through the already-consumed graph fails because saved intermediates have been freed. A fresh forward computation creates a new graph, whose derivative is then added to the existing buffer, producing 24.
The figure separates the recorded operations from the leaf gradient buffer.






Figure 10.3: The operation graph computes derivatives, while a leaf gradient buffer stores their accumulated result.




Code example: A scalar loss creates gradients on tensors that require them.

import torch

x = torch.tensor(2.0, requires_grad=True)
result = 3 * x ** 2 + 1
result.backward()
assert x.grad.item() == 12.0
print(x.grad.item())

try:
    result.backward()
except RuntimeError:
    print("The consumed graph needs a new forward calculation.")
else:
    raise AssertionError("Expected this graph's saved values to be unavailable")

fresh_result = 3 * x ** 2 + 1
fresh_result.backward()
assert x.grad.item() == 24.0
print(x.grad.item())

x.grad = None
(3 * x ** 2 + 1).backward()
assert x.grad.item() == 12.0
print(x.grad.item())
Clearing x.grad prepares its buffer for another independent derivative. It does not recreate the old graph. Conversely, explicitly retaining a graph preserves saved values but does not clear its accumulated gradients. These controls solve different problems.
The operation detach() breaks a tensor’s connection to earlier tracked operations. A torch.no_grad() context prevents recording operations performed inside it. In-place changes can also invalidate values required by backward. Use those controls deliberately when defining which paths should contribute, rather than treating a missing gradient as an optimizer problem.
The forward pass may retain intermediate values for the backward pass, or a training method may recompute them later. This creates a memory cost beyond the parameter arrays themselves. For small models, interpreter overhead and data movement can dominate. Larger tensor operations may instead be limited by arithmetic or memory throughput, so the bottleneck must be measured.

title: 10  Backpropagation
text:
10.5 One training step
The gradients describe local loss changes. Gradient descent subtracts a scaled gradient from the current parameters:
\[
\theta_{\mathrm{new}} = \theta - \eta\,\nabla_{\theta}L(\theta)
\tag{10.11}\]
The positive scalar \(\eta\) is the learning rate, and \(\theta\) collects the parameters. For \(\theta=1\), gradient 3, and \(\eta=0.1\), the next value is \(1-0.1\times3=0.7\). The negative gradient is the steepest first-order decrease direction under the usual Euclidean length constraint. A finite step still needs a suitable scale and does not guarantee a global solution.
For one weight, the same update is:
\[
w_{\mathrm{next}}=w-\mathrm{lr}\,\frac{dL}{dw}
\tag{10.12}\]
The symbol lr denotes the learning rate in this form. The update is a separate operation after the gradient has been calculated.
Complete the running three-example classifier. Its probabilities are approximately \([0.71095,0.45017,0.64566]\) and targets are \([1,0,1]\). The per-example logit differences are \([-0.28905,0.45017,-0.35434]\). Because the objective is a mean, each contributes one third of its local derivative.
The weight gradient is \(X^\top(p-y)/3\). Its first coordinate is \((-0.28905-0.35434)/3\approx-0.21446\). Its second is \((0.45017-0.35434)/3\approx0.03194\). The bias gradient is their three-example mean, approximately \(-0.06441\).
With learning rate 0.1, weights \([0.8,-0.3]\) become approximately \([0.82145,-0.30319]\), and bias 0.1 becomes 0.10644. Recomputing the scores gives approximately \([0.92789,-0.19675,0.62469]\). The mean loss falls from about 0.45893 to 0.45386 for this batch and step. That observed decrease verifies this example, rather than proving every future step must decrease loss.
The runnable code below compares autograd with the analytical gradients before applying the update. torch.no_grad() keeps the parameter assignment outside the next gradient graph. The example recomputes the loss after the update instead of interpreting the old loss value as a new measurement.

Code example: Analytical and automatic gradients for the same three-example batch

import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F

X = torch.tensor([[1.0, 0.0], [0.0, 1.0], [1.0, 1.0]], dtype=torch.float64)
y = torch.tensor([1.0, 0.0, 1.0], dtype=torch.float64)
w = torch.tensor([0.8, -0.3], dtype=torch.float64, requires_grad=True)
b = torch.tensor(0.1, dtype=torch.float64, requires_grad=True)
logits = X @ w + b
loss = F.binary_cross_entropy_with_logits(logits, y)
error = logits.detach().sigmoid() - y
expected_w = X.T @ error / len(y)
expected_b = error.mean()
loss.backward()
assert torch.allclose(w.grad, expected_w)
assert torch.allclose(b.grad, expected_b)
print(loss.item(), w.grad.tolist(), b.grad.item())

with torch.no_grad():
    w -= 0.1 * w.grad
    b -= 0.1 * b.grad
    after = F.binary_cross_entropy_with_logits(X @ w + b, y)
    assert after < loss
    print(w.tolist(), b.item(), after.item())
w.grad = None
b.grad = None
The same method applies to a two-feature example with \(x=[2,-1]\), \(w=[0.5,-0.3]\), \(b=0.1\), and target 1. Its score is \(2(0.5)+(-1)(-0.3)+0.1=1.4\). Using unrounded values, sigmoid gives about 0.80218 and the loss is about 0.22042.
Its logit derivative is \(p-1\approx-0.19782\). Multiplying by the two inputs gives weight derivatives \([-0.39563,0.19782]\), while the bias derivative is \(-0.19782\). At learning rate 0.1, the new weights are approximately \([0.53956,-0.31978]\) and the new bias is 0.11978. Use unrounded intermediate values when checking the step, because rounding a probability before taking its logarithm changes later displayed decimals.
An optimizer step performs the parameter change using gradient buffers and any additional optimizer state. It receives gradients on parameters, rather than raw examples. A typical loop clears previous gradients, computes predictions and loss, calls backward, and then takes an optimizer step. Clearing immediately after the step can also be valid if the intended accumulation boundary remains explicit.
The complete map now separates the training branch from inference. Targets enter the loss calculation independently of the model’s input, and the optimizer follows gradient computation.






Figure 10.4: Training uses targets and gradients to change the model. Inference uses its scores with fixed parameters.



For a library-managed loop, optimizer.zero_grad() prepares the buffers and optimizer.step() applies the update. With set_to_none=True, clearing can leave a buffer absent until a later backward pass supplies it. This is distinct from storing a tensor of zeros, which some update rules treat differently.
The loss surface also limits what an update can guarantee. A convex function never lies above the straight-line interpolation between any two points in its domain. For a differentiable convex objective, a zero gradient identifies a global minimum when such a point exists. This property alone does not make every learning rate converge.
For \(f(w)=w^2\), gradient descent gives \(w_{t+1}=(1-2\eta)w_t\). Its magnitude shrinks when \(0<\eta<1\). At \(\eta=1\), the sign alternates without shrinking. Larger values can make the iterates grow even though the function is convex.
Practical stopping rules include an update budget, small changes in loss or parameters, and validation-based early stopping. A small gradient can also occur near a saddle point or a saturated region. Use the loss history and held-out behavior alongside local derivative size. Section 24.1 compares convex and nonconvex surfaces explicitly.
The following additional runnable example retains the column-shaped binary interface: input \([32,4]\), targets \([32,1]\), weights \([4,1]\), and bias \([1]\). It uses random data to demonstrate shapes and buffer handling. It makes no claim about useful model quality.

Code example: A minimal binary logistic regression step.

import torch

torch.manual_seed(7)

X = torch.randn(32, 4)
y = torch.randint(0, 2, (32, 1)).float()
w = torch.randn(4, 1, requires_grad=True)
b = torch.zeros(1, requires_grad=True)

logits = X @ w + b
loss = torch.nn.functional.binary_cross_entropy_with_logits(logits, y)
loss.backward()
assert w.grad.shape == (4, 1)
assert b.grad.shape == (1,)

with torch.no_grad():
    w -= 0.1 * w.grad
    b -= 0.1 * b.grad
    w.grad.zero_()
    b.grad.zero_()
The weight and bias gradients have shapes \([4,1]\) and \([1]\). The no-grad block changes the parameters and clears both buffers. Using nn.Linear(D,1) with an appropriate stable BCE loss supplies the same model interface. The next chapter compares update rules and their additional state.
crumbs: Part III: From error to learning

title: 10  Backpropagation
text:
10.6 Accumulating a larger batch
A desired batch may require more intermediate storage than the device can hold at once. A microbatch is a smaller group processed as part of one intended batch. Gradient accumulation can combine their contributions before a single optimizer step.
Suppose the intended batch contains the same three examples, split into groups of one and two. To obtain the full-batch mean gradient, divide each group’s sum of losses by 3 before its backward pass. The first contributes one example’s share and the second contributes two. Taking an unweighted mean of the two group means would instead give the lone first example half the total weight.
An equivalent rule weights each microbatch mean by its valid-example count divided by the total valid count. For token losses, count supervised tokens rather than padded positions. Parameters must remain fixed until all the intended contributions have accumulated.
The runnable check compares a full-batch gradient with the accumulated gradients from those unequal groups. Each group receives a fresh forward graph, while the parameter buffers retain the sum. Only after the comparison would an optimizer step be taken.

Code example: Unequal microbatches retain the full-batch mean gradient

import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F

X = torch.tensor([[1.0, 0.0], [0.0, 1.0], [1.0, 1.0]], dtype=torch.float64)
y = torch.tensor([1.0, 0.0, 1.0], dtype=torch.float64)
w = torch.tensor([0.8, -0.3], dtype=torch.float64, requires_grad=True)
b = torch.tensor(0.1, dtype=torch.float64, requires_grad=True)
F.binary_cross_entropy_with_logits(X @ w + b, y).backward()
full_w, full_b = w.grad.clone(), b.grad.clone()
w.grad = None
b.grad = None

for start, stop in [(0, 1), (1, 3)]:
    logits = X[start:stop] @ w + b
    partial = F.binary_cross_entropy_with_logits(logits, y[start:stop], reduction="sum") / len(y)
    partial.backward()

assert torch.allclose(w.grad, full_w)
assert torch.allclose(b.grad, full_b)
print(w.grad.tolist(), b.grad.item())
The gradients agree to numerical precision because the per-example computation and parameter values are the same. A layer whose output depends on the other examples in its batch can break that equivalence. Random operations and differing numerical execution can also change exact results, so the assumptions belong with the comparison.
This distinction completes the training mechanism: a graph determines derivatives, buffers accumulate them, and an update rule changes parameters at a stated boundary. We can now compare those update rules without treating gradients as unexplained inputs.

Chapter checkpoint
A second call to backward fails after the first graph has been consumed. Would clearing parameter gradients recreate that graph? When combining microbatches of one and two examples into a three-example mean, how should their losses be weighted?
Feedback: Clearing a gradient buffer does not recreate saved operations. Recompute the forward graph, or retain it deliberately when the task requires reuse. Divide each microbatch’s summed losses by 3, or weight its mean by its share of the three examples. Take one parameter step after all contributions are accumulated.

title: 11  Momentum and AdamW
text:
11.1 Gradient estimates
Backpropagation has supplied a gradient for each relevant parameter. A training procedure must now decide how far to move and whether previous gradients should influence that step. Different choices can change convergence, memory use, and behavior on held-out examples.
This chapter compares update rules using explicit state and arithmetic. It then separates parameter penalties, learning-rate schedules, and gradient clipping, which affect different parts of the training procedure.
The basic gradient-descent step uses the derivative of a stated objective. Computing it from every training example before each update can be expensive. Full-batch gradient descent uses the whole training set, stochastic gradient descent uses one sampled example, and mini-batch gradient descent uses a group of examples. In common software terminology, SGD also includes mini-batch updates.
For a batch index set \(B\), average its per-example gradients:
\[
g_B=\frac{1}{\lvert B\rvert}\sum_{i\in B}\operatorname{grad}L_i(\theta)
\tag{11.1}\]
The cardinality \(|B|\) is its number of examples, and \(L_i\) is the loss for example \(i\) at the current parameters \(\theta\). With individual gradients \([1,3]\) and \([-1,5]\), the batch gradient is \(([1,3]+[-1,5])/2=[0,4]\).
Under representative sampling, a mini-batch gradient estimates the full empirical-risk gradient. Its value varies with the sampled examples. Increasing batch size generally reduces that sampling variation under comparable conditions, while increasing intermediate storage and changing the number of updates per pass through the dataset.
The update uses that estimate:
\[
\theta_{t+1}=\theta_t-\eta\,\operatorname{grad}L(\theta_t)
\tag{11.2}\]
The index \(t\) counts parameter updates, and \(\eta\) is the learning rate. The formula matches the earlier basic step. Parameter 1 with gradient 3 and learning rate 0.1 becomes 0.7. A larger step can overshoot and increase the loss. A small step may require many updates before the loss changes appreciably.
The figure follows one parameter from its current value through a gradient step. The update moves opposite to the gradient direction, with its size set by the learning rate.
The runnable PyTorch example uses the same three-example classifier as Chapter 10. Creating torch.optim.SGD replaces the manual parameter assignment with a library-managed step. The forward, backward, and buffer-clearing mechanics remain those already derived.
The printed loss is the value calculated before the step. The printed parameters are their values after it. Plain SGD in this configuration uses the current gradient without a persistent momentum or squared-gradient buffer. Adding history changes that behavior.

title: 11  Momentum and AdamW
text:
Figure 11.2: The learning rate scales the parameter update opposite to the gradient direction.





Code example: One optimizer step on the running logistic-regression batch

import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F

X = torch.tensor([[1.0, 0.0], [0.0, 1.0], [1.0, 1.0]])
y = torch.tensor([1.0, 0.0, 1.0])
w = torch.tensor([0.8, -0.3], requires_grad=True)
b = torch.tensor(0.1, requires_grad=True)
optimizer = torch.optim.SGD([w, b], lr=0.1)

optimizer.zero_grad()
loss = F.binary_cross_entropy_with_logits(X @ w + b, y)
loss.backward()
optimizer.step()

print(loss.item(), w.detach(), b.detach())
