title: 15  Recurrent networks
text:
15.1 Sequence outputs
The order of words can change a sentence’s meaning even when its token counts remain identical. A sequence model needs a way to retain information about earlier positions. We begin with a fixed history, then replace that explicit suffix with a learned state.
The progression concerns how a prediction uses context. It also exposes a limitation: a compact recurrent state requires a sequence of dependent updates. The attention mechanism in Chapter 16 will offer a different way to connect positions.
Pooling static embeddings loses order, as Section 13.3 demonstrated. Before choosing an order-sensitive model, establish which outputs the task requires. Different output arrangements lead to different targets and inference procedures.
A sequence acceptor reads an input sequence and returns one decision, such as a review’s sentiment. Sequence labeling returns one label for each input position. A sequence transducer maps an input sequence to an output sequence, whose length need not match the input.
Translation is a transduction task. Token tagging is an aligned case with one label per position. Neither term specifies whether the implementation uses recurrence or attention.
An autoregressive model, introduced in Section 1.2, predicts each output token from an available prefix. Its outputs become inputs to subsequent predictions during generation.
For a batch of \(B\) sequences, one classification target per sequence has shape \([B]\). Tagging \(T\) positions requires targets shaped \([B,T]\). A generated sequence needs its own output length and stopping rule, as in Chapter 7.
These requirements determine which information must reach each prediction. The simplest language-model baseline stores only a short suffix of the preceding text.

title: 15  Recurrent networks
text: Figure 15.2: Sequence tasks differ in the number and alignment of their outputs.

title: 15  Recurrent networks
text:
15.2 Fixed histories
The full next-token distribution conditions on every earlier token. Many exact prefixes occur only once, making direct counting impractical. An n-gram model reduces the history to the most recent \(n-1\) tokens.
This Markov assumption treats that suffix as sufficient for the next prediction.
\[
P(x_{t}\mid x_{<t})\approx P\!\left(x_{t}\mid x_{t-n+1},\ldots,x_{t-1}\right)
\tag{15.1}\]
A bigram model uses one preceding token. A trigram uses two. For example, a trigram approximates \(P(\text{sat}\mid\text{the cat slept})\) by \(P(\text{sat}\mid\text{cat slept})\). It has no way to distinguish earlier prefixes that end with the same two tokens.
Training starts by counting complete history-and-next-token events. For the sentences “cat sat”, “cat sat”, and “cat ate”, insert explicit start and end markers. Each sentence then contributes adjacent bigrams such as \((\text{START},\text{cat})\), \((\text{cat},\text{sat})\), and \((\text{sat},\text{END})\).
The history “cat” has three observed successors: “sat” twice and “ate” once. Maximum-likelihood estimation, or MLE, assigns each successor its observed relative frequency.
\[
P(w_t\mid\mathrm{context})=\frac{\operatorname{count}(\mathrm{context},w_t)}{\operatorname{count}(\mathrm{context})}
\tag{15.2}\]
The denominator counts the successor events for that history. Thus \(P(\text{sat}\mid\text{cat})=2/3\) and \(P(\text{ate}\mid\text{cat})=1/3\). In a separate count row with three occurrences of one continuation among ten events, its probability is \(3/10=0.3\).
Boundary handling matters because the model must represent sentence starts and ends consistently. For higher orders, left padding can supply \(n-1\) start markers. A marker contributes a model event, rather than ordinary article text. Split the corpus before counting to keep evaluation examples out of the estimated probabilities.
The MLE assigns zero probability to an unseen successor under a seen history. A completely unseen history has denominator zero, so the frequency ratio alone does not define its distribution. A vocabulary policy and a fallback rule are necessary before evaluating arbitrary text.
An unknown token collects items excluded from the training vocabulary. Replacing rare training words with that token lets the model estimate events involving it. Merely defining an unknown ID does not create any observed counts for it.
Smoothing reserves probability for events absent from the counts. As a book extension, consider add-alpha smoothing, which adds a positive pseudocount \(\alpha\) to every allowed successor. For history \(h\), the estimate becomes \(P(w\mid h)=[C(h,w)+\alpha]/[C(h)+\alpha|V_{\text{out}}|]\).
Here \(V_{\text{out}}\) is a fixed output vocabulary. With observed successor counts \((2,1,0,0)\) and \(\alpha=1\), the denominator is \(3+4=7\). The probabilities become \((3/7,2/7,1/7,1/7)\) and sum to one.
The unobserved events can now be scored, but probability has been removed from the observed events. A large pseudocount can overwhelm limited data. Backoff instead uses a shorter history when a longer one lacks sufficient evidence. These are modeling choices whose effects require held-out evaluation.
The NLTK experiment in Section 24.3 develops the complete count, score, generation, and persistence workflow. The source notebook requires the MLE procedure and lists smoothing as optional reading. The smoothing calculation here explains an important limitation before we move beyond fixed histories.
Increasing \(n\) exposes more context but creates more possible histories and sparser observations. A learned state offers a different trade-off: it compresses earlier information into a fixed-width vector.

title: 15  Recurrent networks
text:
15.3 Updating recurrent state
A fixed suffix discards everything outside its window. A recurrent neural network, or RNN, instead updates a hidden state as it reads each input. The state can depend on the whole preceding sequence, subject to what its learned update retains.
An RNN cell is the repeated function that combines the current input vector \(x_t\) with the previous state \(h_{t-1}\). In this section, \(x_t\) denotes a floating-point input vector, not the integer token ID used in the n-gram equations.
\[
h_{t}=\phi(W_{x}x_{t}+W_{h}h_{t-1}+b)
\tag{15.3}\]
For input width \(d\) and state width \(H\), \(W_x\) has shape \([H,d]\) and \(W_h\) has shape \([H,H]\). The bias and state have \(H\) coordinates. The same matrices are reused at every step, and \(h_0\) supplies the initial state.
The activation \(\phi\) makes this a nonlinear transition, following Chapter 12. A common choice is \(\tanh\), whose output lies between \(-1\) and \(1\).
For a scalar calculation with identity activation, let \(W_x=2\), \(W_h=0.5\), \(x_t=3\), \(h_{t-1}=4\), and \(b=0\). The next state is \(2(3)+0.5(4)=8\). With both weights equal to one, \(x_t=2\) and \(h_{t-1}=1\) instead produce preactivation 3. A \(\tanh\) activation would turn that preactivation into approximately \(0.9951\).
A two-coordinate example shows the same operation without collapsing the state to a scalar. Set \(x_t=(1,0)\), \(h_{t-1}=(0.5,-0.5)\), \(W_x=I\), \(W_h=0.2I\), and \(b=0\). The preactivation is \((1.1,-0.1)\), giving \(h_t\approx(0.800499,-0.099668)\) after \(\tanh\).
The new state can supply an output immediately. A language-model head maps it to one logit per vocabulary item.
\[
z_{t}=W_{y}h_{t}+b_{y}
\tag{15.4}\]
Here \(W_y\) has shape \([|V|,H]\), \(b_y\) has \(|V|\) coordinates, and \(z_t\) has shape \([|V|]\). For \(h_t=(1,2)\), identity output weights and zero bias give logits \((1,2)\). No extra activation is needed before the stable cross-entropy loss.
For a batch, inputs have shape \([B,T,d]\) and the stored states have shape \([B,T,H]\). A vocabulary head produces logits \([B,T,|V|]\). A tagging head instead uses its label count as the final axis. An acceptor can use a final valid state for one decision.
The recurrence creates a new dependency at every position. Training must assign each error to all the shared parameter uses that contributed to it.

title: 15  Recurrent networks
text:
15.4 Gradients through time
Backpropagation already handles a chain of operations, as Chapter 10 established. Backpropagation through time, or BPTT, applies it to the recurrent cell repeated across sequence positions. Unrolling makes each parameter use visible while retaining one shared parameter tensor.
A loss at the final position depends on earlier states through every intervening transition. For the scalar recurrence \(h_t=\rho h_{t-1}+x_t\), its derivative with respect to a state ten steps earlier is \(\rho^{10}\). If \(\rho=0.5\), that factor is about \(0.000977\). If \(\rho=1.5\), it is about \(57.67\).
A vanishing gradient becomes too small to carry an effective learning signal along this path. An exploding gradient grows excessively. With nonlinear cells, local activation derivatives also enter the product. Matrix transitions can amplify some directions while shrinking others.
Gradient clipping from Section 11.7 bounds a large computed gradient. It does not restore an earlier signal that has already vanished. Truncated BPTT limits the backward path to a chosen segment, usually by detaching the carried state between segments. The state values can continue forward even though later gradients cannot cross that boundary.
For next-token training, teacher forcing supplies the observed previous token as the next decoder input. Writing that input ID as \(u_t\) gives:
\[
u_{t}=x_{t-1}^{\mathrm{gold}}
\tag{15.5}\]
The superscript “gold” identifies the recorded target sequence. An embedding lookup converts \(u_t\) to the floating-point vector consumed by the recurrent cell. The shift, validity mask, and token-loss reduction follow Section 1.2 and Section 8.2.
Generation supplies the model’s selected token instead. Exposure bias describes the resulting difference between observed training prefixes and self-generated prefixes. An early incorrect token can change later inputs and states. Decoding choices remain those in Chapter 7.
Repeated state transformations make retaining information difficult. A gated cell adds a more direct path for carrying selected values forward.

title: 15  Recurrent networks
text:
15.5 Gated memory
A plain RNN transforms its entire state at every step. Long short-term memory, or LSTM, separates a carried cell state \(c_t\) from the exposed hidden state \(h_t\). Learned gates control how much information each coordinate retains, adds, and exposes.
A gate is a vector of sigmoid values between zero and one. The forget gate \(f_t\) controls retained cell content. The input gate \(i_t\) controls the new candidate, and the output gate \(o_t\) controls the exposed state.
Each gate combines the current input with the previous hidden state, using its own matrix and bias.
\[
\begin{aligned} i_{t}&=\sigma(W_{i}x_{t}+U_{i}h_{t-1}+b_{i}),\\ f_{t}&=\sigma(W_{f}x_{t}+U_{f}h_{t-1}+b_{f}),\\ o_{t}&=\sigma(W_{o}x_{t}+U_{o}h_{t-1}+b_{o}) \end{aligned}
\tag{15.6}\]
For hidden width \(H\), the input matrices have shape \([H,d]\) and the recurrent matrices have shape \([H,H]\). Concatenating \(x_t\) with \(h_{t-1}\) and joining the matrices gives an equivalent single affine calculation. A gate preactivation of zero produces sigmoid value \(0.5\).
The candidate \(g_t\) proposes new cell content through \(\tanh\). The symbol \(\odot\) means coordinatewise multiplication. The complete state update is:
\[
\begin{aligned} g_{t}&=\tanh(W_{g}x_{t}+U_{g}h_{t-1}+b_{g}),\\ c_{t}&=f_{t}\odot c_{t-1}+i_{t}\odot g_{t},\\ h_{t}&=o_{t}\odot\tanh(c_{t}) \end{aligned}
\tag{15.7}\]
The forget term retains part of \(c_{t-1}\), and the input term adds part of \(g_t\). The output gate then selects how much of \(\tanh(c_t)\) becomes visible in \(h_t\). Gates can preserve one coordinate while replacing another.
For one coordinate, take \(c_{t-1}=0.5\), \(g_t=0.4\), \(f_t=0.8\), \(i_t=0.3\), and \(o_t=0.6\). Retained content is \(0.8(0.5)=0.4\), and new content is \(0.3(0.4)=0.12\). Thus \(c_t=0.52\) and \(h_t=0.6\tanh(0.52)\approx0.286620\).
In a separate half-open-gate example, \(f_t=i_t=o_t=0.5\), \(c_{t-1}=0\), and \(g_t=0.38\). The new cell value is \(0.19\), and the exposed state is \(0.5\tanh(0.19)\approx0.093873\).
Holding the gates fixed, the direct derivative of \(c_t\) with respect to \(c_{t-1}\) is \(f_t\). Values near one can preserve this part of the gradient across steps. Other paths pass through the gates’ dependencies, so an LSTM does not eliminate every gradient problem.
A gated recurrent unit, or GRU, uses update and reset gates without a separate cell-state tensor. It offers another controlled recurrent update with less carried state than an LSTM of the same width. Both still depend on the previous step.

title: 15  Recurrent networks
text:
15.6 Layers, directions, and cost
A gated cell defines one transition. A library layer applies it across a sequence and may stack several layers or run in both directions. These choices change the returned tensors and the information available to each output.
A deep recurrent network feeds one recurrent layer’s outputs into another. A bidirectional network combines a forward pass with a reverse pass. The latter uses later input positions, so it requires the relevant complete input sequence.
The following PyTorch example supplies two sequences with five steps and three input features. It uses two bidirectional LSTM layers, each with hidden width four. The example checks dimensions rather than training a predictor.

Code example: Deep bidirectional LSTM dimensions

import torch
import torch.nn as nn

torch.manual_seed(7)
batch, steps, input_width, hidden_width = 2, 5, 3, 4
inputs = torch.randn(batch, steps, input_width)

lstm = nn.LSTM(
    input_size=input_width,
    hidden_size=hidden_width,
    num_layers=2,
    batch_first=True,
    bidirectional=True,
)
outputs, (final_hidden, final_cell) = lstm(inputs)

print(outputs.shape)       # [batch, steps, 2 * hidden_width]
print(final_hidden.shape)  # [layers * directions, batch, hidden_width]
print(final_cell.shape)
assert outputs.shape == (2, 5, 8)
assert final_hidden.shape == final_cell.shape == (4, 2, 4)
The output shape is \([2,5,8]\): each position contains four coordinates from each direction of the top layer. The final hidden and cell tensors both have shape \([4,2,4]\). Their first axis combines two layers and two directions.
To obtain both completed directional states, use the final-state tensor. The reverse half of the output at the last input position has only begun its reverse traversal. It is not the completed reverse summary of the sequence.
For padded batches, select final valid positions or use an appropriate packed-sequence procedure. Processing padding as ordinary steps can change the returned state. Bidirectional processing also requires correct lengths when identifying each sequence’s boundaries.
Bidirectionality suits a complete-input classification or tagging task. It leaks future information in causal next-token generation. An encoder may read a complete source sequence bidirectionally while a separate output generator remains causal.
Recurrence has a compact carried state, but its critical path contains \(T\) dependent updates for \(T\) positions. Training also stores intermediate values for backward computation unless recomputation or truncation changes that requirement. Increasing the state width adds matrix operations and parameters at every step.
The character-model experiment in Section 24.4 connects these output shapes to training and generation. Its prefixes and decoding comparisons test how the carried state affects later predictions.
Attention changes the connection between positions: a query can directly combine information from several permitted sources. Chapter 16 develops that calculation and its different memory costs.

Chapter checkpoint
A trigram assigns identical predictions to two different paragraphs. Their last two tokens match. Is more training data sufficient to make its predictions differ?
Feedback: More counts can refine the shared conditional distribution, but the model still uses the same two-token history for both paragraphs. Distinguishing their earlier context requires changing the representation of history.
A bidirectional LSTM achieves unusually low next-token loss. Which dependency would you inspect before accepting the result?
Feedback: Check whether reverse states include the target or later tokens. A causal predictor must exclude that information. Compare it with a unidirectional model under the same valid-token loss and data split.

title: 16  Attention mathematics
text:
16.1 Preparing attention vectors
A recurrent state carries earlier information through every intervening update. Attention gives an output position a more direct connection to several source positions. It calculates a separate weight for each permitted source, then combines their vectors.
The calculation has three stages: prepare comparison and content vectors, normalize their scores, and form a weighted sum. Visibility rules belong inside that calculation because they determine which information may affect the result.
Suppose the representation at “sat” needs information from the sequence “The cat sat”. Instead of compressing every earlier position into one recurrent state, attention can compare the current position with each available source.
A query is the vector used for one output position’s comparisons. A key is a source vector used in those comparisons. A value is the source content that the resulting weights combine. Query and key widths must match, while value width may differ.
Learned projection matrices transform input vectors into these three roles. For input matrix \(X\) with one token per row, the projections are:
\[
Q=XW_{Q}
\tag{16.1}\]
\[
K=XW_{K}
\tag{16.2}\]
\[
V=XW_{V}
\tag{16.3}\]
Here \(X\) has shape \([T,D]\), with \(T\) token positions and input width \(D\). The projection shapes determine query/key width \(d_k\) and value width \(d_v\).
\[
W_{Q}\in\mathbb{R}^{D\times d_{k}},\quad W_{K}\in\mathbb{R}^{D\times d_{k}},\quad W_{V}\in\mathbb{R}^{D\times d_{v}}
\tag{16.4}\]
Consequently, \(Q\) and \(K\) have shape \([T,d_k]\), while \(V\) has shape \([T,d_v]\). These are values computed for the current input. The projection matrices are parameters shared across inputs and updated through the task loss.
For a fully specified example, let the three input rows be \((1,0,0)\), \((0,1,0)\), and \((0,0,1)\). Choose projection matrices whose rows are the vectors in the following table. Multiplying by these inputs selects each corresponding row.
These hand-selected vectors demonstrate arithmetic, rather than learned English relationships. We will follow the third query through the score, normalization, output, and mask calculations without changing its input values.

title: 16  Attention mathematics
text:
16.2 Scores and weighted values
The prepared vectors define what will be compared and combined. Scaled dot-product attention compares a query with every key, dividing each dot product by \(\sqrt{d_k}\).
\[
\mathrm{scores}=\frac{QK^{T}}{\sqrt{d_{k}}}
\tag{16.5}\]
An individual score is:
\[
\operatorname{score}_{i,j}=\frac{q_i\cdot k_j}{\sqrt{d_k}}
\tag{16.6}\]
The score matrix has one row per query and one column per key. For the third query above, all three dot products equal one: each key matches one nonzero query coordinate. Since \(d_k=4\), its scaled score row is \((0.5,0.5,0.5)\).
Scaling controls the typical score magnitude. If query and key coordinates are independent, zero-mean, and unit-variance, their dot product has variance \(d_k\). Division by \(\sqrt{d_k}\) returns that variance to one. Learned vectors need not satisfy these assumptions exactly, so scaling does not guarantee unsaturated scores.
An attention weight is a normalized coefficient produced by applying softmax across the keys in one query row. An attention matrix \(A\) contains all those rows. The softmax mechanics are established in Chapter 6.
Equal scores \((0.5,0.5,0.5)\) produce weights \((1/3,1/3,1/3)\). Their exponentials are all approximately \(1.648721\), and each is divided by their sum, approximately \(4.946164\).
The attention output combines value vectors using those weights.
\[
O=AV
\tag{16.7}\]
Equivalently, one output row is:
\[
\operatorname{out}_i=\sum_j\alpha_{i,j}v_j
\tag{16.8}\]
For the third position, \(o_3=(v_1+v_2+v_3)/3=(1/3,1/3,1/3,1/3)\). The resulting four-coordinate vector contains contributions from all three sources.






Figure 16.2: Scaled query-key scores become attention weights. The third row averages three four-coordinate values.



Before any attention dropout, nonnegative weights sum to one over the permitted sources. The result is a convex combination, meaning a weighted average with those constraints. Later output projections can change its range and coordinates.
Changing a query changes this combination. Hold the keys and values fixed, but replace \(q_3\) with \((2,0,0,0)\). Raw scores become \((2,0,2)\) and scaled scores become \((1,0,1)\). Softmax produces approximately \((0.422319,0.155362,0.422319)\), giving output \((0.422319,0.155362,0.422319,0.422319)\).
The first and third sources now receive more weight. This controlled change isolates the query’s role. Replacing an actual input token can change its query, key, and value together, depending on the projections.






Figure 16.3: Changing one query shifts attention weights while the keys and values remain fixed.



A separate two-key case illustrates score sharpness. With \(q=(1,0)\), \(k_1=(1,0)\), \(k_2=(0,2)\), and \(d_k=2\), the scaled scores are \((1/\sqrt2,0)\). Their weights are approximately \((0.669762,0.330238)\).
For values \((10,0)\) and \((0,2)\), that row gives output approximately \((6.69762,0.660477)\). If a different query instead produces scaled scores \((2,0)\), its weights are approximately \((0.880797,0.119203)\). The same values then produce \((8.80797,0.238406)\).
These are different score rows, so they yield different mixtures. The softmax axis also matters: normalizing across queries would make output positions compete with one another, rather than distributing each query’s weight across its sources.
The following independent two-coordinate example uses three queries and keys. It prints row sums and context vectors, then plots a heatmap with query rows and key columns.

Code example: Scaled dot-product attention and a token-to-token heatmap

import math
import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import seaborn as sns

tokens = ["the", "cat", "sat"]
Q = torch.tensor([[1.0, 0.0], [0.0, 1.0], [1.0, 1.0]])
K = torch.tensor([[1.0, 0.0], [0.0, 1.0], [1.0, 1.0]])
V = torch.tensor([[2.0, 0.0], [0.0, 2.0], [1.0, 1.0]])

scores = Q @ K.T / math.sqrt(Q.shape[-1])
weights = F.softmax(scores, dim=-1)
context = weights @ V

print(weights.sum(dim=-1), context)
sns.heatmap(
    weights.numpy(),
    xticklabels=tokens,
    yticklabels=tokens,
    annot=True,
)
plt.xlabel("key position")
plt.ylabel("query position")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.savefig("attention-three-token-heatmap.png", dpi=160)
plt.close()
assert torch.allclose(weights.sum(dim=-1), torch.ones(3))
assert context.shape == (3, 2)
Each row sums to one, and the context matrix has shape \([3,2]\). To inspect the plot, choose one query row and compare its key weights. A large weight describes one intermediate contribution. It does not establish a complete explanation for a model’s final prediction.
The calculation so far allows every source. A causal or padded input requires explicit exclusions before normalization.

title: 16  Attention mathematics
text:
16.3 Visibility masks
A next-token predictor must not use the answer while constructing its prediction. An attention mask specifies which key positions each query may read. A causal mask excludes future positions, and a padding mask excludes positions that do not belong to the input.
For aligned query and key positions, an additive causal mask is:
\[
M_{i,j}=\begin{cases}-\infty,&j>i,\\0,&\text{otherwise.}\end{cases}
\tag{16.9}\]
The mask contributes zero to allowed scores and negative infinity to excluded scores. Thus query position \(i=2\) cannot read key position \(j=4\). Combining this mask with the score matrix gives the normalized weights:
\[
A=\operatorname{softmax}\!\left(\frac{QK^{T}}{\sqrt{d_{k}}}+M\right)
\tag{16.10}\]
For finite allowed scores, \(\exp(-\infty)=0\) makes an excluded key’s weight zero. Masking after softmax would leave the retained weights incorrectly normalized unless they were normalized again.
In the three-token example, the third query can read all three positions. To test a real exclusion, also declare the second key invalid. Its score row becomes \((0.5,-\infty,0.5)\), its weights become \((0.5,0,0.5)\), and its output becomes \((0.5,0,0.5,0.5)\).
The value at the excluded second position can change without affecting that output. The following code verifies the original uniform result, causal exclusions, and this padding exclusion. It also rejects a query with no valid keys.

Code example: Causal and padding exclusions in the three-token calculation

import math
import torch

X = torch.eye(3)
WQ = torch.tensor([[1., 0., 0., 0.], [0., 1., 0., 0.], [1., 0., 1., 0.]])
WK = torch.tensor([[1., 1., 0., 0.], [0., 1., 1., 0.], [1., 0., 0., 1.]])
WV = torch.tensor([[1., 0., 0., 1.], [0., 1., 0., 0.], [0., 0., 1., 0.]])
Q, K, V = X @ WQ, X @ WK, X @ WV

def attend(q, k, v, allowed):
    if not torch.all(allowed.any(dim=-1)):
        raise ValueError("Every query must have an allowed key")
    scores = q @ k.T / math.sqrt(q.shape[-1])
    scores = scores.masked_fill(~allowed, float("-inf"))
    weights = torch.softmax(scores, dim=-1)
    return weights, weights @ v

causal = torch.ones(3, 3, dtype=torch.bool).tril()
weights, output = attend(Q, K, V, causal)
assert torch.allclose(output[2], torch.full((4,), 1/3))
assert torch.count_nonzero(weights.triu(1)) == 0

valid_keys = torch.tensor([True, False, True])
allowed = causal & valid_keys.unsqueeze(0)
weights, output = attend(Q, K, V, allowed)
assert torch.allclose(weights[2], torch.tensor([.5, 0., .5]))
assert torch.allclose(output[2], torch.tensor([.5, 0., .5, .5]))
changed_values = V.clone()
changed_values[1] = 1000.
assert torch.allclose(attend(Q, K, changed_values, allowed)[1], output)
print(weights, output)
try:
    attend(Q, K, V, torch.zeros_like(causal))
except ValueError:
    print("Rejected a query without a valid source")
else:
    raise AssertionError("All-masked rows must be rejected")
An all-masked row has no distribution to normalize. A basic softmax over only negative infinities produces invalid values. This implementation raises an error. Other systems may define a zero output, but that policy must be explicit and consistent with later layers.
With the shifted targets from Section 1.2, the representation at input position \(i\) predicts token \(i+1\). It may therefore read its own input and earlier inputs. Including the diagonal does not reveal the next-token target.
Causal masking allows a training sequence’s attention rows to be calculated together when all input tokens are supplied. During generation, the next input token is still unknown until the current prediction is selected. Masked parallel training does not remove that generation dependency.

title: 16  Attention mathematics
text:
16.4 Self-attention and cross-attention
The computation depends on queries, keys, values, and visibility. Their source determines whether information moves within one sequence or between two sequences.
In self-attention, the same representation sequence supplies \(Q\), \(K\), and \(V\). Bidirectional self-attention allows valid positions on either side of a query. Causal self-attention permits the current position and earlier positions, subject to other exclusions such as padding.
In cross-attention, queries come from the sequence being updated, while keys and values come from a separate source. If that source has \(T_k\) positions and the query sequence has \(T_q\) positions, the attention matrix is rectangular.
Object | Shape for one attention calculation | |—|—| | Query matrix \(Q\) | \([T_q,d_k]\) | | Key matrix \(K\) | \([T_k,d_k]\) | | Value matrix \(V\) | \([T_k,d_v]\) | | Scores and weights | \([T_q,T_k]\) | | Output \(O\) | \([T_q,d_v]\) |
Two target queries reading five source positions produce a \([2,5]\) weight matrix. Multiplying by five three-coordinate values produces a \([2,3]\) output. A batch adds the same leading batch axis to these objects.






Figure 16.4: Two target queries weight five source values, producing two output vectors with three coordinates each.



An encoded source sentence can supply keys and values for a generated translation. A multimodal model can use image representations as the source for text queries. The score and weighted-sum calculation remains the one established above.
There is no universal triangular cross-attention mask. The task determines which source positions are available. Chapter 18 compares these visibility choices across complete architectures.

title: 16  Attention mathematics
text:
16.5 Attention cost
Direct connections shorten the path between positions, but they create many pairwise comparisons. The number of query-key pairs is \(T_qT_k\). For full self-attention over \(T\) positions, it is \(T^2\).
\[
\mathrm{work}_{\mathrm{attention}}=\mathcal{O}(T^{2}d_{k}),\quad \mathrm{memory}_{\mathrm{scores}}=\mathcal{O}(T^{2})
\tag{16.11}\]
The score calculation performs a \(d_k\)-coordinate dot product for every pair. Mixing the values adds work proportional to \(T^2d_v\). Storing a complete score or weight matrix requires \(T^2\) entries per sequence for this single calculation.
Increasing \(T\) from 1,000 to 2,000 increases pair count from one million to four million. At four bytes per materialized score, those matrices require four and sixteen million bytes respectively. These figures exclude projections, values, gradients, and other model state.
Optimized attention kernels can process tiles and maintain normalization statistics without storing the entire score matrix. They preserve the mathematical attention result up to floating-point effects. This reduces memory traffic without eliminating the pairwise arithmetic of exact dense attention.
The cache used during generation is a separate storage concern, developed in Chapter 21. Chapter 17 first combines several attention calculations with positional information and feature transformations into a complete transformer block.

Chapter checkpoint
An excluded source receives zero weight, but the remaining weights sum to 0.7. What ordering error would you inspect?
Feedback: Check whether masking occurred after softmax. Excluding scores before normalization redistributes the full weight across allowed keys. A deliberate dropout step is a separate operation and needs separate interpretation.
A cross-attention layer has seven queries and eleven source values of width five. What output shape should it return, and which axis should softmax normalize?
Feedback: Its weight matrix is \([7,11]\), normalized across the eleven source positions. Its output is \([7,5]\), with one vector for each query.

title: 17  Transformer blocks
text:
17.1 Multiple attention heads
Attention combines information from permitted positions. A deep sequence model also needs to distinguish order, preserve useful signals, and transform the features at each position. A transformer block brings those operations together while keeping a consistent representation width.
We first develop its components, then follow their tensors through a complete layer. A final variant replaces one feature transformation with several selectively activated networks.
One attention calculation produces one set of source weights per query. Multi-head attention provides several such calculations, allowing different learned projections to combine source information in different ways.
An attention head has its own query, key, and value projections. Each head applies the score, mask, normalization, and value mixture from Chapter 16.
\[
\operatorname{head}_i=\operatorname{Attention}(XW_{Q,i},XW_{K,i},XW_{V,i})
\tag{17.1}\]
For model width \(D\) and \(H\) heads, a common configuration sets each head’s width to \(d_h=D/H\). That configuration requires \(D\) to be divisible by \(H\). Other designs can use different projection widths, but this chapter uses equal widths.
The head outputs are concatenated along their feature axis. An output projection then mixes those concatenated coordinates and returns model width \(D\).
\[
\operatorname{MHA}(X)=\operatorname{concat}(\operatorname{head}_1,\ldots,\operatorname{head}_H)W_O
\tag{17.2}\]
The output projection does not introduce new token-to-token comparisons. Each head has already combined positions through its own attention weights.
Implementations often calculate all projections together in shape \([B,T,D]\). They then split the last axis into heads and move the head axis before the token axis.
\[
Q_{\mathrm{heads}}=\operatorname{reshape}(Q,B,T,H,d_h)\mathbin{.}\operatorname{permute}(0,2,1,3)
\tag{17.3}\]
Here \(B\) is batch size, \(T\) is sequence length, and \(d_h\) is head width. The reshape first produces \([B,T,H,d_h]\). The permutation \((0,2,1,3)\) then produces \([B,H,T,d_h]\). Reshaping alone does not perform this axis exchange.
For \(B=2\), \(T=4\), \(D=8\), and \(H=2\), the intermediate shape is \([2,4,2,4]\) and the attention-ready shape is \([2,2,4,4]\). One head’s vectors have shape \([2,4,4]\). Two heads concatenate back to width eight.
The following index example uses unequal token and head counts so their roles remain visible. Head 0 receives coordinate pairs \((0,1)\), \((4,5)\), and \((8,9)\) from the three tokens.
For different query and source lengths, the complete shapes are \(Q:[B,H,T_q,d_h]\) and \(K,V:[B,H,T_k,d_h]\). Scores have shape \([B,H,T_q,T_k]\), normalized over the final source axis. The output has shape \([B,H,T_q,d_h]\) before recombination.
Heads need not specialize into stable linguistic categories. Their value depends on training and available width. Increasing their count while fixing total width makes each head narrower. Section 24.5 compares at least two heads under controlled inputs.

title: 17  Transformer blocks
text:
Code example: Tracing coordinate values through the head split

import torch

q = torch.arange(12).reshape(1, 3, 4)
split = q.reshape(1, 3, 2, 2)
heads = split.permute(0, 2, 1, 3)
print(heads[0, 0])
assert torch.equal(heads[0, 0], torch.tensor([[0, 1], [4, 5], [8, 9]]))
restored = heads.permute(0, 2, 1, 3).reshape(1, 3, 4)
assert torch.equal(restored, q)

title: 17  Transformer blocks
text:
17.2 Position information
Multiple heads supply different comparisons, but content vectors alone do not identify a token’s location. Without positional information or an order-dependent mask, self-attention is permutation-equivariant: reordering its input rows reorders its output rows correspondingly.
The sentences “dog bites man” and “man bites dog” illustrate why order matters. A causal mask supplies an ordering constraint through visibility. Position information can additionally represent particular locations or distances between tokens.
An absolute positional encoding assigns a vector to each position and adds it to the token representation. Those vectors may be learned or constructed from a fixed rule. A relative position bias instead changes attention scores according to the distance between query and source positions.
Attention with Linear Biases, or ALiBi, assigns each head a positive slope \(m_h\). For an allowed causal source \(j\le i\), it subtracts a distance penalty from the scaled dot product.
\[
\operatorname{score}_{i,j,h}=\frac{q_i^{T}k_j}{\sqrt{d_k}}-m_h(i-j),\quad j\le i,\quad m_h>0
\tag{17.4}\]
A head with slope \(0.1\) subtracts \(0.3\) for distance three. The bias changes the softmax weights without changing the query or key vectors. Future positions still receive the causal mask’s negative infinity.
Rotary positional embedding, or RoPE, incorporates position by rotating paired query and key coordinates. For a pair \((a,b)\) at position \(t\), a rotation frequency \(\omega\) gives \((a\cos(t\omega)-b\sin(t\omega),\ a\sin(t\omega)+b\cos(t\omega))\).
Different coordinate pairs use different frequencies. Let \(R_t\) denote one such rotation. The rotated dot product is \((R_iq)^\top(R_jk)=q^\top R_{j-i}k\), so it depends on the relative angle between positions.
For a two-coordinate example, \((1,0)\) at angle zero remains \((1,0)\). Rotating it by \(90^\circ\) gives \((0,1)\). Comparing these two rotated vectors produces dot product zero, while comparing two unrotated copies produces one.






Figure 17.2: Rotating query and key pairs changes their relative angle while preserving each pair’s length.



RoPE changes the comparison vectors before their dot product. It does not append an extra value vector. The rotation preserves a vector pair’s length while changing its direction.
A positional rule that can be evaluated at larger indices does not guarantee accurate long-context predictions. Training lengths, frequencies, attention patterns, and data all affect behavior beyond the observed range. Test the required lengths rather than inferring capability from the encoding alone.

title: 17  Transformer blocks
text:
17.3 Residuals and normalization
After attention combines positions, its output must enter the next transformation. Repeatedly replacing every representation can make a deep stack difficult to optimize. A residual connection adds a transformation to its input, allowing the layer to learn an adjustment.
For \(y=x+F(x)\), the derivative is \(I+J_F\), where \(J_F\) is the Jacobian of the transformation. The direct path contributes the identity term. It provides another gradient route, although cancellation or growth can still occur.
Both sides of the addition must have compatible dimensions. Transformer sublayers normally return the full model width \(D\) before adding to the incoming representation, called the residual stream. If one coordinate is 2 and its computed adjustment is \(0.3\), the result is \(2.3\).
Layer normalization, or LayerNorm, normalizes the features of each token independently. For one \(D\)-coordinate vector, it computes the feature mean \(\mu\) and population variance \(\sigma^2\).
\[
\operatorname{LN}(x)=\frac{\gamma(x-\mu)}{\sqrt{\sigma^{2}+\varepsilon}}+\beta
\tag{17.5}\]
The learned vectors \(\gamma\) and \(\beta\) scale and shift the normalized coordinates. The positive constant \(\varepsilon\) keeps the denominator defined when variance is small. No statistics are combined across examples or token positions.
For \(x=(2,4)\), the mean is 3 and the variance is 1. Ignoring a small \(\varepsilon\) and using unit scale with zero shift gives approximately \((-1,1)\). The separate vector \((1,3)\) has mean 2 and also produces approximately \((-1,1)\) under those settings.
Root mean square normalization, or RMSNorm, divides by the root mean square of the features without subtracting their mean.
\[
\operatorname{RMSNorm}(x)=\frac{\gamma x}{\sqrt{\operatorname{mean}_{j}(x_j^{2})+\varepsilon}}
\tag{17.6}\]
For \(x=(3,4)\), the mean square is \(12.5\) and its square root is approximately \(3.535534\). With unit scale and negligible \(\varepsilon\), the result is approximately \((0.848528,1.131371)\). Unlike LayerNorm, this operation does not center the vector.
Both methods preserve the token and batch axes. RMSNorm avoids computing and subtracting the mean, although its practical performance depends on the implementation and hardware.
The axes matter when comparing this operation with batch normalization, or BatchNorm. For an array of examples shaped \([N,C]\), BatchNorm computes a mean and variance for each of the \(C\) channels across the \(N\) examples. With rows \((2,4)\) and \((1,3)\), its channel means are \((1.5,3.5)\). LayerNorm instead uses each row’s own features, giving the row means 3 and 2 calculated above. Changing the other examples in a batch can therefore change a training-time BatchNorm result.
By default, PyTorch’s BatchNorm1d tracks running statistics during training and uses them during evaluation. Setting track_running_stats=False uses current batch statistics in both modes. For input shaped \([N,C,L]\), it combines the example and length axes when calculating each channel’s statistics. The PyTorch 2.11 BatchNorm1d contract specifies these choices. The transformer block here uses LayerNorm over each token’s feature width, so it needs no batch-statistics estimate for evaluation.
A pre-norm block normalizes the input before applying the sublayer and adding its result to the original input.
\[
x_{l+1}=x_l+F(\operatorname{LN}(x_l))
\tag{17.7}\]
A post-norm block applies normalization after the residual addition.
\[
x_{l+1}=\operatorname{LN}(x_l+F(x_l))
\tag{17.8}\]
In the pre-norm form, the residual stream bypasses that normalization. In the post-norm form, the whole residual sum passes through it. If a post-norm residual sum is \((1,3)\), its centered values are \((-1,1)\) before scale and shift.
Replacing LayerNorm with RMSNorm gives a different pre-norm variant. These layouts affect gradient paths and training behavior. A direct residual path helps optimization, but does not guarantee stable training at arbitrary depth.

title: 17  Transformer blocks
text:
17.4 Feed-forward layers
Attention changes a token by combining information from other positions. The feed-forward network, or FFN, then transforms that token’s coordinates using the same network at every position. This operation introduces no new cross-position reads.
For one token represented as a column vector, a basic FFN is the MLP from Chapter 12:
\[
\operatorname{FFN}(x)=W_2\phi(W_1x+b_1)+b_2
\tag{17.9}\]
The first matrix expands the width, \(\phi\) supplies a nonlinear activation, and the second matrix returns to width \(D\). One common intermediate width is \(4D\).
\[
W_1\in\mathbb{R}^{4D\times D},\quad W_2\in\mathbb{R}^{D\times4D}
\tag{17.10}\]
For \(D=768\), the intermediate width is 3,072. Across a batch, an input \([B,T,D]\) becomes \([B,T,4D]\) and returns to \([B,T,D]\). These two matrices contain about \(8D^2\) weights before biases, explaining why the FFN can account for substantial parameters and arithmetic.
The scalar case \(x=1\), \(W_1=2\), \(b_1=0.5\), identity activation, \(W_2=3\), and \(b_2=1\) gives output \(3(2+0.5)+1=8.5\). Identity activation isolates the affine arithmetic here. A useful nonlinear FFN applies an activation between its projections.
The Gaussian error linear unit, or GELU, multiplies a value by the standard normal cumulative probability at that value.
\[
\operatorname{GELU}(x)=x\Phi(x)
\tag{17.11}\]
Here \(\Phi(x)\) is the probability that a standard normal variable is at most \(x\). Thus \(\operatorname{GELU}(0)=0\) and \(\operatorname{GELU}(1)\approx0.841345\). Negative inputs are smoothly suppressed rather than abruptly set to zero as in ReLU.
A gated linear unit, or GLU, multiplies one projected branch by a gate derived from another. The SiLU activation, also called Swish for this form, is \(\operatorname{SiLU}(b)=b\sigma(b)\). SwiGLU uses that activation in its gating branch.
\[
\operatorname{SwiGLU}(x)=W_c\!\left[(W_a x)\odot\operatorname{SiLU}(W_bx)\right],\quad\operatorname{SiLU}(u)=u\sigma(u)
\tag{17.12}\]
Here \(W_a,W_b\) have shape \([H_f,D]\), and \(W_c\) has shape \([D,H_f]\). The two expanded branches multiply coordinatewise before the output projection. Biases are omitted to keep this operation visible.
For scalar branches \(a=2\) and \(b=0\), SwiGLU’s intermediate value is \(a\operatorname{SiLU}(b)=2(0)(0.5)=0\). A sigmoid-only GLU would instead give \(a\sigma(b)=1\). The factor \(b\) is necessary to distinguish the two activations.
For \(a=2\) and \(b=1\), the SwiGLU intermediate is \(2\sigma(1)\approx1.462117\). These gates act on features within one token. They serve a different role from attention weights over source positions.

title: 17  Transformer blocks
text:
17.5 Assembling the block
The components now have compatible interfaces. A transformer block alternates attention across positions with an FFN at each position, adding a residual around each sublayer. Repeating the block creates network depth.
Using pre-LayerNorm, the two updates are:
\[
\begin{aligned}X_1&=X+\operatorname{Attention}(\operatorname{LN}(X)),\\X_2&=X_1+\operatorname{FFN}(\operatorname{LN}(X_1))\end{aligned}
\tag{17.13}\]
Here Attention includes the multiple-head calculation and its output projection. Both \(X_1\) and \(X_2\) retain shape \([B,T,D]\). Positional information must be supplied by the selected encoding or attention rule.
Take \(B=1\), \(T=2\), \(D=4\), and \(H=2\). Combined projections have shape \([1,2,4]\). Reshaping to \([1,2,2,2]\) first means [batch, token, head, feature]. Permuting to [batch, head, token, feature] leaves the numerical shape unchanged but changes which values each attention calculation reads.
The combined head output has shape \([1,2,2,2]\), with one \([1,2,2]\) result per head. Recombining heads restores $[1,2,4]`. An FFN can expand it to \([1,2,16]\) before returning to \([1,2,4]\) for the residual addition.






Figure 17.3: Pre-normalized attention and feed-forward updates each return to the model width for a residual addition.



The following PyTorch layer uses LayerNorm and GELU. It receives prepared vectors of shape \([2,4,8]\), applies two attention heads, and returns the same outer shape. The supplied causal mask blocks future keys.

Code example: One pre-normalized transformer layer

import torch
import torch.nn as nn

class TransformerLayer(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, width=8, heads=2, hidden=16):
        super().__init__()
        self.norm1 = nn.LayerNorm(width)
        self.attention = nn.MultiheadAttention(width, heads, batch_first=True)
        self.norm2 = nn.LayerNorm(width)
        self.ffn = nn.Sequential(
            nn.Linear(width, hidden),
            nn.GELU(),
            nn.Linear(hidden, width),
        )

    def forward(self, x, attention_mask=None):
        normalized = self.norm1(x)
        mixed, weights = self.attention(
            normalized,
            normalized,
            normalized,
            attn_mask=attention_mask,
            average_attn_weights=False,
        )
        x = x + mixed
        x = x + self.ffn(self.norm2(x))
        return x, weights

torch.manual_seed(7)
x = torch.randn(2, 4, 8)
blocked = torch.ones(4, 4, dtype=torch.bool).triu(1)
layer = TransformerLayer().eval()
output, weights = layer(x, attention_mask=blocked)
print(x.shape, output.shape, weights.shape)
print(weights.mean(dim=1).shape)
assert output.shape == (2, 4, 8)
assert weights.shape == (2, 2, 4, 4)
assert torch.count_nonzero(weights.triu(1)) == 0
changed = x.clone()
changed[:, -1] += 10 * torch.arange(8)
changed_output, _ = layer(changed, attention_mask=blocked)
assert torch.allclose(output[:, :-1], changed_output[:, :-1], atol=1e-6)
The returned per-head attention weights have shape \([2,2,4,4]\). Averaging their head axis gives \([2,4,4]\), which is also the library’s default return format when head averaging is enabled. Inspecting separate heads therefore requires an explicit setting.
For this MultiheadAttention API, a two-dimensional attention mask has shape \([T_q,T_k]\). A three-dimensional per-example, per-head mask has shape \([B H,T_q,T_k]\). A Boolean True entry blocks a source here, unlike the allowed-position Boolean mask used by the helper in Section 16.3.
Padding can be supplied separately with key_padding_mask shaped $[B,T_k]`. All-masked rows still require a defined policy. Match the specific API’s mask contract rather than assuming every attention interface uses the same Boolean convention.
The compact example uses no dropout. When included in training, dropout can act on attention weights or sublayer outputs, following Section 11.5. Evaluation disables it. Disabling gradient recording is a separate choice.
After the final block, a language-model output head projects each token representation to vocabulary logits.
\[
\operatorname{logits}=x_{\mathrm{final}}W_{\mathrm{vocab}}^{T}
\tag{17.14}\]
Here \(x_{\text{final}}\) has shape \([B,T,D]\), and \(W_{\text{vocab}}\) has shape \([|V|,D]\). The result has shape \([B,T,|V|]\). A model may tie these weights to its input embedding table, with the gradient consequences described in Section 13.2.
The block defines the transformation. Chapter 18 will choose its permitted inputs and training targets. Before that comparison, one useful variant changes which FFN parameters execute for each token.

title: 17  Transformer blocks
text:
17.6 Mixture of experts
A dense FFN activates the same matrices for every token. A mixture-of-experts, or MoE, layer contains several alternative FFNs and selects only a subset for each input. Each alternative is an expert, and the selection module is a router.
For token vector \(x\in\mathbb R^D\) and \(E\) experts, a router matrix with shape \([E,D]\) produces \(E\) scores. Softmax converts them to probabilities \(g\). The set \(\mathcal T_k(g)\) contains the indices of the largest \(k\) probabilities.
\[
g=\operatorname{softmax}(W_{\mathrm{gate}}x),\quad y=\sum_{e\in\mathcal{T}_{k}(g)}g_{e}^{(k)}f_{e}(x)
\tag{17.15}\]
Each selected expert \(f_e\) returns a \(D\)-coordinate vector. In this formulation, the selected weights are renormalized: \(g_e^{(k)}=g_e/\sum_{j\in\mathcal T_k(g)}g_j\). Their weighted outputs can therefore be added back to the residual stream.
For router scores \((\log 7,\log 3,0)\), softmax gives \((7/11,3/11,1/11)\). Selecting the largest two entries and renormalizing gives \((0.7,0.3)\). If their scalar outputs are 2 and 5, the mixture is \(0.7(2)+0.3(5)=2.9\).
Across \(B\) sequences of \(T\) tokens, router scores have shape \([B,T,E]\). The selected expert outputs retain width \(D\), and the final mixture has shape \([B,T,D]\).






Figure 17.4: Top-two routing renormalizes the selected weights before combining the expert outputs.



Sparse activation means only some expert parameters execute for a token. It can increase total parameter capacity without activating every expert each time. Router computation, dispatch, and communication still add cost, and all expert weights need storage somewhere.
Load balancing encourages a useful distribution of tokens across experts. If most tokens select one expert, it becomes a bottleneck while others receive little training. Capacity limits may also require a policy for overflow tokens.
One training approach perturbs router scores with Gaussian noise before selecting the largest entries. This changes which experts receive examples during exploration. An auxiliary loss can also penalize uneven total gate weight across a batch. The sparsely gated MoE paper develops noisy gating and balancing objectives.
For positive expert importance values \(I_e\), the coefficient of variation is their standard deviation divided by their mean. Importance totals \((9,1)\) have mean five and population standard deviation four, so their squared coefficient is \(0.64\). Totals \((5,5)\) give zero. Adding a scaled penalty encourages balanced importance during training. It does not guarantee balanced traffic in each inference batch, and equal gate weight need not mean equal execution time.
An expert capacity limits how many assigned tokens it can process in a dispatch. If capacity is two and three tokens select it, the implementation needs an overflow rule, such as rerouting or skipping that expert branch. State the actual rule because it changes the computation. Increasing capacity reduces overflow risk while increasing memory requirements.
Top-\(k\) selection is discrete. Gradients pass through selected expert computations and their weights, while the selection boundary itself is not a smooth operation. Balancing objectives and routing rules affect both training and runtime behavior.
MoE is a choice for conditional computation within a model. It does not require multiple input modalities. The following chapter compares architecture and objective choices independently of this FFN variant.

Chapter checkpoint
A head split has the expected shape but produces different attention weights after a refactor. What evidence would distinguish a shape check from an axis check?
Feedback: Trace identifiable coordinate values through reshape and permutation, then reconstruct the original tensor. Equal dimension sizes can hide an incorrect axis exchange.
A claimed SwiGLU implementation returns 1 when its branches are \(a=2\) and \(b=0\). Which operation is missing?
Feedback: SiLU multiplies the sigmoid by its own input. The SwiGLU intermediate should be \(a b\sigma(b)=0\). Returning 1 indicates a sigmoid-only gate in this example.
An MoE model has more parameters but no latency improvement. Which costs would you measure?
Feedback: Measure active expert computation, routing and dispatch, communication, and the distribution of tokens across experts. Total parameter count alone does not determine per-token latency.

title: 18  Transformer architectures
text:
18.1 Architecture families
A transformer block defines how representations change. The complete architecture also determines which inputs each prediction can use and where its targets come from. Those choices connect the same block components to classification, text completion, and translation.
We compare information flow first, then construct the corresponding training records and inference interfaces. This separates a model’s structure from the application expressed through it.
The block in Chapter 17 preserves a sequence of representations. Its visibility mask and connections determine which sequence those representations describe. Three common architecture families organize that information differently.
An encoder-only transformer creates representations of an available input sequence, commonly using bidirectional self-attention. A decoder-only transformer uses causal self-attention to support left-to-right prediction. An encoder-decoder transformer represents a source sequence with an encoder and generates a separate target sequence with a decoder.
The encoder-decoder’s target side uses causal self-attention over earlier target inputs. Its cross-attention reads the encoded source, following Section 16.4. Source and target lengths can differ.
The application does not uniquely determine the family. A decoder can classify an article by generating its category text. An encoder can supply vectors for retrieval or feed a token-labeling head. These interfaces require different target formats even when the user asks for the same final decision.
Architecture also does not uniquely determine the training objective. The objective must respect available information, but an encoder can learn from classification, reconstruction, or other suitable targets.

title: 18  Transformer architectures
text: Example task | Visible information | Output and target | |—|—|—| | Encoder-only review classification | All valid review tokens | One pooled representation feeds class logits, compared with the review label | | Decoder-only continuation | The current input token and preceding inputs | Each eligible position produces logits for its following token | | Encoder-decoder translation | Complete encoded source and the available target prefix | Each target position predicts the next target-language token |

title: 18  Transformer architectures
text:
18.2 Training objectives
A legal attention pattern establishes what the model can see. A training objective specifies which prediction errors change its parameters. Comparing the target sets makes the differences between model families concrete.
Causal language modeling predicts a sequence through its next-token conditional probabilities. Its summed loss is:
\[
L_{\mathrm{CLM}}=-\sum_t\log P_{\theta}(x_t\mid x_{<t})
\tag{18.1}\]
The target shift and valid-position reduction are established in Section 1.2 and Section 8.2. For IDs \([4,8,9]\), the manual input-target pairs are \([4,8]\) and \([8,9]\). This familiar alignment remains the same inside a causal transformer.
If two targets receive probabilities \(0.5\) and \(0.25\), their summed loss is approximately \(2.079442\). Averaging instead gives approximately \(1.039721\) per supervised token. State which reduction is being compared.
Masked language modeling, or MLM, predicts selected hidden tokens from the remaining context. Let \(M\) contain the selected target positions.
\[
L_{\mathrm{MLM}}=-\sum_{t\in M}\log P_{\theta}(x_t\mid x_{\mathrm{visible}})
\tag{18.2}\]
For “the cat sat”, select the middle token and supply “the [MASK] sat”. The target is “cat” at the selected position. The model may use both neighboring words, but it must not read the unchanged target token at that position.
Only selected positions contribute to this simplified masked objective. With two target probabilities \(0.8\) and \(0.4\), their summed loss is \(-\log(0.8)-\log(0.4)\approx1.139434\). Original token IDs elsewhere supply context rather than additional targets in this record.
Actual masking recipes can also replace selected tokens with random words or retain some unchanged inputs. Those choices alter the training corruption process and must be recorded explicitly. The simple example above uses explicit masking throughout.
Original BERT also used next sentence prediction, or NSP, alongside masked-token loss. Its input paired two text segments, and a binary classifier predicted whether the second followed the first in the source. Their combined objective trained token reconstruction and a segment-level decision. Later encoder models need not use NSP, so masked-token training alone does not imply this additional objective.
The pair uses the structural tokens from Section 3.3: [CLS] A [SEP] B [SEP]. BERT’s final representation at [CLS] feeds the NSP classifier. Learned segment embeddings also tell the model whether each token belongs to A or B. The separator marks a boundary, while the segment embedding adds membership information at every position. These distinct roles are shown in the original BERT input specification.
Sequence-to-sequence training predicts a target sequence conditioned on a separate source. Its objective is:
\[
L_{\mathrm{seq2seq}}=-\sum_t\log P_{\theta}(y_t\mid y_{<t},x_{\mathrm{source}})
\tag{18.3}\]
Here \(x_{\text{source}}\) is the full source and \(y_{<t}\) is the earlier target prefix. During training, teacher forcing supplies the recorded earlier target tokens, as in Section 15.4. The encoder provides source representations independently of that target shift.
For two target probabilities \(0.5\) and \(0.25\), the summed loss is again approximately \(2.079442\). The arithmetic matches the causal example, while the conditional information includes a separate source sequence.
Some encoder-decoder pretraining uses denoising, which reconstructs clean text from a corrupted version. Missing spans become targets, and the corrupted text supplies the source. This uses the same source-target interface as other conditional sequence tasks.
These objectives evaluate different conditions and target sets. Their raw losses cannot be compared fairly without matching tokenization, reduction, and evaluation protocol. Masked-token conditional probabilities also do not automatically form the left-to-right sequence likelihood used by a causal model.

title: 18  Transformer architectures
text:
18.3 Model interfaces
An objective becomes executable only when its input and target records match the model interface. A pretrained checkpoint contains parameters learned before the current task-specific adaptation. Loading it does not determine how a new dataset should be formatted.
For encoder classification, one record can contain a review’s token IDs, its validity mask, and one integer class label. A task head consumes the encoder representation. Its loss compares class logits with that label, using the classification mechanics in Chapter 8.
For a decoder-only instruction model, a record combines the instruction, optional evidence, and answer into one token sequence. At generation time, only the instruction and available evidence are supplied. At training time, a loss mask can supervise answer tokens while keeping the prompt as visible context.
For an encoder-decoder model, the source instruction and target answer are separate sequences. Source padding and target padding can therefore have different lengths and masks. The target decoder receives shifted target inputs, usually prepared from labels by the model’s supported training interface.
The model class must match that architecture. Hugging Face’s AutoModelForSequenceClassification supplies a task head, AutoModelForCausalLM supplies a causal generation head, and AutoModelForSeq2SeqLM supports an encoder-decoder generation interface. Their label conventions must be checked for the actual checkpoint and library version.
Some causal language-model APIs shift labels internally, allowing labels initially copied from the input IDs. Applying another manual shift would misalign predictions. The manual calculation in Section 8.2 establishes what the API must implement, without requiring every API to accept the same tensors.
The distinction from Section 1.1 concerns what probability is modeled. A discriminative classifier estimates \(P(y\mid x)\) for labels. A generative model can describe \(P(x)\) or a joint distribution \(P(x,y)\). Conditional generation produces structured or textual outputs given an input context.
Prompted classification, extraction, translation, and open-ended writing can all use conditional token generation. The interface changes how the task is expressed, while the decoder still produces token distributions. Generated label text may require parsing and validity checks that an integer class head avoids.
For a causal sequence with conditional probabilities \(0.5\), \(0.4\), and \(0.25\), the sequence probability is \(0.05\). This follows the factorization in Section 1.2. Changing architecture or prompt format does not remove the need to define what sequence and conditioning information that probability describes.
The paired model experiment in Section 24.6 uses causal and encoder-decoder checkpoints with their respective formats. It compares task outputs under one rubric rather than treating their raw training tensors as interchangeable.

title: 18  Transformer architectures
text:
18.4 Iterative generation
Causal generation commits to successive tokens through a growing prefix. Another approach begins with an incomplete sequence and refines several positions over multiple passes. This changes the generation procedure as well as its dependencies.
A diffusion language model learns to reverse a corruption process applied to text representations. In masked-token approaches, training hides tokens at varying corruption levels and learns to recover them. Generation repeatedly predicts and reveals or revises selected positions. Large Language Diffusion Models develops one such formulation.
For an illustrative three-position output, a procedure might begin with “[MASK] [MASK] [MASK]”, retain “cat” at the middle position, and refine the remaining positions. The actual sampler determines which proposals to keep, which to mask again, and when to stop. This is a mechanism sketch, not a claimed output from a trained model.






Figure 18.2: An illustrative sampler fills several positions across dependent refinement passes.



Several positions can be processed together within a pass, but refinement passes still depend on earlier passes. Cost therefore depends on output length, number of passes, architecture, and implementation. Parallel updates alone do not establish lower latency or better output quality.
This comparison concerns text generation. It is separate from the expert routing in Section 17.6 and the model-compression methods in Section 20.6. Those choices change activated or stored parameters rather than defining this refinement procedure.
All these models still need suitable training examples. Chapter 19 examines how corpus selection, packing, and compute allocation shape the distribution on which an objective is optimized.

Chapter checkpoint
Two systems classify the same review. One returns class logits and the other generates a category string. Which parts of their evaluation can be shared, and which need different checks?
Feedback: Both can be evaluated against the same category targets and split. The generative system also needs a rule for parsing invalid or unexpected label text. Its token loss is not directly the classifier’s class loss.
A masked-token model has a lower loss than a causal model. Does this show that it is better at continuation?
Feedback: Not by itself. It may see right context and predict a different subset of tokens. Evaluate both on the intended task with an appropriate common protocol.

title: 19  Pretraining data and scaling
text:
19.1 Curating the corpus
The architecture and objective define what a model can learn from an example. The corpus determines which examples it receives, while the compute budget limits how many updates can be made. Pretraining quality depends on those decisions together.
The progression from fixed histories to recurrent states and attention changes how context enters a prediction. Large transformer training also combines many parameters with large corpora and sustained optimization. The forward, loss, backward, and update cycle remains the one in Section 10.5.
Training on more text does not guarantee more useful evidence. Repeated documents, broken extraction, and an unsuitable domain mixture can change the errors the model learns to reduce. Corpus curation selects and prepares the material that contributes to the objective.
Filtering removes or downweights records according to explicit criteria, such as language, extraction quality, or intended content scope. Privacy and licensing requirements also constrain which records belong in the corpus. A filter changes the training distribution, so its effects should be inspected across sources and languages.
Deduplication detects exact or near-duplicate examples. Exact matching catches identical records, while near-duplicate methods can find repeated passages with small changes. Overly broad matching can remove distinct examples, so thresholds need sample review.
Repeating one record gives its patterns more influence on the loss. Removing duplicates therefore changes both the token count and the relative weight of evidence. It may also reduce memorization caused by excessive repetition.
Evaluation contamination occurs when training includes evaluation examples or closely related answers. It can raise a reported score without demonstrating generalization. Keep evaluation sets separate and check suspected overlaps using the split principles in Chapter 9.
Record which filtering and deduplication rules were applied, their removal counts, and representative retained and rejected examples. A changed corpus should be explainable through those decisions, rather than only its final token count.
After selecting records, training still needs a rule for how often to sample each remaining source.

title: 19  Pretraining data and scaling
text: Figure 19.2: Removing duplicate documents before splitting keeps the repeated text together. Only the training branch supplies training batches.

title: 19  Pretraining data and scaling
text:
19.2 Mixing sources
A corpus can contain code, books, articles, and other sources in very different quantities. Source-mixture weights specify how often a sampler selects each source. They need not match the sources’ raw sizes.
Let \(P_s\) describe source \(s\), and let \(\alpha_s\ge0\) be its sampling probability. The resulting mixture is:
\[
P_{\mathrm{data}}=\sum_s\alpha_sP_s,\quad\sum_s\alpha_s=1
\tag{19.1}\]
The sampler first chooses a source with probability \(\alpha_s\), then draws an example from it. With code weight \(0.3\) and book weight \(0.7\), ten draws contain three code examples and seven book examples in expectation. An actual group of ten can differ.
The sampling unit matters. If code examples average two tokens and book examples average six, those expected draws contribute six code tokens and forty-two book tokens. Code then supplies \(6/48=12.5\%\) of tokens despite accounting for \(30\%\) of examples.
Thus an example mixture is not automatically a token mixture. For a mean loss over valid tokens, longer examples contribute more target positions. A mean of per-example means would weight examples differently, following the reduction discussion in Section 8.2.
Oversampling selects a source more often than its raw corpus share would imply. This can strengthen a scarce domain, but may repeat the same examples many times. Track both processed tokens and unique material to distinguish added training exposure from added evidence.
The chosen objective then creates labels from those records. Causal, masked, and source-target formats follow Chapter 18. Changing the source weights alters the empirical distribution of their losses without changing the underlying gradient mechanism.
Sampling decides which examples enter a batch. Packing decides how their token positions share the allocated tensor space.

title: 19  Pretraining data and scaling
text:
19.3 Packing sequences
Padding every short document to the model’s full context length can waste allocated positions. Sequence packing places several shorter examples into a longer training array. Its boundary rules determine whether those examples remain independent.
A separator token makes a boundary visible in the text, but does not by itself block attention across it. If independent documents are intended, an attention mask must stop queries in one document from reading another. A corresponding loss mask must exclude unintended boundary transitions.
Consider document A with tokens [BOS, 4, 8, EOS] and document B with [BOS, 6, EOS]. Packing them into eight positions gives [BOS, 4, 8, EOS, BOS, 6, EOS, PAD].
The first seven input positions have following targets [4, 8, EOS, BOS, 6, EOS, PAD]. For independent-document training, valid target indicators are [1, 1, 1, 0, 1, 1, 0]. Predicting B’s BOS from A’s EOS is excluded, as is predicting padding.
Within each document, attention remains causal. Queries at B’s positions can read B’s prefix but cannot read A. This combines the visibility and validity rules from Section 16.3 with the target reduction from Section 8.2.
A different corpus policy may deliberately train one continuous stream across separators. That is a different conditioning assumption and should be recorded. A packed tensor’s shape does not reveal which policy was used.
Supervised-token utilization measures the share of allocated positions that contribute targets to the objective.
\[
\operatorname{utilization}=\frac{\mathrm{supervised\,tokens}}{\mathrm{allocated\,positions}}
\tag{19.2}\]
If 900 of 1,024 allocated positions are supervised, utilization is \(900/1024=0.878906\), or about \(87.9\%\). The small packed example above has five supervised targets among eight allocated positions.
This measure differs from hardware utilization. Boundary markers, masked prompts, and padding can occupy real tensor positions without contributing loss. Kernel efficiency, sequence lengths, and device scheduling also affect elapsed time.
Packing can reduce wasted space, but it cannot repair an unsuitable corpus or objective. Once the data procedure is defined, the remaining planning question is how to divide compute between model size and training exposure.

title: 19  Pretraining data and scaling
text:
19.4 Allocating compute
A larger model costs more to process each token. Under a fixed training budget, increasing parameter count usually leaves fewer tokens to train on. Compute-optimal training chooses their combination to minimize the selected loss within that budget.
A scaling law is an empirical relationship fitted to measured runs. One useful form separates a limiting loss from parameter- and data-related corrections.
\[
L(N,D)\approx L_{\infty}+aN^{-\alpha}+bD^{-\beta}
\tag{19.3}\]
Here \(N\) is parameter count, \(D\) is processed training-token count, and \(a,b,\alpha,\beta\) are positive fitted constants. The symbol \(D\) denotes tokens in this section, rather than the hidden width used in earlier chapters.
A simple dense-transformer planning estimate is \(C\approx6ND\) floating-point operations. It captures major parameter-dependent forward and backward work. Attention length, architecture, and implementation can require a more detailed estimate.
For \(N=10^9\) parameters and \(D=20\times10^9\) tokens, this estimate gives \(C=1.2\times10^{20}\) operations. Doubling parameters and halving tokens leaves the product, and thus this estimated compute, unchanged. It does not leave the fitted loss unchanged.
Substituting \(D=C/(6N)\) into the loss estimate gives \(L(N)\approx L_\infty+aN^{-\alpha}+b(6N/C)^\beta\). Increasing \(N\) reduces its parameter correction but increases its data correction. Differentiating with respect to \(\log N\) balances these effects at \(\alpha aN^{-\alpha}=\beta b(6N/C)^\beta\).
For this simplified fit, the balance implies \(N_{\text{opt}}\propto C^{\beta/(\alpha+\beta)}\) and \(D_{\text{opt}}\propto C^{\alpha/(\alpha+\beta)}\). When the exponents are similar, both allocations grow approximately with the square root of compute.
The Chinchilla study found approximately balanced growth of parameters and tokens within its studied range. Its 70-billion-parameter model used 1.4 trillion training tokens. The resulting twenty-to-one ratio motivates a familiar planning heuristic:
\[
D_{\mathrm{tokens}}\approx20N_{\mathrm{params}}
\tag{19.4}\]
Under that heuristic, a seven-billion-parameter model suggests roughly 140 billion training tokens. This is an estimate from a particular training-cost objective, rather than a universal target for every corpus and architecture.
A separate arithmetic example illustrates how estimated loss components combine. A limiting term of 1.0, parameter correction of 0.2, and data correction of 0.1 give 1.3. If a separately estimated optimization gap adds 0.05, the result is 1.35. These hypothetical values are not a fitted forecast.
Training compute, parameter count, and token count are coupled. They cannot all be varied independently while retaining a fixed compute budget. Fitted trends also depend on data quality, training recipes, and the range of observed runs.
Deployment adds another objective. A smaller model trained longer may be useful when its lower serving cost matters across many requests. Evaluate total training and serving requirements alongside quality, rather than selecting a model from parameter count alone.
Once a base model exists, adapting it can be more practical than repeating pretraining. Chapter 20 compares changes to context, behavior, and trainable parameters.

Chapter checkpoint
A sampler draws 30% of its documents from code. Why might code contribute much less than 30% of the token loss?
Feedback: Its documents may be shorter or contain fewer supervised positions. Inspect the sampling unit, valid target counts, and loss reduction before changing the weights.
Packed documents contain separator tokens. What additional evidence establishes that they are independent training examples?
Feedback: Inspect attention across document boundaries and the labels at each boundary. Separators alone do not block conditioning, and a full tensor can still contain invalid cross-document targets.

text:
Chapters in this part
A pretrained model may need different task behavior or lower response costs. Prompting can change its context, adaptation can change its parameters, and serving can manage reusable state.
Chapter 20 compares fine-tuning methods, including low-rank adaptation and quantization. Chapter 21 follows prompt processing and one-token decoding through the KV cache, batching, and latency constraints.
These choices use the same tensors, losses, and attention operations already established. Part VI maps them to software and non-text inputs.

title: 20  Low-rank adaptation and preference alignment
text:
20.1 Prompting and retrieved context
A pretrained model may know the relevant language yet miss a task’s facts, output format, or preferred behavior. Those failures call for different interventions. Some can be addressed through input context, while others require changing parameters or training targets.
This chapter starts from the missing capability and follows what each intervention changes. It then separates the training objective, the parameters allowed to move, and the numerical format used to store them.
Before continuing training, test whether the model can perform the task when its instructions and evidence are explicit. Prompting supplies those instructions through the input. In-context examples demonstrate the desired input-output pattern within that same context.
For a review classifier, a prompt might request exactly positive or negative, then show one labeled example of each. The next review follows without its label. This changes the conditional input while leaving the parameters fixed.
Compare the instruction alone with the instruction plus examples on the same held-out reviews. Inspect classification errors and invalid output formats separately. Examples consume context space, and their wording or order can affect the result.
When required facts live outside the model, retrieval-augmented generation, or RAG, supplies selected evidence before generation. Its complete text procedure here is to index source passages, retrieve relevant passages for a query, include them in the prompt, and generate an answer. Record the passages supporting that answer so it can be checked.
The conditional distribution becomes:
\[
P_{\theta}(y\mid\mathrm{prompt},\mathrm{retrieved\,context})
\tag{20.1}\]
Here \(\theta\) remains fixed, and \(y\) is the answer. As a hypothetical observation, useful evidence might raise an answer’s probability from \(0.2\) to \(0.6\) without changing a weight. Irrelevant or misleading evidence can instead reduce answer quality.
Retrieval addresses access to changing or extensive source material. It also adds indexing, search, and context-processing costs. A retrieval failure and an answer-generation failure require different corrections, as the final system experiment in Section 24.7 demonstrates.
Prompting and retrieval can be combined with later fine-tuning. If the failure persists despite sufficient evidence and clear instructions, fine-tuning on targeted examples may improve the reliability of its responses.
