title: 20  Low-rank adaptation and preference alignment
text:
20.2 Supervised fine-tuning
Fine-tuning continues training from a pretrained checkpoint. Supervised fine-tuning, or SFT, uses examples of desired inputs and outputs. Instruction tuning is SFT whose records contain instructions and expected responses, sometimes with additional evidence.
The training objective remains a loss on the target outputs. For a causal instruction model, prompt tokens condition the answer, while a loss mask can restrict supervision to answer positions. The architecture-specific formats are established in Section 18.3.
Suppose a toy record has prompt IDs \([11,12]\) and answer IDs \([21,22,9]\), where 9 is the answer’s end token. The combined input is \([11,12,21,22,9]\). For an API that shifts labels internally, response-only labels are \([-100,-100,21,22,9]\).
After that internal shift, the last prompt input predicts the first answer token. The next answer input predicts the following answer token, and the final supervised prediction is the end token. The two ignored prompt positions supply context but no direct target loss in this record.
Do not apply an additional manual shift to an API that already performs it. Padding validity, response boundaries, and empty-answer handling need explicit checks. The reduction over valid targets follows Section 8.2.
Full fine-tuning allows base parameters to change under the update rule from Chapter 11. One simple gradient step is:
\[
\theta^{\prime}=\theta-\eta\nabla L_{\mathrm{task}}(\theta)
\tag{20.2}\]
For scalar \(\theta=1\), gradient \(0.4\), and learning rate \(0.1\), the result is \(\theta'=0.96\). Larger models apply the same principle through an optimizer and many parameter tensors.
Fine-tuning can strengthen a stable task format, decision boundary, or instruction pattern. A small or narrow dataset can also cause overfitting. Catastrophic forgetting is loss of useful earlier behavior during adaptation.
Mixing several tasks or retaining representative earlier examples can reduce pressure toward a narrow behavior. It also increases data preparation and may dilute improvement on the main target task. Parameter-efficient updates can still cause forgetting, so preserving frozen base weights does not remove the need to evaluate the adapted model.
Compare held-out task performance before and after training, and retain tests of important base behavior. Tune learning rate and training duration on validation data rather than assuming that more updates are beneficial. Save the exact base checkpoint, tokenizer, record format, and target-mask procedure.
The course uses reasoning language model, or RLM, for a model trained to produce intermediate solution steps before an answer. For example, a training response can show \(3\times4=12\), then \(12+2=14\), and finally give 14. SFT can supervise that entire response using the same target-mask rule.
Intermediate steps consume additional generated tokens and can contain errors even when they sound plausible. Assess the answer and, where possible, the validity of each step. The displayed text does not by itself reveal the computation inside the model. RLM describes a training and response behavior here, rather than a separate attention architecture.
The adaptation experiment in Section 24.6 supplies a complete data and evaluation protocol. Some desired behaviors are easier to express through comparisons between answers than through one reference answer. Preference objectives use that additional form of supervision.

title: 20  Low-rank adaptation and preference alignment
text:
20.3 Learning from preferences
SFT imitates supplied outputs. Preference learning instead uses a judgment that one response is better than another for the same prompt. Alignment describes training and evaluation intended to bring behavior closer to the selected instructions, preferences, or constraints.
A reward model assigns a score \(r_\phi(x,y)\) to response \(y\) for prompt \(x\). One way to train it uses preferred and rejected pairs, increasing the preferred response’s score relative to the rejected response. The score reflects its training judgments and can be inaccurate outside them.
Reinforcement learning from human feedback, or RLHF, can use this scorer to improve a response-generating policy. Here a policy is the model’s conditional distribution over responses. A reference policy remains fixed to provide a comparison point.
A common objective balances expected reward against a Kullback-Leibler penalty, using the divergence defined in Section 8.4.
\[
\max_{\pi}\mathbb{E}_{x}\!\left[\mathbb{E}_{y\sim\pi(\cdot\mid x)}[r_{\phi}(x,y)]-\beta\operatorname{KL}\!\left(\pi(\cdot\mid x)\mathbin{\|}\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(\cdot\mid x)\right)\right]
\tag{20.3}\]
For each prompt, \(\beta>0\) controls the penalty for departure from the reference distribution. The expectation includes responses sampled from the policy being trained. With reward 2, divergence \(0.5\), and \(\beta=0.2\), the penalized value is \(2-0.2(0.5)=1.9\).
Proximal Policy Optimization, or PPO, is one policy-update method used in RLHF. It limits changes to action-probability ratios through a clipped objective while learning from sampled responses and their scores. That clipping differs from clipping a gradient norm.
Reinforcement learning from AI feedback, or RLAIF, uses model-generated judgments for some feedback. The evaluation must still test whether those judgments reflect the intended criteria. Optimizing an imperfect scorer can increase its score without improving the actual task.
Direct Preference Optimization, or DPO, trains from preferred and rejected responses without fitting a separate reward model and running an online reward-optimization loop. Its loss compares each response’s policy log probability with its reference log probability. Direct Preference Optimization derives this formulation.
\[
-\log\sigma\!\left(\beta\left((\log\pi_{\theta}(y_w\mid x)-\log\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(y_w\mid x))-(\log\pi_{\theta}(y_l\mid x)-\log\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(y_l\mid x))\right)\right)
\tag{20.4}\]
Here \(y_w\) is the preferred response and \(y_l\) is the rejected response. Each response log probability is the sum of its token log probabilities, with the prompt used as conditioning context. The reference parameters remain fixed.
Take policy log probabilities \(-2.5\) for the preferred response and \(-3.5\) for the rejected response. Let both reference log probabilities be \(-4\). The reference-relative values are then \(1.5\) and \(0.5\).
With \(\beta=0.5\), their scaled difference is \(0.5(1.5-0.5)=0.5\). The sigmoid is approximately \(0.622459\), and the loss is \(-\log(0.622459)\approx0.474077\). Both response probabilities increased relative to the reference in this example, but the preferred response increased more.
The following small calculation verifies the loss and its local derivatives with respect to the two policy log probabilities.

Code example: DPO pair loss from response log probabilities

import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F

policy_logp = torch.tensor([-2.5, -3.5], dtype=torch.float64, requires_grad=True)
reference_logp = torch.tensor([-4., -4.], dtype=torch.float64)
relative = policy_logp - reference_logp
margin = 0.5 * (relative[0] - relative[1])
loss = -F.logsigmoid(margin)
loss.backward()
print(margin.item(), loss.item(), policy_logp.grad)
assert torch.isclose(loss, torch.tensor(0.4740769841801067, dtype=torch.float64))
assert policy_logp.grad[0] < 0 < policy_logp.grad[1]
The derivatives are approximately \(-0.188770\) for the preferred log probability and \(0.188770\) for the rejected one. They favor a larger reference-relative preference gap. Actual parameter gradients also depend on how the policy produces these log probabilities.
Preference training does not guarantee factual correctness, stable general behavior, or agreement across evaluators. Test those properties separately. The chosen objective also leaves open how many parameters should be allowed to change.

title: 20  Low-rank adaptation and preference alignment
text:
20.4 Low-rank updates
Updating every weight can require substantial gradient and optimizer memory. Parameter-efficient fine-tuning, or PEFT, changes only selected or added parameters. Several PEFT choices change different parts of the interface. A task head adds trainable output layers, while selective tuning updates a chosen subset of existing weights. A bottleneck adapter inserts a narrow trainable transformation inside the frozen network. With input width eight and bottleneck width two, its two matrices contain \(8(2)+2(8)=32\) weights before biases.
Soft prompt tuning learns additional input vectors while retaining the base weights. Four prompt vectors of width eight contain 32 trainable values and add four input positions. These are learned continuous vectors, whereas the ordinary prompt in Section 20.1 supplies fixed token IDs. Their equal parameter count does not make a soft prompt equivalent to an internal adapter.
Low-Rank Adaptation, or LoRA, represents an update to a frozen matrix through two smaller trainable factors.
The rank concept from Section 14.3 applies to the update here, rather than to a compressed data matrix. For base weight \(W\in\mathbb R^{d_{\text{out}}\times d_{\text{in}}}\), the effective weight is:
\[
W_{\mathrm{eff}}=W+\frac{\alpha}{r}BA
\tag{20.5}\]
Factor \(A\) has shape \([r,d_{\text{in}}]\), and \(B\) has shape \([d_{\text{out}},r]\). Their product has the same shape as \(W\) and rank at most \(r\). The scale \(\alpha/r\) controls its contribution.
For a four-by-four identity base, choose \(r=1\), \(\alpha=1\), \(A=[1,0,-1,2]\), and \(B=[1,2,0,-1]^\top\). Their product is:
\[
BA=\left[\begin{aligned}1&\quad 0&\quad -1&\quad 2\\2&\quad 0&\quad -2&\quad 4\\0&\quad 0&\quad 0&\quad 0\\-1&\quad 0&\quad 1&\quad -2\end{aligned}\right]
\tag{20.6}\]
Each row is a multiple of \(A\), showing its rank-one structure. For input \(x=(1,0,1,0)^\top\), \(Ax=0\), so the adapter contributes zero and the output remains \(x\).
For \(x=(1,0,0,0)^\top\), \(Ax=1\) and \(BAx=(1,2,0,-1)^\top\). Adding the identity base output gives \((2,2,0,-1)^\top\). The same adapter can therefore leave one input unchanged while changing another.
The two factors contain eight trainable values, compared with sixteen in a full four-by-four update. More generally:
\[
\operatorname{params}_{\mathrm{LoRA}}=r(d_{\mathrm{in}}+d_{\mathrm{out}})
\tag{20.7}\]
For a \(4096\times4096\) weight and \(r=8\), each factor contains 32,768 values. The total is 65,536, compared with 16,777,216 base values, or \(0.390625\%\). This fraction excludes other adapted layers, biases, and any additional trainable modules.






Figure 20.3: The frozen base output and the low-rank BA contribution are added for the same input.



A frozen weight still participates in forward computation. Gradients can pass through its operation to earlier trainable components without accumulating an update for that weight. LoRA commonly starts with nonzero random \(A\) and zero \(B\), giving a zero initial adapter contribution.
At that initialization, \(B\) can receive a gradient while \(A\) initially receives zero through the product. Initializing both factors to zero would block both product gradients. The following calculation verifies the complete matrix example and this initialization behavior.

Code example: A complete rank-one update and its initial gradients

import torch

W = torch.eye(4)
A = torch.tensor([[1., 0., -1., 2.]])
B = torch.tensor([[1.], [2.], [0.], [-1.]])
delta = B @ A
print(delta)
x_unchanged = torch.tensor([1., 0., 1., 0.])
x_changed = torch.tensor([1., 0., 0., 0.])
assert torch.equal((W + delta) @ x_unchanged, x_unchanged)
assert torch.equal((W + delta) @ x_changed, torch.tensor([2., 2., 0., -1.]))

A = A.clone().requires_grad_()
B = torch.zeros(4, 1, requires_grad=True)
output = W @ x_changed + B @ (A @ x_changed)
output.sum().backward()
assert W.grad is None
assert torch.count_nonzero(A.grad) == 0
assert torch.equal(B.grad, torch.ones(4, 1))
print(A.grad, B.grad)
Setting requires_grad=False excludes a tensor from gradient accumulation. The optimizer must also contain the intended trainable parameters and execute a step. The flag alone neither updates weights nor proves that the optimizer was configured correctly.
For inference, additive linear paths can be merged into one matrix.
\[
W_{\mathrm{merged}}=W+\frac{\alpha}{r}BA
\tag{20.8}\]
Merging removes the separate adapter branch but makes switching adapters less convenient. Supported PEFT models expose a merge operation such as merge_and_unload(). Quantized bases can require reconstruction or requantization, so merging may alter numerical results and needs validation.
LoRA reduces trainable parameter state, but the base weights and activation computation remain. Quantization addresses the base-weight storage component separately.

title: 20  Low-rank adaptation and preference alignment
text:
20.5 Quantized bases
Quantization represents values with a smaller set of stored codes. Dequantization reconstructs approximate numerical values from those codes for computation. Fewer bits can reduce weight storage while introducing reconstruction error.
A simple uniform quantizer uses scale \(s\) and zero point \(z\): \(q=\operatorname{clip}(\operatorname{round}(w/s)+z,q_{\min},q_{\max})\). Its reconstruction rule is:
\[
\hat{x}=\mathrm{scale}\cdot(q-\mathrm{zero\,point})
\tag{20.9}\]
The stored code identifies a level. Values between levels are rounded, and values beyond the representable range are clipped. The reconstructed number can therefore differ from the original even before any model calculation.






Figure 20.4: A quantized code needs both its scale and zero point to reconstruct a numerical value.



Block quantization gives smaller groups of values their own scales. This limits how far one outlier can stretch a shared range, at the cost of more scale metadata. For block \(b\) and value index \(i\):
\[
\hat{w}_{b,i}=s_b(q_{b,i}-z_b)
\tag{20.10}\]
With code 13, scale \(0.1\), and zero point 3, the reconstructed weight is \(0.1(13-3)=1\). Double quantization also compresses the collection of block scales.
\[
\hat{s}_b=s_s(q_b^{s}-z_s)
\tag{20.11}\]
If the scale code is 8, its reconstruction scale is \(0.01\), and its zero point is zero, the reconstructed block scale is \(0.08\). Using that reconstructed scale with weight code 13 and zero point 3 gives \(0.8\). This second approximation changes the reconstructed weight again.
NormalFloat 4, or NF4, uses sixteen nonuniform reconstruction levels with greater resolution near zero. It was designed for approximately normally distributed normalized weights. An NF4 code selects a lookup level that is then scaled, rather than using the uniform zero-point formula above.
Quantized Low-Rank Adaptation, or QLoRA, combines a frozen quantized base with trainable LoRA factors. Its forward calculation can be represented as:
\[
y=\operatorname{dequant}(W_{4\mathrm{bit}})x+\frac{\alpha}{r}BAx
\tag{20.12}\]
Low-bit codes determine how the base is stored. A supported floating-point compute dtype, such as bfloat16, determines how reconstructed values participate in arithmetic. The adapter path retains trainable values in a suitable higher precision. QLoRA combines this approach with NF4, double quantization, and memory-management techniques.
The following setup function expects an actual causal-model checkpoint, its revision, and compatible projection names. It uses PyTorch, Transformers, PEFT, bitsandbytes, and hardware that supports the selected quantized path and compute dtype. The PEFT quantization guide specifies preparation before adapter insertion.

Code example: Preparing a compatible quantized causal model for adapter training

import torch
from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, BitsAndBytesConfig
from peft import LoraConfig, get_peft_model, prepare_model_for_kbit_training

def make_qlora(checkpoint_id, revision, target_modules):
    quantization = BitsAndBytesConfig(
        load_in_4bit=True,
        bnb_4bit_quant_type="nf4",
        bnb_4bit_compute_dtype=torch.bfloat16,
        bnb_4bit_use_double_quant=True,
    )
    base = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(
        checkpoint_id, revision=revision,
        quantization_config=quantization,
    )
    base = prepare_model_for_kbit_training(base)
    config = LoraConfig(
        r=8, lora_alpha=16, target_modules=target_modules,
        bias="none", task_type="CAUSAL_LM",
    )
    model = get_peft_model(base, config)
    model.print_trainable_parameters()
    trainable = [key for key, parameter in model.named_parameters() if parameter.requires_grad]
    if not trainable:
        raise RuntimeError("No trainable adapter parameters were attached")
    return model
Rank 8 and \(\alpha=16\) give adapter scale 2. The caller chooses projection names that exist in the checkpoint, such as q_proj and v_proj for a compatible architecture. Adapting all supported linear layers is a broader choice with a different trainable parameter count.
The printed parameter report should show which values are trainable. It does not establish that a training batch fits in memory. Activations, optimizer state, reconstruction buffers, and the device’s kernels also matter. Chapter 23 examines these storage lifetimes.
The complete experiment in Section 24.6 specifies the checkpoints, target records, and before-and-after evaluation. Quantization and low-rank updates should be assessed against that task evidence, rather than inferred from compression ratios.

title: 20  Low-rank adaptation and preference alignment
text:
20.6 Distillation and pruning
Adapters reduce the cost of changing a base, but the deployed model can still be large. Knowledge distillation trains a student model from outputs supplied by a teacher model. Pruning removes selected parts of a model’s existing parameter structure.
Distillation can use teacher-generated answers as training examples. It can also match teacher probability distributions or selected intermediate representations. Matching probabilities requires compatible output meanings, and comparing intermediate values may require an additional projection when their widths differ.
Soft teacher targets preserve alternatives that a single hard label discards. If a teacher assigns \((0.7,0.2,0.1)\), a student can learn that the second class is a more plausible alternative than the third. A cross-entropy or KL objective from Chapter 8 measures the distribution mismatch.
For teacher distribution \((0.75,0.25)\) and student distribution \((0.5,0.5)\), their cross-entropy is \(0.693147\) and the teacher entropy is approximately \(0.562335\). The KL divergence is therefore approximately \(0.130812\). The teacher’s uncertainty remains part of the target.
Some methods soften both distributions with a temperature before comparing them. That changes the training target and requires a defined temperature and loss scale. Other methods match teacher answers directly and do not require shared token-level distributions.
A small language model has fewer parameters relative to the compared larger model. There is no universal size boundary implied here. A smaller student can lower storage and computation, but the teacher’s quality does not automatically transfer to it.
Pruning uses a stated criterion to remove weights, channels, attention heads, or larger structures. Unstructured pruning removes individual weights. Structured pruning removes complete groups that an implementation can more readily exclude from dense operations.
Setting many weights to zero does not guarantee less memory or faster dense matrix multiplication. The storage format and kernels must exploit the removed structure. Quality can also fall, requiring further training or a less aggressive pruning decision.
These choices change different objects. Distillation changes the student’s supervision, pruning changes retained structure, and quantization changes numerical representation. LoRA constrains an update, while the expert routing in Section 17.6 selects active computation. A model can combine several of them.
Choose the intervention from the observed failure and resource constraint. Measure task quality, retained base behavior, and the relevant memory or latency cost. Chapter 21 follows the adapted model into the request-processing loop where those serving costs become visible.

Chapter checkpoint
A model’s facts are outdated, but its response format is reliable. What experiment would distinguish an evidence problem from a behavior problem?
Feedback: Evaluate the same questions with current, relevant evidence supplied in context. Inspect whether retrieval found the evidence and whether generation used it correctly before selecting a training change.
Both LoRA factors start at zero and remain unchanged. What derivative explains the failure?
Feedback: Each factor’s product gradient contains the other factor. Both zero factors block both gradients through that path. A zero output contribution can instead use one nonzero factor and one zero factor.
Four-bit base weights fit in device memory, but training fails during backward. Which memory categories remain to be measured?
Feedback: Inspect saved activations, gradients and optimizer state for trainable parameters, temporary reconstruction buffers, and other runtime allocations. Base-weight storage is only one part of training memory.

title: 21  KV cache and serving
text:
21.1 Prefill and decode
A generated answer grows one token at a time. Recomputing the entire prefix for every prediction would repeat much of the same transformer work. A key-value cache preserves reusable attention state, while a serving scheduler decides how requests share computation and memory.
We follow one request first, then examine cache capacity, user-visible timing, and shared scheduling. This keeps the model’s state transitions connected to the costs that an application measures.
The causal block in Chapter 17 cannot change an earlier representation when a later token is appended. Under fixed weights and inference settings, its earlier keys and values can therefore be reused.
Prefill processes the available prompt and computes attention keys and values for its positions at every layer. The KV cache stores those keys and values. It does not need to store every earlier logit or complete hidden representation.
The final valid prompt position already produces logits for the first output token. Selecting that token uses the decoding rule from Chapter 7. A separate forward pass on the newly selected token is needed only to produce the following token’s logits.
Decode repeatedly processes the newest selected token, calculates its query, key, and value at each layer, and appends the new key and value. Its query reads the earlier cache together with the newly processed position.
\[
\mathrm{cache}_t=\operatorname{append}(\mathrm{cache}_{t-1},K_t,V_t)
\tag{21.1}\]
For a three-token prompt, prefill creates three cached positions and produces the distribution for token four. Processing token four extends the cache to four positions and produces the distribution for token five. If generation stops after selecting token four, that token need not be processed into the cache.
The cache therefore counts processed positions, not necessarily every token already emitted. In a simple batch, prompt IDs have shape \([B,T_{\text{prompt}}]\) and prefill logits have shape \([B,T_{\text{prompt}},|V|]\). Selecting the final valid position gives logits \([B,|V|]\).
A subsequent decode input has shape \([B,1]\). Each layer reuses its earlier state and calculates only the new position’s transformation. For a right-padded batch, logits[:, -1, :] may select padding, so the final valid position or the model’s supported padding convention matters.
The new query still reads the permitted earlier keys and values. Its attention work grows with current context length even though earlier projections are reused. Caching reduces repeated computation without making each step independent of the prefix size.

title: 21  KV cache and serving
text:
21.2 Cache capacity
Reusing earlier values saves arithmetic but retains state for every active request. Its size depends on layer count, cached positions, numerical format, and the number of key-value heads.
In standard multi-head attention, each query head has corresponding key and value projections. Multi-query attention, or MQA, shares one key-value head across several query heads. Grouped-query attention, or GQA, shares one key-value head within each group of query heads.
These variants retain several query comparisons while reducing the number of stored key and value vectors. They are architecture choices, rather than a safe switch for arbitrarily discarding heads from an already trained model.
For one layer, the logical cache tensors have shape:
\[
K,V\in\mathbb{R}^{B\times H_{\mathrm{KV}}\times T\times d_h}
\tag{21.2}\]
Here \(B\) is the number of requests in a uniform-length batch, \(H_{\text{KV}}\) is key-value head count, \(T\) is cached length, and \(d_h\) is head width. With \(L\) layers and \(s\) bytes per stored scalar, total logical storage is:
\[
\mathrm{bytes}=2\cdot\mathrm{layers}\cdot B\cdot H_{\mathrm{KV}}\cdot T\cdot d_h\cdot s
\tag{21.3}\]
The factor two counts both keys and values. Appending one processed position for every request in that batch increases storage by:
\[
\Delta\mathrm{bytes}_{\mathrm{per\ token}}=2LBH_{\mathrm{KV}}d_hs
\tag{21.4}\]
For one request, one layer, one key-value head, width two, and two-byte values, a three-position cache uses 24 bytes. Processing another token increases it to 32 bytes. Each of its key and value tensors changes from \([1,1,3,2]\) to \([1,1,4,2]\).






Figure 21.3: Processing one more position adds a key and a value, increasing this cache from 24 to 32 bytes.



A separate example uses two layers, four key-value heads, width eight, one request, and two-byte storage. At five positions, each key or value tensor holds 160 values, or 320 bytes. Across both layers and both tensors, the total is 1,280 bytes.
Processed positions | Total logical cache bytes | |—:|—:| | 5 | 1,280 | | 6 | 1,536 | | 7 | 1,792 | | 8 | 2,048 |
Each additional processed position adds 256 bytes. The decode input remains \([1,1]\), while the attention operation reads the growing cache and returns the next vocabulary-logit vector.
The following function estimates this logical storage in gibibytes, where one GiB is \(1024^3\) bytes.

Code example: A simple KV-cache memory estimate.

def kv_cache_gib(
    layers, batch, kv_heads, seq_len, head_dim,
    bytes_per_value=2,
):
    bytes_total = (
        2 * layers * batch * kv_heads * seq_len
        * head_dim * bytes_per_value
    )
    return bytes_total / 1024**3

print(
    kv_cache_gib(
        layers=32, batch=1, kv_heads=8,
        seq_len=8192, head_dim=128,
    )
)
assert kv_cache_gib(32, 1, 8, 8192, 128) == 1.0
For 32 layers, eight key-value heads, 8,192 positions, width 128, and two-byte values, the result is one GiB per request. A model with 32 query heads would use four times as much cache if it also stored 32 key-value heads of that width.
For unequal request lengths, sum their cached positions instead of using one common \(BT\). Physical allocation also includes partially filled blocks and metadata. Shared prefixes can reduce duplication. Model weights, temporary activations, and other serving state are separate memory categories.

title: 21  KV cache and serving
text:
21.3 Latency and throughput
Cache capacity determines which requests can be admitted, but an application experiences waiting time and streaming speed. Define timing at the request boundary before comparing an optimization.
Time to first token, or TTFT, is the delay from submitting a request to receiving its first output token. A useful decomposition is:
\[
\mathrm{TTFT}=\mathrm{queue\ time}+\mathrm{prefill\ time}+\mathrm{first\ token\ selection\ and\ delivery\ time}
\tag{21.5}\]
The final term includes selecting and delivering the first token, which is produced from prefill’s final-position logits. It is not inherently a separate transformer decode forward pass. If queueing takes eight milliseconds, prefill twenty, and remaining first-token processing five, TTFT is 33 milliseconds.
Time per output token, or TPOT, describes a request’s spacing between output tokens after its first token. If \(n\ge2\) tokens arrive at times \(t_1,\ldots,t_n\), its mean interval is:
\[
\mathrm{TPOT}_{\mathrm{request}}=\frac{t_n-t_1}{n-1},\quad n\ge2
\tag{21.6}\]
A one-token response has no such interval. Report distributions across requests or intervals, with the aggregation rule stated, because a mean can hide long pauses.
Aggregate throughput counts output tokens from all requests per unit time. If a batch produces forty tokens in 200 milliseconds, its throughput is 200 tokens per second. The reciprocal, five milliseconds per aggregate token, is not the TPOT experienced by each request.
For example, four active requests can each produce one token every twenty milliseconds. Across ten steps, they produce forty tokens in 200 milliseconds, while each stream has twenty-millisecond intervals. Batching raises total output rate without making each individual stream emit a token every five milliseconds.
Prefill often exposes large matrix operations over many positions. Decode processes fewer new positions per request and repeatedly reads weights and cache values. Whether either phase is limited by arithmetic, memory bandwidth, or scheduling depends on the workload and hardware.
Measure prompt and output lengths, active request counts, numerical formats, and arrival patterns alongside timings. An optimization can improve throughput while increasing queueing or delaying individual streams.

title: 21  KV cache and serving
text:
21.4 Scheduling requests
Requests arrive at different times and finish after different output lengths. A simple fixed batch can leave completed slots unused while a long request continues. Continuous batching admits and removes requests between model steps.
The scheduler combines currently active inputs, then routes each output back to its request. Token history, cache positions, validity rules, and sampling state remain separate. The stopping rules are those in Chapter 7.
A larger active batch can use hardware more efficiently, but may increase waiting or processing time for a particular request. Head-of-line blocking occurs when a long operation prevents later work from progressing on a shared schedule.
Chunked prefill splits an incoming prompt into smaller pieces that can be interleaved with existing decode work. Each chunk retains the prompt’s earlier state and correct positions.
Suppose one request has a twelve-token prompt while two others are decoding. An uninterrupted prefill processes all twelve prompt tokens before the existing requests receive their next scheduled step. With four-token chunks, a possible schedule is prefill four, decode, prefill four, decode, then prefill four.
In this illustrative schedule, the new prompt completes later because other work is interleaved. The existing streams encounter shorter interruptions. Actual timing also depends on how efficiently each chunk executes.






Figure 21.4: Four-token prefill chunks let existing decode streams take steps before the new prompt finishes.



Continuous batching decides which requests share a step. Chunking limits the amount of prompt work admitted at once. Both require a cache allocator that can accommodate changing request lengths without moving every earlier value.

title: 21  KV cache and serving
text:
21.5 Paged cache blocks
Reserving one large contiguous cache region for every request can waste space when lengths are uncertain. PagedAttention divides a request’s logical cache into fixed-size blocks and maps them to physical blocks that need not be adjacent. A block table tells the attention kernel where each logical segment resides. PagedAttention introduces this organization for language-model serving.
Consider a simplified allocator with four token positions per block. A nine-position request needs three logical blocks. Its block table might map them to physical blocks \([5,1,9]\).
Zero-based token position 6 belongs to logical block \(\lfloor6/4\rfloor=1\) at offset \(6\bmod4=2\). The block table maps it to physical block 1, offset 2. Token position 8 maps to physical block 9, offset 0.
The request occupies twelve allocated positions, of which nine contain values. Its last block has three unused slots. The internal fragmentation in this example is the space reserved inside that partially filled block.
Appending positions 9, 10, and 11 fills the remaining slots. Position 12 requires another physical block and a new table entry. The earlier logical positions keep their meanings even if physical blocks are scattered in memory.
The kernel uses the mapping while reading keys and values. Allocation can therefore grow without requiring one adjacent region for the entire sequence. It still needs metadata and suitable access patterns, and block size affects wasted capacity and management cost. The vLLM design description explains the kernel-side layout.
When a request finishes, blocks can return to the free pool once no other request references them. Reference counts or an equivalent mechanism are needed if multiple requests share cached prefixes.

title: 21  KV cache and serving
text:
21.6 Prefix reuse and offloading
The per-request cache avoids recomputing a growing continuation. A prefix cache extends reuse across requests whose initial token sequences match. Their shared prompt state can be computed once and referenced by later requests.






Figure 21.5: Matching requests reference one immutable prefix while keeping separate writable suffix blocks.



Reuse requires the same effective model weights, including active adapters, and a compatible cache interpretation. Token IDs, position handling, attention settings, and any input features affecting the prefix must match. Similar-looking text is insufficient if its tokenization differs.
Shared blocks must remain unchanged while other requests reference them. If a request needs to extend a partially shared block, a copy-on-write policy can allocate its own copy before modification. Other requests retain their original prefix state.
Prefix caching can reduce repeated prompt processing. It does not directly remove queueing or the work of generating a new suffix. Full-prefix hits also require a valid way to obtain the next-token logits, since stored keys and values alone are not those logits. The vLLM prefix-caching guide describes the scope of its reuse.
Cache offloading stores selected cache blocks in another memory tier, such as host memory, when accelerator capacity is tight. A later attention operation must make any required offloaded values available again. The capacity saving therefore introduces transfer and scheduling costs.
For two long requests whose caches do not fit together, offloading can admit more stored context. A decode step may then wait for required blocks to transfer. Compare capacity, transfer time, TTFT, and TPOT under the actual request mix.
High-level model.generate(use_cache=True) supports an initial inspection of state reuse with a compatible model. Serving runtimes such as vLLM, SGLang, and TensorRT-LLM add scheduling and memory-management choices. Their precise controls differ, so engine-specific flags are not interchangeable transformer operations.
Cache layout and scheduling aim to preserve the model’s computation while changing its execution. Numerical kernels and sampling state can still affect reproducibility. Check output behavior as well as speed when changing a serving configuration.
The same representation and resource questions extend beyond text. Chapter 22 examines the additional input processing required for images, audio, and tables.

Chapter checkpoint
A three-token prompt has just produced its first output token. How many positions must already be in its ordinary KV cache?
Feedback: Three prompt positions. The selected fourth token enters the cache when a subsequent forward pass processes it to predict token five, if generation continues.
An optimization doubles aggregate throughput while the spacing within each response is unchanged. Is its TPOT twice as good?
Feedback: No. More concurrent streams can raise throughput while each stream keeps the same token intervals. Report per-request timing separately from total token rate.
A prefix string is unchanged after switching adapters. Can the old prefix state be reused automatically?
Feedback: No. The effective weights changed, so the cached keys and values may differ. The reuse key must account for the active model and adapter configuration.

title: 22  Images, audio, and multimodal models
text:
22.1 Image features and patches
A transformer receives vectors, but pixels, audio samples, and table fields have different structures. Their first representation must preserve the information the task needs. Connecting these representations to text also requires a suitable training objective or generation interface.
This chapter follows each input through its conversion, then distinguishes matching across modalities from generating an answer about them. The final comparison asks which model structure is justified by the data and task.
An image contains neighboring pixels on a two-dimensional grid. A model can exploit those local relationships before combining information over a larger region. A convolution applies a shared weighted filter to local neighborhoods.
For unit stride, one output value is:
\[
Y_{i,j,c_{\mathrm{out}}}=b_{c_{\mathrm{out}}}+\sum_{u,v,c_{\mathrm{in}}}W_{u,v,c_{\mathrm{in}},c_{\mathrm{out}}}X_{i+u,j+v,c_{\mathrm{in}}}
\tag{22.1}\]
Here \(X\) is the input feature map, \(W\) contains filter weights, and \(b\) is the output-channel bias. Indices \(i,j\) identify an output location, \(u,v\) identify filter offsets, and the channel indices select input and output features. Deep-learning libraries usually implement this unflipped-filter form, mathematically a cross-correlation, under the convolution name.
For a two-by-two patch \([[1,2],[3,4]]\), a kernel of ones and zero bias produces \(1+2+3+4=10\). Moving the kernel to another neighborhood reuses the same learned weights.
Stride is the distance between successive filter positions. Padding supplies values around the input border. With dilation one, kernel width \(k\), stride \(s\), and padding \(p\) on both sides, one output dimension is:
\[
n_{\mathrm{out}}=\left\lfloor\frac{n_{\mathrm{in}}+2p-k}{s}\right\rfloor+1
\tag{22.2}\]
The floor counts complete filter placements. For input width five, kernel width three, no padding, and stride one, the output width is three. A valid configuration must permit at least one placement.
Repeated filters share a detection rule across image locations. After nonlinear activation, spatial pooling or strided layers can reduce resolution, allowing later features to combine information from a wider input region. Sharing a filter does not make the complete classifier invariant to every translation, crop, or background change.
A wolf classifier that relies on snow may succeed on familiar photographs and fail on wolves against other backgrounds. Keep subject and background variation in the evaluation design. This is the same shortcut-learning problem as the spurious text features discussed in Section 9.1.
A convolutional neural network, or CNN, stacks these local transformations. A residual network, or ResNet, adds compatible inputs around learned convolutional branches. The residual mechanism is the one from Section 17.3.
A vision transformer, or ViT, instead processes a sequence of projected image regions called patch tokens. Dividing an image of height \(H\) and width \(W\) into nonoverlapping square patches of side \(P\) gives:
\[
N_{\mathrm{patches}}=\left(\frac{H}{P}\right)\left(\frac{W}{P}\right)
\tag{22.3}\]
This expression assumes \(P\) divides both dimensions. Otherwise preprocessing must crop or pad explicitly. Flattening each \(P\times P\) patch with \(C\) channels creates \(P^2C\) values. A learned matrix projects that vector to model width \(D\).
\[
Z=\operatorname{flatten}(\mathrm{patches})W_{\mathrm{patch}},\quad Z\in\mathbb{R}^{B\times N\times D}
\tag{22.4}\]
Here \(W_{\text{patch}}\) has shape \([P^2C,D]\), and \(Z\) has shape \([B,N,D]\) for \(N\) patches. Position information preserves their locations, using the principles in Section 17.2.
A \(224\times224\) image with \(16\times16\) patches produces \(14\times14=196\) positions. An additional classification token would make 197. Halving patch side length to eight gives 784 patch positions, four times as many. Their full pairwise attention count increases by a factor of sixteen.
In a separate smaller example, a \(32\times32\) RGB image with \(8\times8\) patches produces sixteen tokens. Each patch contains \(8(8)(3)=192\) values. Projection to width 64 gives shape \([B,16,64]\) before any optional classification token.
Patch projection itself can be implemented by a convolution whose kernel and stride both equal the patch size. The following code applies that operation to two RGB images, then converts the spatial output grid into a sequence.
The grid has shape \([2,64,14,14]\), and the sequence has shape \([2,196,64]\). flatten(2) combines the spatial axes, while transpose(1,2) puts patch positions before features. Subsequent transformer blocks consume those vectors after the model’s position and token conventions are applied.
Local filters and patch attention encode different assumptions about useful relationships. Neither representation by itself explains how an image should match a sentence.

title: 22  Images, audio, and multimodal models
text:
Figure 22.2: The identity path preserves an input while the learned branch adds a compatible correction.
















Figure 22.3: Sixteen image patches each become a 192-value row, then project to 64 model coordinates.





Code example: Patchifying an image with a strided convolution

import torch
import torch.nn as nn

torch.manual_seed(7)
images = torch.randn(2, 3, 224, 224)
patch_projection = nn.Conv2d(in_channels=3, out_channels=64, kernel_size=16, stride=16)

patch_grid = patch_projection(images)          # [2, 64, 14, 14]
patch_sequence = patch_grid.flatten(2).transpose(1, 2)  # [2, 196, 64]

print(patch_grid.shape)
print(patch_sequence.shape)
assert patch_grid.shape == (2, 64, 14, 14)
assert patch_sequence.shape == (2, 196, 64)

title: 22  Images, audio, and multimodal models
text:
22.2 Matching images and text
An image-retrieval task needs a comparable score for an image and a text query. Contrastive Language-Image Pre-training, or CLIP, learns separate image and text encoders whose outputs can be compared. Its training data supplies matching image-caption pairs. The CLIP paper develops this paired supervision.
For \(B\) pairs, normalize their embedding vectors and compute a similarity matrix \(S\) with shape \([B,B]\). Row \(i\) compares image \(i\) with every caption. Column \(j\) compares caption \(j\) with every image. The recorded matches occupy the diagonal.
A contrastive loss rewards matched pairs relative to comparison candidates. CLIP uses both image-to-text and text-to-image cross-entropy, with temperature \(\tau>0\):
\[
L_{\mathrm{CLIP}}=\frac{1}{2}\left[\operatorname{CE}\!\left(\frac{S}{\tau},y\right)+\operatorname{CE}\!\left(\frac{S^{T}}{\tau},y\right)\right]
\tag{22.5}\]
Here \(y=(0,\ldots,B-1)\) supplies zero-based diagonal class indices to the code. Each cross-entropy receives scaled similarity logits and averages its batch. The final factor one half averages the two directions.
Consider temperature-scaled scores \(S/\tau=\begin{bmatrix}\log9&0\\\log2&\log8\end{bmatrix}\). The first image row gives its correct caption probability \(9/(9+1)=0.9\). The second gives its correct caption probability \(8/(2+8)=0.8\).
The image-to-text loss is \([-\log(0.9)-\log(0.8)]/2\approx0.164252\). Reversing the direction requires normalizing the columns of the same matrix. Their correct-image probabilities are \(9/11\) and \(8/9\).
The text-to-image loss is \([-\log(9/11)-\log(8/9)]/2\approx0.159227\). Averaging both directions gives approximately \(0.161739\). The following calculation verifies all three values.

Code example: The two directions of a contrastive batch loss

import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F

scaled_scores = torch.log(torch.tensor([[9., 1.], [2., 8.]], dtype=torch.float64))
targets = torch.arange(2)
image_loss = F.cross_entropy(scaled_scores, targets)
text_loss = F.cross_entropy(scaled_scores.T, targets)
loss = (image_loss + text_loss) / 2
print(image_loss.item(), text_loss.item(), loss.item())
assert abs(image_loss.item() - 0.164252033486018) < 1e-9
assert abs(text_loss.item() - 0.159226865559) < 1e-9
assert abs(loss.item() - 0.161739449523) < 1e-9






Figure 22.4: The same image-text score matrix gives two losses by normalizing rows and columns separately.



The batch provides comparison candidates without separately listing every negative example. However, an unmatched caption can still correctly describe another image. Such ambiguous pairs can give a misleading training signal and require attention to dataset construction.
At inference, either encoder can supply a vector for similarity-based retrieval. CLIP’s matching score does not itself generate a caption or answer a question. A task requiring text output needs an additional generation component.
Image captioning generates a description conditioned on visual features. Visual question answering, or VQA, also conditions on a question. A vision encoder can supply projected vectors to a language decoder through a supported combined-input or cross-attention interface.
The conditional-generation mechanics follow Chapter 18. The visual preprocessing and connection to the language model must match its training. A generic feature vector cannot simply be inserted into any unrelated text model.
Two other representation choices clarify this distinction. A vector-quantized variational autoencoder, or VQ-VAE, selects entries from a learned codebook, a finite table of vectors, to represent encoded input regions. Its decoder reconstructs the input from those selected vectors. Neural Discrete Representation Learning introduces this approach.
For encoded vector \((0.9,0.1)\) and codebook entries \((0,0)\), \((1,0)\), and \((0,1)\), the nearest entry is \((1,0)\). Its squared distance is \(0.02\), compared with \(0.82\) and \(1.62\) for the others. The selected entry’s index can be treated as a discrete token.
Training combines reconstruction with terms that keep the encoder outputs and codebook entries close. Nearest-entry selection is discrete. A common gradient approximation treats that selection as an identity operation for the encoder’s backward path. This is different from uniformly rounding a stored weight in Section 20.5.
The Vision-and-Language Transformer, or ViLT, processes projected image patches and text tokens together, avoiding a separate heavy convolutional region-feature stage. The ViLT paper describes this joint interaction architecture. It differs from CLIP’s separate encoders and pairwise output comparison.
In merged attention, image and text vectors enter one sequence after projection to a compatible width. Modality indicators distinguish their origins, while position information retains spatial or textual relationships. With two image patches and three text tokens, full self-attention compares five positions through a \(5\times5\) score matrix, excluding extra special tokens.
Cross-attention can instead connect separate streams. Three text queries attending to two image positions produce a \(3\times2\) score matrix. The query, key, and value mechanics remain those in Chapter 16. Separate encoders whose final vectors are only compared, as in CLIP, do not by themselves perform this cross-attention.
ViLT combines objectives for matching paired inputs, reconstructing selected text tokens, and relating words to patches. These supervision signals act on a representation where the modalities already interact. Cropping and flipping can expand image training variation, but an augmentation must preserve the caption or label’s meaning. Flipping an image described as “the cup on the left” can violate that condition.
The combined experiment in Section 24.7 evaluates retrieval separately from captioning and answering. That separation shows whether an error arose in matching evidence, interpreting the image, or producing the answer.

title: 22  Images, audio, and multimodal models
text:
22.3 Audio samples and spectral frames
An audio recording changes over time rather than across an image grid. A waveform is a sequence of sampled amplitudes. Its sampling rate states how many samples represent one second, and its channels represent separate recorded signals.
Pulse-code modulation, or PCM, stores quantized amplitude samples. Bit depth controls the available amplitude codes. Sampling rate and bit depth describe different properties: temporal sampling and amplitude resolution.
A 44.1 kHz, 16-bit stereo recording stores 44,100 sample frames per second, each containing two channel values. Its uncompressed sample payload is \(44{,}100\times2\times2=176{,}400\) bytes per second, excluding headers. A model expecting mono at another rate needs an explicit channel conversion and resampling step.
A frequency analysis can reveal oscillations in these samples. Applying one Fourier transform to a whole recording does not retain a separate description of when each frequency occurs. The short-time Fourier transform, or STFT, analyzes a sequence of local windows instead.
For the complete-frame convention used here, each window contains \(N\) samples and the hop \(R>0\) is the distance between window starts. Frame \(m\) begins at sample \(mR\). Its transform is:
\[
X[m,k]=\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}x[mR+n]w[n]\exp\!\left(-\frac{2\pi i kn}{N}\right)
\tag{22.6}\]
The local index \(n\) runs from zero to \(N-1\), so the waveform value is \(x[mR+n]\). The window \(w[n]\) weights those samples. The frequency-bin index is \(k\), and \(i\) denotes the imaginary unit. The complex result records magnitude and phase for that frame and frequency.
For four samples \((1,0,-1,0)\) and a rectangular window, the zero-frequency component is their sum, zero. The four-point transform is \((0,2,0,2)\) under this convention. The nonzero components capture the alternating structure that the zero-frequency sum misses.
The discrete Fourier transform, or DFT, is the finite transform evaluated above. A fast Fourier transform, or FFT, is an efficient algorithm for computing it. The FFT does not itself choose the windows or advance through time.
An inverse DFT reconstructs the windowed samples when the full complex coefficients and matching normalization are retained. Magnitudes alone discard phase. A mel representation also combines frequency bins, so it generally cannot be inverted to the original waveform exactly. Spectral features are a modeling choice: some systems learn directly from waveform samples.
Moving to another frame must advance the waveform indices. For samples \([0,0,0,0,1,1,1,1]\), window length four and hop four give zero-frequency sums zero and four. Shifting only the window while reusing the first four waveform samples would miss the second segment.
The number of complete left-aligned frames is:
\[
F=\left\lfloor\frac{S-N}{R}\right\rfloor+1,\quad S\ge N
\tag{22.7}\]
Here \(S\) is the total sample count, and the expression assumes \(S\ge N\). Starts \(0,R,2R,\ldots\) are valid when \(mR+N\le S\). Counting from frame zero produces the final plus one. If \(S<N\), this convention yields zero complete frames and handles that case separately.
For \(S=8\), \(N=4\), and \(R=4\), starts zero and four give two frames. For \(S=10\), \(N=4\), and \(R=3\), starts zero, three, and six give three. Centering or padding in a library call can produce a different frame count.
The following NumPy calculation checks the spectrum, advancing frame indices, and the short-input case under this exact convention.

Code example: Complete spectral frames with explicit sample indices

import numpy as np

def complete_stft(samples, window, hop):
    samples = np.asarray(samples, dtype=float)
    window = np.asarray(window, dtype=float)
    if samples.ndim != 1 or window.ndim != 1 or len(window) == 0:
        raise ValueError("Use one-dimensional samples and a nonempty window")
    if not isinstance(hop, int) or hop <= 0:
        raise ValueError("Hop must be a positive integer")
    width = len(window)
    starts = range(0, len(samples) - width + 1, hop)
    frames = [np.fft.fft(samples[start:start + width] * window) for start in starts]
    return np.stack(frames) if frames else np.empty((0, width), dtype=complex)

single = complete_stft([1, 0, -1, 0], np.ones(4), 4)
shifted = complete_stft([0, 0, 0, 0, 1, 1, 1, 1], np.ones(4), 4)
np.testing.assert_allclose(single[0], [0, 2, 0, 2])
np.testing.assert_allclose(shifted[:, 0], [0, 4])
assert shifted.shape == (2, 4)
assert complete_stft(np.arange(10), np.ones(4), 3).shape == (3, 4)
assert complete_stft([1, 2], np.ones(4), 2).shape == (0, 4)
print(single, shifted[:, 0])
Stacking the frame spectra produces a time-frequency matrix. A mel filterbank groups spectral energy into perceptually spaced frequency bands. A mel spectrogram records these band values over time, often followed by logarithmic scaling.
Whisper is an encoder-decoder speech model that processes log-mel audio features and generates text tokens. Its overall feature-to-encoder-to-decoder path is described in Robust Speech Recognition. This chapter’s four-sample example illustrates the transform, not Whisper’s actual preprocessing dimensions.






Figure 22.5: Encoded audio supplies cross-attention context while the causal decoder predicts text tokens.



The model’s expected sample rate, window settings, channel handling, and feature scaling must be preserved. Recognition quality can differ across languages, recording conditions, and domains. A strong result on one language or dataset does not establish performance on another.
Different output requirements explain the other audio systems discussed in the course. wav2vec 2.0 learns speech representations from waveform input. It masks latent positions and trains a contrastive prediction against quantized targets. Fine-tuning with transcriptions then supports speech recognition. This representation-learning model is not a waveform decoder.
AudioLM instead generates audio continuations through discrete token sequences. Semantic tokens describe longer-range structure, while acoustic tokens retain details needed by an audio codec’s decoder. Predicting more tokens extends an audio prompt, and decoding their acoustic representation returns a waveform. Text token generation alone cannot reconstruct those acoustic details.
SpeechVerse connects representations from a speech model to a language model through a small set of trainable parameters. Audio and a textual instruction can then condition a text response, such as a transcription or task answer. The speech and text base models stay frozen in its described training setup. Its interface combines the adaptation principle from Chapter 20 with the cross-modal connections discussed above.
These systems have different outputs: recognition text, generated audio, or an instruction-conditioned answer. Choose an evaluation that matches the output. A correct transcript does not establish natural audio synthesis, and plausible audio does not establish transcription accuracy.

title: 22  Images, audio, and multimodal models
text:
22.4 Tabular fields
A table row has distinct fields whose types and units can differ. Its column order is usually a schema convention rather than the time or spatial order of a signal. The representation should preserve field identity and missing-value meaning.
Categorical values can select embedding rows, following Chapter 13. Numeric values can be standardized using training-set statistics or passed through learned projections. Missing values need an explicit indicator or handling rule rather than an accidental ordinary value.
TabTransformer uses attention over categorical field embeddings. Other tabular transformer designs also turn numeric fields into vectors. The details differ, so a schema-to-vector mapping must identify both the value and its field.
In the original TabTransformer arrangement, the contextual categorical vectors are concatenated with normalized numerical fields before an MLP predicts the target. For three categorical vectors of width four and two numeric values, that classifier receives \(3(4)+2=14\) coordinates. This separates attention over categories from the final mixed-field prediction.
For a design that represents every field, \(B\) records with \(F\) fields can produce a tensor \([B,F,D]\). Attention compares fields within each record. It does not make identically encoded values from different columns interchangeable.
The course also compares gradient-boosted decision trees, an ensemble that adds trees sequentially to improve the current predictions under a loss. Trees partition feature values through decision rules, providing a different way to model nonlinear field interactions.
A regularized linear model and boosted trees provide useful comparison points for supervised tables. Match their training and validation splits and compare quality, missing-value behavior, and resource cost. A transformer can be useful when its representations or transfer learning offer an advantage, but table format alone does not establish that advantage.

title: 22  Images, audio, and multimodal models
text:
22.5 Choosing the input model
Each conversion preserves some structure and discards other detail. A model choice should follow the required output and observed errors, together with the cost of processing its representations.
Input or task | Representation and comparison | |—|—| | Image classification | Compare local convolutional features with patch-based models under the required resolution and data budget | | Speech transcription | Preserve the time axis and preprocessing contract, then compare suitable sequence models on the target recordings | | Supervised table | Preserve field types and missing values, with linear and tree baselines alongside richer models | | Image-text retrieval | Compare normalized representations and inspect the ranking of relevant candidates | | Captioning or VQA | Evaluate generated text conditioned on image features, separating visual errors from response errors |
The expensive stage can be input feature extraction, attention over many patches or frames, or output generation. Expert routing, if present, follows Section 17.6 and adds its own scheduling costs. It is not an input modality.
The final system exercise in Section 24.7 records component outputs and combined failures. Chapter 23 first examines how these representations occupy tensor storage, so memory measurements can be interpreted correctly.

Chapter checkpoint
Halving a square patch’s side length leaves image resolution unchanged. How do patch count and full pairwise attention count change?
Feedback: Each image dimension contains twice as many patches, giving four times as many positions. Their full pair count grows by sixteen, excluding optional extra tokens.
A CLIP model retrieves the right image but cannot answer how many objects it contains. Which capability is still missing from that result?
Feedback: Retrieval establishes a matching result, not accurate visual counting or conditional answer generation. Test those components separately before judging the combined system.
Two audio frames have different sample values but identical computed spectra. Which indexing error would you check first?
Feedback: Verify that frame \(m\) reads \(x[mR+n]\). Reusing \(x[n]\) can repeatedly analyze the first window instead of advancing through the waveform.
