title: 23  Tensor storage and execution
text:
23.1 Tensor size and storage
A model can fit a mathematical shape contract and still exceed device memory or spend time copying data. Shape describes the logical array. Storage, layout, and tensor lifetime explain the resources that executing it requires.
The tensor basics in Section 2.2 already support the earlier models. This chapter follows their physical representation, then connects shared storage and training state to useful memory measurements.
Estimating memory starts with the values an operation must represent. A tensor’s shape lists the lengths of its axes, and its dtype specifies the numerical representation of each element. Its device identifies where its values reside, such as CPU memory or a CUDA GPU.
Creation establishes both the initial values and their representation. torch.tensor([1, 2]) infers an integer dtype, while an explicit dtype=torch.float32 produces floating-point values. Choose the dtype from the operation’s contract: token IDs index a table, while learned weights participate in floating-point arithmetic.
zeros and ones initialize every element to a known value. arange(start, stop, step) generates a sequence excluding the stop value. linspace(start, stop, steps) requests a count of evenly spaced values, including both endpoints when that count exceeds one.
empty allocates a tensor without assigning useful initial values. Its contents must be written before they influence a result. It saves initialization work only when the subsequent operation overwrites every element that will be read.
Random initialization requires a distribution as well as a shape. rand samples uniformly from \([0,1)\), while randn uses a normal distribution with mean zero and standard deviation one. normal accepts other means and standard deviations. poisson draws nonnegative counts using supplied nonnegative rates. These choices model different quantities and cannot be exchanged just because their output shapes agree.
For reproducible small checks, set a random seed and record the environment. A seed controls a random-number sequence, but it does not guarantee identical results across every device or library version. The initialization discussion in Section 12.3 explains how the distribution affects learning.
The logical element count is:
\[
\operatorname{numel}(X)=\prod_i d_i
\tag{23.1}\]
Here \(d_i\) is the length of axis \(i\). A tensor with shape \([2,3,4]\) contains 24 logical elements. For fixed element size, their logical byte count is:
\[
\mathrm{logical\ bytes}(X)=\operatorname{numel}(X)\cdot\mathrm{bytes\ per\ element}
\tag{23.2}\]
Float32 uses four bytes per element, so this example represents \(24(4)=96\) bytes of values. The estimate excludes object metadata, allocator overhead, and unrelated tensors.
Storage is the underlying allocation that holds values. Several tensor objects can refer to the same storage. A small slice may also keep a much larger allocation alive. Consequently, adding every tensor’s logical byte count can double-count shared values or miss unused portions of retained storage.
The following example preserves the earlier \([4,8,16]\) batch. Its three axes represent examples, sequence positions, and hidden features. Inspecting those meanings alongside dtype and device establishes what later operations receive.
It reports 512 logical elements and 2,048 logical bytes on CPU. requires_grad is false, so this creation does not request gradient tracking. The values themselves are irrelevant to the size calculation.
For dense strided tensors, untyped_storage().nbytes() reports the size of the underlying storage. It does not establish how much additional memory that tensor required, because another tensor may own the same allocation. Device-wide allocator measurements answer a different question, revisited in Section 23.5.

title: 23  Tensor storage and execution
text:
Code example: PyTorch tensors carry dimensions, dtype, and device metadata.

import torch

x = torch.randn(4, 8, 16, dtype=torch.float32)
print(x.shape)   # batch=4, sequence=8, hidden=16
print(x.dtype)   # float32
print(x.device)  # cpu unless moved to cuda
print(x.numel(), x.numel() * x.element_size())
assert x.numel() == 512
assert x.numel() * x.element_size() == 2048
assert not x.requires_grad

title: 23  Tensor storage and execution
text:
23.2 Axes and broadcasting
The logical shape also determines whether an operation is valid. Before optimizing a tensor path, identify what each axis means and which axes the operation combines.
A feature vector has shape \([D]\), a batch of feature vectors \([B,D]\), and a token-ID batch \([B,T]\). Embedding lookup adds a feature axis, producing \([B,T,E]\). A language-model head then replaces the hidden width with a vocabulary axis, producing logits \([B,T,V]\).
For the matrix convention used in Chapter 5, a linear transformation is:
\[
X\in\mathbb{R}^{B\times D_{\mathrm{in}}},\quad W\in\mathbb{R}^{D_{\mathrm{in}}\times D_{\mathrm{out}}},\quad Y=XW+b\in\mathbb{R}^{B\times D_{\mathrm{out}}}
\tag{23.3}\]
The input \(X\) has shape \([B,D_{\mathrm{in}}]\), and the mathematical matrix \(W\) has shape \([D_{\mathrm{in}},D_{\mathrm{out}}]\). Contracting the shared input dimension leaves \([B,D_{\mathrm{out}}]\). Thus a \(2\times3\) input and a \(3\times4\) matrix produce a \(2\times4\) result.
PyTorch nn.Linear stores a parameter \(A\) with shape \([D_{\mathrm{out}},D_{\mathrm{in}}]\). The same operation is therefore \(XA^T+b\), with \(A=W^T\). Keeping these symbols separate avoids treating one stored matrix as both orientations.
Broadcasting applies an operation across compatible axes without requiring the caller to create repeated copies of the smaller operand. Dimensions align from the right. At each aligned axis, their lengths must agree or one must be one. Missing leading axes behave as length one.
For bias \(b\) with shape \([4]\) and output shape \([2,4]\), broadcasting adds the same four bias values to both rows. It does not turn this elementwise addition into matrix multiplication. A bias of shape \([2]\) would fail this contract, despite having one value per example.
Vectorization expresses a collection of operations through tensor kernels rather than a Python loop over examples. One matrix multiplication can process the whole batch. This often reduces interpreter overhead, but a valid vectorized expression can still create large intermediate tensors.
An operation can also change its input storage. x.exp() returns elementwise exponentials in a new tensor. The trailing underscore in x.exp_() means it writes the result into x. Likewise, x.add_(b) modifies x, including values visible through any other tensor sharing that storage.
Comparisons expose a second distinction. x.gt(0) produces a Boolean mask for values greater than zero. x.gt_(0) overwrites the original tensor with zero and one in its existing dtype. It destroys the original values and does not turn a floating-point tensor into a Boolean tensor.

Code example: Comparison masks and changes to existing values

import torch

x = torch.tensor([-1., 0., 2.])
mask = x.gt(0)
assert mask.dtype == torch.bool
assert mask.tolist() == [False, False, True]
assert x.tolist() == [-1., 0., 2.]
x.gt_(0)
assert x.dtype == torch.float32 and x.tolist() == [0., 0., 1.]

a = torch.tensor([0., 1.])
b = a.exp()
assert a.tolist() == [0., 1.]
a.exp_()
assert torch.allclose(a, b)
print(mask, x, a)
The ordinary comparison preserves \([-1,0,2]\). Its in-place counterpart changes the original to \([0,0,1]\). The exponential example similarly distinguishes a retained input from overwritten values. During training, an in-place change may invalidate a value needed for backward computation. Autograd checks many such conflicts, but avoiding unnecessary mutation makes the dependency easier to inspect.
For attention, Section 17.1 establishes the head layout \([B,H,T,d_h]\). Permuting axes preserves the values’ intended relationships only when the storage interpretation follows those axes. The next section makes that interpretation explicit.

title: 23  Tensor storage and execution
text:
23.3 Views, strides, and copies
A transpose can exchange axes without moving every value. It changes how logical coordinates address existing storage. A view is a tensor that shares storage with another tensor, while a copy has its own allocation.
A stride is the change in storage position, measured in elements, when one coordinate increases by one. The storage offset locates the tensor’s first logical element within its underlying storage. For a two-dimensional tensor:
\[
\operatorname{element\ offset}(i,j)=o_0+i s_0+j s_1
\tag{23.4}\]
Here \(o_0\) is the storage offset and \(s_0,s_1\) are the strides. To obtain a byte offset, multiply the entire element offset by the dtype’s element size.
Consider values \([0,1,2,3,4,5]\) arranged as a \(2\times3\) matrix. Its strides are \([3,1]\) and its storage offset is zero. Coordinate \((1,2)\) reads element offset \(1(3)+2(1)=5\).
Transposing gives shape \([3,2]\) and strides \([1,3]\), while retaining the same six stored values. Its coordinate \((2,1)\) also reads offset \(2(1)+1(3)=5\). The axes changed, but the address still identifies the same value.
The second row of the original matrix has shape \([3]\) and storage offset three. Its logical size is twelve float32 bytes, yet it shares the original 24-byte storage. This is why a slice’s element count is not its full retained allocation.
Contiguous layout places values in the expected adjacent order for a specified memory format. With the usual row-major format, the last axis advances by one element. The transposed matrix above is not contiguous in that format.
view() changes shape only when the existing strides support the requested grouping. Contiguity is sufficient for many common reshapes, but not required for every possible view. Calling view() on the transpose to flatten it fails because its logical traversal cannot use one consistent stride.
reshape() returns a view when possible and otherwise copies. contiguous() returns the original tensor when it already has the requested layout, or copies it into that layout. clone() explicitly creates a copy. Code that depends on shared storage must not assume that every reshape() shares values.
The following trace checks shape, stride, offsets, and storage sharing. It also shows a noncontiguous slice whose evenly spaced values can still form a one-dimensional view.

Code example: Shared storage, transpose, reshape and an evenly strided view

import torch

x = torch.arange(6, dtype=torch.float32).reshape(2, 3)
t = x.T
row = x[1]
assert x.stride() == (3, 1) and t.stride() == (1, 3)
assert row.storage_offset() == 3
assert row.numel() * row.element_size() == 12
assert row.untyped_storage().nbytes() == 24
assert x.untyped_storage().data_ptr() == t.untyped_storage().data_ptr()
assert x[1, 2].item() == t[2, 1].item() == 5
try:
    t.view(-1)
except RuntimeError:
    print("The transpose cannot use a flat view")
else:
    raise AssertionError("Expected an incompatible view")
flat_copy = t.reshape(-1)
assert flat_copy.tolist() == [0, 3, 1, 4, 2, 5]
assert flat_copy.untyped_storage().data_ptr() != x.untyped_storage().data_ptr()
assert x.contiguous() is x
assert t.contiguous().is_contiguous()

spaced = torch.arange(12).reshape(3, 4)[:, ::2]
flat_view = spaced.view(-1)
assert not spaced.is_contiguous()
assert flat_view.stride() == (2,)
assert flat_view.tolist() == [0, 2, 4, 6, 8, 10]
assert flat_view.untyped_storage().data_ptr() == spaced.untyped_storage().data_ptr()
print(x.shape, t.shape, row.storage_offset(), flat_view.stride())
The transpose shares storage, but its flattened reshape uses a copy. The final slice retains every second column of a \(3\times4\) matrix. Its offsets are \(0,2,4,6,8,10\), so a flat view with stride two is valid.
Sharing can extend beyond PyTorch objects. torch.from_numpy uses the same CPU memory as a supported NumPy array and retains its numerical dtype. Changing either object therefore changes the other’s values. By contrast, torch.tensor(array) copies the input values.
For a supported CPU tensor without gradient tracking, .numpy() normally exposes shared memory too. detach().cpu().numpy() disconnects the graph and transfers to CPU when needed, but does not promise a separate copy if the tensor is already on CPU. Add .copy() to obtain an independent NumPy array when later mutation must be isolated.

Code example: NumPy sharing and explicit copies

import numpy as np
import torch

array = np.array([1., 2., 3.], dtype=np.float64)
shared = torch.from_numpy(array)
copied = torch.tensor(array)
array[0] = 9.
assert shared.dtype == torch.float64
assert shared[0].item() == 9. and copied[0].item() == 1.
roundtrip = shared.numpy()
roundtrip[1] = 8.
assert shared[1].item() == 8.
isolated = shared.detach().cpu().numpy().copy()
isolated[2] = 7.
assert shared[2].item() == 3.
scalar = torch.tensor(4.)
assert scalar.shape == torch.Size([]) and scalar.item() == 4.
print(shared, copied, isolated)
The first mutation changes both the NumPy array and its shared tensor, while the copied tensor retains the old values. The conversion back to a NumPy array shares the tensor’s storage. A final NumPy copy isolates subsequent changes. Never change data needed by an unfinished backward computation through a shared NumPy view: those writes can bypass PyTorch’s normal mutation checks.
A tensor with one value can be scalar-shaped, with shape \([]\), or retain an axis, such as \([1]\). .item() extracts its value as a Python scalar in either case. It requires exactly one element and removes the tensor interface, so it is useful for logging rather than differentiable computation.
Copying a transpose into contiguous order can help a later kernel, but it adds allocation and transfer work. Measure the complete operation sequence before deciding that the copy improves performance. A kernel may already support the original strides efficiently.

title: 23  Tensor storage and execution
text:
23.4 Training state and tensor lifetimes
Storage sharing explains individual tensors, while memory exhaustion often depends on how many tensors remain alive together. Training retains parameters, gradients, saved activations, and optimizer state for different purposes.
The forward and backward sequence is taught in Chapter 10. Here its consequence is lifetime: backward computation may need values created during the forward pass. Autograd retains the information necessary for those derivatives until the graph is released or deliberately retained.
A leaf tensor is not the result of an operation recorded in the current autograd graph. A trainable leaf parameter can have requires_grad=True and grad_fn=None. Intermediate tensors produced by recorded differentiable operations usually carry a grad_fn describing their backward operation.
detach() creates a tensor without that autograd connection, but it shares storage with the original. It does not release every reference to the graph and does not create an independent value copy. Use detach().clone() when both disconnection and separate storage are required.






Figure 23.2: A tensor’s storage and gradient links differ from the optimizer’s separate state arrays.



A dense gradient buffer has the same logical shape as its parameter:
\[
\operatorname{shape}(G_{\theta})=\operatorname{shape}(\theta)
\tag{23.5}\]
Here \(G_\theta\) stores the derivatives of the scalar loss with respect to entries of \(\theta\). A linear weight with shape \([4,3]\) therefore receives a dense .grad tensor with shape $[4,3]`. Some operations support sparse gradients, whose storage is different despite the same logical parameter shape.
The optimizer mechanics in Chapter 11 determine which additional state persists between updates. Adam normally maintains two moment arrays for each updated parameter:
\[
\operatorname{state}_{\mathrm{Adam}}(\theta)=\{m_{\theta},v_{\theta}\},\quad\operatorname{shape}(m_{\theta})=\operatorname{shape}(v_{\theta})=\operatorname{shape}(\theta)
\tag{23.6}\]
The first moment \(m_\theta\) and second moment \(v_\theta\) each have the parameter’s shape. Implementations also keep small step counters and may allocate temporary update buffers.
One million float32 parameters occupy 4 MB. Float32 gradients add 4 MB, and two float32 Adam moments add 8 MB. These four arrays alone total 16 MB, using decimal megabytes.
This is a component estimate, not a complete training peak. Saved activations and temporary tensors add memory. Some mixed-precision arrangements also retain a higher-precision parameter copy. Quantization and sharding change the accounting, so inspect the actual implementation.






Figure 23.3: Parameters, gradients, and Adam moments total 16 MB in this example, before activations and temporary buffers.



Inference usually omits gradients and optimizer state but still needs parameters, active intermediate values, and request state such as the KV cache from Chapter 21. Calling model.eval() changes modules’ evaluation behavior. It does not by itself disable autograd tracking. A suitable no_grad() or inference_mode() context controls that separate concern.
Saving an output tensor in a Python list can also retain its graph during training. For a scalar log, storing loss.item() avoids keeping the loss tensor. Such extraction may synchronize device execution, so logging frequency can affect timing.

title: 23  Tensor storage and execution
text:
23.5 Devices, precision, and measurement
The same tensor expression can run on CPU or GPU, but its operands need compatible placement. Moving only a model or only its batch leaves the linear operation with mismatched devices.
A CUDA device is a GPU execution and memory target exposed by PyTorch, commonly cuda:0. The following example moves the model and constructs its input on the selected device. CPU remains a valid fallback for checking the interface.

Code example: Moving a model and its batch to one device

import torch
import torch.nn as nn

# The same code runs on a GPU when CUDA is available and on CPU otherwise.
device = torch.device("cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu")
model = nn.Linear(3, 2).to(device)
features = torch.tensor([[1.0, 0.0, -1.0]], device=device)

logits = model(features)
assert logits.device == features.device == next(model.parameters()).device
print(device, logits.shape)
assert logits.shape == (1, 2)
The result has shape \([1,2]\) and shares its device with the model and features. A CPU run checks placement logic. It does not measure GPU throughput or exercise CUDA kernels.
to(device) returns a tensor on the requested device, potentially allocating and copying when placement changes. It may return the original object when no conversion is required. Moving a CUDA tensor to a CPU-only NumPy path also requires an explicit transfer, with gradient tracking handled appropriately.
Mixed precision uses different floating-point dtypes for different operations or state. Lower-precision matrix operations can reduce memory traffic and use faster hardware paths. Sensitive reductions and optimizer state may retain higher precision. The mathematical operation remains the same, but rounding and representable range can change its numerical result.
A floating-point format divides its bits among a sign, an exponent and a fraction. The exponent mainly determines the range of magnitudes. The fraction determines how closely nearby values can be represented within that range.
Format | Sign bits | Exponent bits | Fraction bits | Bytes per value | | — | — | — | — | — | | float32 | 1 | 8 | 23 | 4 | | float16 | 1 | 5 | 10 | 2 | | bfloat16 | 1 | 8 | 7 | 2 |
Float16 and bfloat16 therefore have the same storage width but different numerical behavior. Bfloat16 retains float32’s exponent width while representing fewer nearby values. Around 1, adjacent representable values are spaced by approximately 0.000977 in float16 and 0.0078125 in bfloat16. These gaps grow at larger magnitudes.
Underflow loses values too small for the format, potentially rounding them to zero. Overflow exceeds its finite range. Gradient scaling temporarily multiplies the loss to reduce underflow during the backward calculation, then removes that scale before the optimizer update. It cannot repair every source of numerical instability.
Check loss values, gradients, and evaluation behavior against an appropriate reference. Float16 training may require gradient scaling to avoid underflow. The choice of dtype should follow the hardware, operation and training setup.
Data parallelism replicates a model across devices that process different local batches. An all-reduce combines corresponding gradients across replicas so their optimizer updates remain consistent. Communication and synchronization add costs, and changing total batch size can change optimization behavior.
The memory question also determines the measurement. torch.cuda.memory_allocated() counts tensor memory managed by the CUDA allocator. memory_reserved() includes memory the allocator retains for reuse. Neither is identical to the sum of every live tensor’s logical size or every byte shown by a system-level GPU monitor.
GPU kernels execute asynchronously relative to the host in many operations. A host timer around a launch can therefore measure dispatch instead of completion. Use CUDA events or explicit synchronization around a bounded benchmark, include warmup, and specify whether transfers are included.
Resetting peak-memory statistics before a representative operation helps isolate its peak. Report the batch, sequence length, dtype, and whether the run trains or serves. Those conditions connect the measurement to the tensor lifetimes and layouts studied here.
The complete experiments in Chapter 24 combine these checks with task quality. The library map in ?sec-ch-m2-library-map connects each interface to its earlier explanation and practical exercise.

Chapter checkpoint
A tensor slice has twelve logical bytes but its storage reports 24 bytes. Is either measurement necessarily wrong?
Feedback: No. The slice can expose three float32 elements while retaining a six-element shared allocation. Neither measurement alone establishes its additional device allocation.
A transpose becomes slower after adding contiguous(), although the following matrix kernel becomes faster. What should the comparison include?
Feedback: Include allocation and copying in the complete path. The kernel’s improvement must repay those costs under the actual reuse pattern.
An inference run calls eval() but still retains a growing graph. Which separate controls and references should you inspect?
Feedback: Check gradient-tracking context and stored output references. Evaluation mode alone does not disable autograd, and retained tensors can keep computation history alive.

title: 24  Experiments and system integration
text:
24.1 Logistic regression and optimizer comparisons
A correct small calculation does not establish that a trained system solves its task. These experiments connect the earlier mechanisms to complete datasets, controlled comparisons, and inspectable failures. Each result needs enough recorded information for another person to reproduce the comparison and assess its conclusion.
The short code examples below check particular interfaces and calculations. The full protocols require training or inference on the specified data. Their result tables are instructions for collecting evidence, not claims that those experiments have already been completed.
Keep source task statements and visible notebook outputs. Label plots with the measured quantity, axes, and configuration, using shared scales for comparisons. Record dataset and model revisions, preprocessing, splits, seeds, package versions, and hardware. Explain conclusions from the observed evidence rather than from the expected ranking of methods.
The first experiment makes every trainable value accessible. Its purpose is to connect a change in the update rule to a change in loss and held-out classification. It follows the SST-2 assignment in LLM_Architectures,_hometask_1.ipynb and the introductory PyTorch classifier notebook.
Checking one update. Start with the two-feature example below. The affine score from Chapter 5, stable binary loss from Chapter 8, and backward computation from Chapter 10 already define its mechanics.
\[
X\in\mathbb{R}^{B\times D},\quad w\in\mathbb{R}^{D},\quad z=Xw+b\in\mathbb{R}^{B}
\tag{24.1}\]
For batch size \(B\) and feature width \(D\), inputs have shape \([B,D]\), weights \([D]\), and logits \([B]\). With \(B=2,D=5\), the same rule produces two scores from a \(2\times5\) input. The binary batch objective is:
\[
L=-\frac{1}{B}\sum_{i=1}^{B}\left[y_i\log p_i+(1-y_i)\log(1-p_i)\right],\quad p_i=\sigma(z_i)
\tag{24.2}\]
Here \(p_i=\sigma(z_i)\) and \(y_i\in\{0,1\}\). For labels \((1,0)\) and probabilities \((0.8,0.25)\), the mean loss is approximately \(0.255413\) nats. A logits-based implementation avoids taking logarithms of rounded probabilities.
Compare the resulting gradients with the manual derivatives from Section 10.2, then verify one SGD update. Clearing accumulated gradients and rebuilding a forward graph are separate requirements. The assertions compare the manual and automatic derivatives and verify the changed weights.
Preparing SST-2. The source code loads SetFit/sst2, while its description also links the Stanford dataset. Record the actual dataset identifier and revision so the experiment can be reproduced. Use the supplied train and validation partitions.
Apply consistent cleaning: lowercase text, retain the selected letters, digits, spaces, and punctuation, and handle hyphens explicitly. Fit a count vocabulary on training sentences only. Retain the 10,000 most frequent tokens, or report the smaller limit used for available memory.
For vocabulary [movie, good, bad], good movie good becomes [1,2,0]. Reuse the fitted mapping on validation examples, including its out-of-vocabulary rule. The feature construction is taught in Chapter 4.
Implementing the classifier. Build weights, bias, affine scores, sigmoid probabilities, and prediction thresholding from PyTorch primitives. Provide zero and small-random initialization options. Keep the model, loss, and mini-batch training function separate so the experiments can reuse them.
Implement stable binary cross-entropy from logits and compare it with binary_cross_entropy_with_logits. Also compare the one-logit formulation with two-class softmax and one-hot targets, following Chapter 8. Test extreme logits as well as ordinary values.
The source’s 1e-15 probability clamp is insufficient to keep float32 probabilities below one. Use the stable logits expression rather than copying that numerical error. The classification threshold belongs in evaluation and must not replace probabilities inside the loss.
During mini-batch SGD, save detached copies of weights and bias after each update. At every epoch, record unregularized training log loss and a justified metric on both train and validation data. Return the final parameters and batch-wise parameter history. A two-feature decision-boundary plot helps interpret the introductory example, while the SST-2 run needs high-dimensional diagnostics.
Comparing learning rate and batch size. Run the source’s complete grid while keeping preprocessing, data partitions, epoch budget, and initialization policy fixed:
Show comparable heatmaps with learning rate on the horizontal axis and batch size on the vertical axis. Use the histories to distinguish faster progress, oscillation, divergence, and overfitting. A fixed epoch budget implies different update counts for different batch sizes, so report both epochs and updates.
Comparing L1 penalties. Add \(\lambda\sum_j|w_j|\) to the training objective, using the convention from Chapter 11. Compare \(\lambda\in\{0,10^{-4},10^{-3},10^{-2},10^{-1}\}\) with other settings fixed. The source recommends learning rate 0.1 and batch size 100 for this comparison.
Compare zero and small-random initialization. Record training stability, train and validation metrics, and the count of weights whose magnitude exceeds \(10^{-7}\). Plot that count and the training metric against \(\lambda\), alongside validation behavior. Plot selected shrinking weights against update number.
Ordinary SGD with an L1 subgradient need not produce exact zeros. Describe the threshold used for the reported count rather than claiming exact feature elimination. The source’s optional proximal-descent bonus is explained in Chapter 11, with the small-magnitude branch corrected.
Comparing optimizer paths. The assignment also requires a separate experiment on two functions. It is not replaced by the sentiment classifier’s learning-rate grid. Compare GD, Momentum, AdaGrad, and Adam using their rules from Chapter 11.
The convex function is \(f(x,y)=x^2+4y^2\). Its gradient is \((2x,8y)\), and its minimum is at \((0,0)\). The six-hump function is:
\[
f(x,y)=\left(4-2.1x^2+\frac{x^4}{3}\right)x^2+xy+\left(-4+4y^2\right)y^2
\tag{24.3}\]
Its two global minima lie approximately at \((0.0898,-0.7126)\) and \((-0.0898,0.7126)\), with value about \(-1.0316\). It also has local minima. Begin from a nonoptimal point, such as the source’s \((-2,-1.5)\), and compare additional starts to investigate that dependence.
Save \((x_t,y_t)\) and function value after each step. Plot values against iteration and trajectories over function contours, showing all optimizers on comparable axes. Change hyperparameters deliberately. Then inspect oscillation, progress, and the final parameter values. Explain why a setting effective on the bowl may behave differently on the six-hump surface.
The classifier and surface experiments reveal different aspects of optimization. The next experiment adds a learned text representation while preserving a separate evaluation decision.

title: 24  Experiments and system integration
text:
Code example: Logistic-regression forward, loss, and backward checks

import torch.nn as nn

import torch

# Rows are examples; columns are features.
X = torch.tensor([[1.0, 0.0], [0.0, 1.0]])
y = torch.tensor([1.0, 0.0])
w = torch.tensor([0.2, -0.1], requires_grad=True)
b = torch.tensor(0.0, requires_grad=True)

# The affine score is the logistic-regression logit.
logits = X @ w + b
loss = torch.nn.functional.binary_cross_entropy_with_logits(logits, y)
loss.backward()
assert logits.shape == (2,)
assert w.grad.shape == w.shape
assert b.grad.shape == b.shape
error = (torch.sigmoid(logits.detach()) - y) / len(y)
assert torch.allclose(w.grad, X.T @ error)
assert torch.allclose(b.grad, error.sum())
before = w.detach().clone()
expected = before - 0.1 * (X.T @ error)
with torch.no_grad():
    w -= 0.1 * w.grad
    b -= 0.1 * b.grad
assert torch.allclose(w, expected)
print(loss.item(), w.detach(), b.detach())









Learning rates | Batch sizes | Evidence for every combination | |—|—|—| | 0.01, 0.03, 0.1, 0.3, 1.0 | 50, 100, 200 | Final train and validation log loss and metric, with convergence histories |

title: 24  Experiments and system integration
text:
24.2 Text classification with learned embeddings
The AG News assignment tests whether learned token vectors support useful document predictions. It follows LLM_Architectures_hometask_2_Tel_Aviv.ipynb, from tokenizer training through error analysis. This section is the complete classification protocol referenced by the earlier representation chapters.
Preparing the comparisons. Keep the dataset’s test partition for final evaluation and create a validation partition within training data. Fit both BPE and WordPiece on training text only, recording normalization, vocabulary limits, and special tokens. Chapter 3 explains their construction.
Write five comparison sentences and display both token sequences beside each sentence. Explain the differences actually observed, including rare or fragmented words. A tokenizer’s output alone does not establish that one method will improve the classifier.
Train Word2Vec on the BPE-tokenized training sentences with the objective from Chapter 14. Compare CBOW and skip-gram at embedding widths 50, 100, and 200, giving six settings. Keep or explicitly report window size, minimum frequency, training epochs, seed, and other changed settings.
For three example tokens, show vector dimensions and nearest neighbors. Report each Word2Vec vocabulary size and explain its difference from the tokenizer vocabulary. Frequency filtering can remove valid tokenizer tokens. Define the fallback for those tokens before constructing document vectors.
Building the classifier. Map token IDs to learned vectors, then pool valid token positions into one vector per article. Chapter 13 defines lookup, pooling, and padding exclusion. Mean and sum pooling are source options. Explain any alternative and handle documents with no usable tokens explicitly.
An article representation of width \(E\) enters an MLP with one to three hidden layers, nonlinear activation, and four output logits. Record hidden widths, activation, optimizer, learning rate, batch size, and epoch count. Chapter 12 supplies the nonlinear layer mechanics.
The original small example verifies this interface with two documents, two tokens each, and three embedding coordinates:

Code example: Pooled token vectors and four-class MLP logits

import torch
import torch.nn as nn
torch.manual_seed(7)

# A real run obtains these token vectors from the trained Word2Vec model.
token_vectors = torch.tensor([
    [[1.0, 0.0, 0.5], [0.5, 1.0, 0.0]],
    [[0.0, 1.0, 0.5], [1.0, 0.5, 0.0]],
])
article_vectors = token_vectors.mean(dim=1)
classifier = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(3, 8), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(8, 4))
labels = torch.tensor([0, 2])

logits = classifier(article_vectors)
loss = nn.CrossEntropyLoss()(logits, labels)
assert article_vectors.shape == (2, 3)
assert logits.shape == (2, 4)
print(loss.item())
It produces article vectors \([2,3]\), four-class logits \([2,4]\), and a scalar cross-entropy loss. Both positions are valid in this toy batch. Real padded batches need the validity-aware pooling from Chapter 13.
State whether the pretrained embeddings remain frozen. If they are trainable, classifier gradients also change their rows, and the Word2Vec initialization becomes a starting point rather than a fixed representation. Comparing frozen and trainable versions is a useful book extension, separate from the source’s six Word2Vec settings.
An MLP can classify pooled features because their width is fixed. Pooling loses order information, however, so the classifier cannot recover distinctions absent from those features. Compare that limit with the sequence models in Chapter 15.
Evaluating the result. Select architecture and training settings using validation evidence. Then compute test accuracy and a confusion matrix as required by the source. Optional F1 measurements add detail but do not replace accuracy. Chapter 9 explains the metrics and selection boundary.
Display three incorrect predictions with original text, true label, and predicted label. Relate patterns to tokenization, representation, or classification evidence. Neighbor quality alone is not the final classifier result, and an unexplained error pattern is not evidence of a specific internal cause.
The source also asks for a proposed input-influence method, without requiring its implementation. One option removes a token or phrase and compares the original class score under the same model. Explain that deletion changes the input and can create unnatural text, so this is a sensitivity test rather than proof of human-like reasoning.
Conclude which Word2Vec objective and width supported the chosen task, citing the comparison results. The next experiment removes learned vectors entirely to expose sequence probabilities through counts.

title: 24  Experiments and system integration
text:
24.3 N-gram counts and generation
The NLTK tutorial gives a fixed-history baseline whose probabilities can be traced to observed counts. It follows Ngram_Language_Model_with_NLTK_(1).ipynb. The count estimator and unseen-event problem are taught in Section 15.2.
Building counts. The source tutorial uses a text article saved as language-never-random.txt. Load its text, split it into sentences, tokenize each sentence, and lowercase tokens consistently. Inspect the first sentence before constructing counts. Begin the small check below with already tokenized sentences. For order \(n\), add \(n-1\) start and end markers around each sentence, keeping sentence boundaries explicit. padded_everygram_pipeline supplies training sequences containing grams up to that order and vocabulary data for fitting.
A vocabulary cutoff determines which observed words retain their own entries. NLTK’s Vocabulary maps excluded or unseen tokens to <UNK>. Inspect known and rare tokens after applying that mapping, because it changes the counts the estimator receives.
The original two-sentence check remains useful before the library workflow:

Code example: Padded bigram counts and maximum-likelihood probability

from collections import Counter

sentences = [["<s>", "the", "cat", "</s>"], ["<s>", "the", "dog", "</s>"]]
bigrams = Counter(
    (left, right)
    for sentence in sentences
    for left, right in zip(sentence, sentence[1:])
)
contexts = Counter(left for left, _ in bigrams.elements())

probability = bigrams[("the", "cat")] / contexts["the"]
assert probability == 0.5
print(bigrams, probability)
In that count table, the precedes cat once and dog once. Each continuation has probability one half. Neither this example nor an unsmoothed MLE model automatically resolves an unseen history.
Fit NLTK MLE(n) on the padded everygrams. Inspect unigram counts, one history’s continuation counts, and its conditional score. Compare logscore with the base-two logarithm of that probability. NLTK’s base-two log scores differ from the natural-log loss convention used elsewhere in this book.
Generating and restoring a model. Generate a continuation with a fixed text_seed and random_seed. Keep the raw tokens so boundary symbols remain inspectable. For readable text, remove boundary markers under an explicit rule and detokenize with TreebankWordDetokenizer.
The following complete small example covers vocabulary mapping, fitting, inspection, generation, and the source’s dill save/reload operation. It reloads only the file this example just created.

Code example: NLTK vocabulary, counts, generation and model persistence

from pathlib import Path
import math
import dill
from nltk.lm import MLE, Vocabulary
from nltk.lm.preprocessing import padded_everygram_pipeline
from nltk.tokenize.treebank import TreebankWordDetokenizer

sentences = ["the cat sat".split(), "the dog sat".split()] * 2
sentences.append("the hare sat".split())
training, vocabulary_tokens = padded_everygram_pipeline(2, sentences)
vocabulary = Vocabulary(vocabulary_tokens, unk_cutoff=2)
model = MLE(2, vocabulary=vocabulary)
model.fit(training)
assert model.vocab.lookup("hare") == "<UNK>"
assert model.vocab.lookup("unseen") == "<UNK>"
assert model.counts[2][("the",)]["cat"] == 2
assert model.counts[2][("the",)]["<UNK>"] == 1
probability = model.score("cat", ["the"])
assert probability == 2 / 5
assert math.isclose(model.logscore("cat", ["the"]), math.log2(probability))
generated = model.generate(8, text_seed=["the"], random_seed=42)
readable = TreebankWordDetokenizer().detokenize(
    [token for token in generated if token not in {"<s>", "</s>"}]
)
print(model.counts.unigrams, model.counts[2][("the",)])
print(probability, generated, readable)
path = Path("tiny-ngram-model.pkl")
with path.open("wb") as target:
    dill.dump(model, target)
with path.open("rb") as source:
    restored = dill.load(source)
assert restored.score("cat", ["the"]) == probability
assert restored.generate(8, text_seed=["the"], random_seed=42) == generated
The reloaded model must reproduce the conditional score and the same seeded token sequence. Saving only generated text would not preserve the estimator. Record library versions with the artifact, because serialization and generation behavior can depend on them.
Book extension: unseen events and evaluation. The source lists smoothing classes as optional further reading. It does not perform the smoothing and held-out-perplexity comparison requested here. Keep that extension distinguishable from the original tutorial.
Use the add-alpha mechanism in Section 15.2 to compare one zero-count continuation with its smoothed probability. Evaluate on held-out sentences using the same vocabulary and boundary conventions. Chapter 8 explains how mean negative log probability determines perplexity.
An unsmoothed zero probability gives infinite perplexity. A finite smoothed result resolves that numerical failure but does not prove useful language prediction. Report model order, cutoff, smoothing settings, and several generated continuations alongside the loss.

title: 24  Experiments and system integration
text:
24.4 Character sequences and recurrent generation
An n-gram model limits context to an explicit history length. The character-level assignment replaces that table with learned recurrent state. It uses dinosaur names in the second part of LLM_Architectures_hometask_2_Tel_Aviv.ipynb.
Preparing sequences. Add < and > around each name, then create character-to-ID and ID-to-character mappings. The source illustrates anna as <anna>. Preserve the same mapping across training, validation, and generation.
Split whole names before concatenating each partition and constructing overlapping windows. Alternatively, split a source stream first and prevent windows from crossing that split. Randomly separating already-overlapping windows can place nearly identical character spans in both partitions.
Construct a dataset with __len__ and __getitem__, accepting a sequence length and input names or file path. For each start position, return an input window of length \(T\) and the next-character targets of length \(T\). For <anna> and \(T=4\), input <ann pairs with target anna.
Create training and validation loaders with a recorded batch size. Ensure the vocabulary covers validation characters under a declared policy. Do not silently assign a new ID that exceeds the model’s output width.
Tracing and training the model. One-hot encode an ID tensor \([B,T]\) into floating-point inputs \([B,T,V]\). An LSTM of width \(H\) produces sequence states \([B,T,H]\). The output head maps these to next-character logits \([B,T,V]\).
The recurrence, gates, and state shapes follow Chapter 15. On one fixed batch, print each layer’s output shape and inspect probabilities over the final vocabulary axis. Align every timestep’s logit with its shifted target before reducing cross-entropy.
Train for a fixed epoch budget while recording training and validation loss. Reset state between independent examples or document intentional state carryover. If carrying state across truncated segments, detach at the chosen backward boundary as explained in Chapter 15.
Comparing generation. Supply several prefixes to the trained model. Process the full prefix, then carry recurrent state while feeding back each selected character. Stop at > or a recorded maximum length.
Compare greedy decoding with sampling from the full vocabulary, then vary top-\(k\) and temperature. Chapter 7 contains the selection mechanics. Hold the model and prefix fixed for each comparison and record seeds, because different samples alone cannot establish an improvement.
The original small code checks one untrained LSTM and a top-three distribution:

Code example: Character LSTM state and top-k sampling

import torch
import torch.nn as nn
torch.manual_seed(7)

vocab_size, hidden_width = 6, 8
inputs = torch.nn.functional.one_hot(
    torch.tensor([[0, 1, 2]]),
    vocab_size,
).float()
lstm = nn.LSTM(vocab_size, hidden_width, batch_first=True)
output_head = nn.Linear(hidden_width, vocab_size)

states, recurrent_state = lstm(inputs)
logits = output_head(states[:, -1])
top_values, top_ids = torch.topk(logits, k=3, dim=-1)
probabilities = torch.softmax(top_values, dim=-1)

assert states.shape == (1, 3, hidden_width)
assert top_ids.shape == (1, 3)
print(top_ids, probabilities)
Its hidden states have shape \([1,3,8]\), and the selected candidates have shape \([1,3]\). It does not train a name generator or execute the feedback loop. The complete experiment must add those stages before interpreting name quality.
Keep generated names beside the settings and loss histories. Discuss repeated fragments, incomplete endings, prefix sensitivity, and plausible new combinations using the actual outputs. Attention next provides a different way to inspect information access across a sequence.

title: 24  Experiments and system integration
text:
24.5 Attention under controlled changes
The attention assignment tests how changing an input affects the weights and output values. It follows the second part of From_Finetuning_to_Attention_Inside_LLMs.ipynb. The complete mechanism is in Chapter 16, and head layouts are in Section 17.1.
Start with the original two-position calculation below. Save projected \(Q,K,V\), unmasked scores, the mask, masked scores, row-wise weights, and weighted outputs. Label both heatmap axes by token and position.

Code example: Scaled attention values and row-normalization checks

import torch

# Two query positions, two key positions, and scalar values.
Q = torch.tensor([[1.0, 0.0], [0.0, 1.0]])
K = torch.tensor([[1.0, 0.0], [0.0, 1.0]])
V = torch.tensor([[2.0], [6.0]])
scale = Q.shape[-1] ** 0.5
scores = Q @ K.T / scale
causal_mask = torch.triu(torch.full_like(scores, float("-inf")), diagonal=1)
masked_scores = scores + causal_mask
weights = torch.softmax(masked_scores, dim=-1)
output = weights @ V
assert scores.shape == (2, 2)
assert output.shape == (2, 1)
assert weights[0, 1].item() == 0.0
assert torch.allclose(weights.sum(dim=-1), torch.ones(2))
The first query cannot read the second key under the causal mask. Every valid row sums to one. In a separate scalar check, weights \([0.25,0.75]\) and values \([2,6]\) produce output five. Compare an unmasked hand calculation and library result before adding masks.
Changing one word. Use the cat sat on the mat, then replace cat with dog. Define one fixed token-to-vector lookup and keep all projection matrices unchanged. Unchanged token IDs must retrieve identical vectors in both runs.
The source’s newly sampled random embeddings would change more than the selected word. Reusing a fixed lookup corrects that experimental control. A toy lookup can show arithmetic effects but cannot establish linguistic meaning in random vectors.
Compare the changed token’s projections, affected score row and column, normalized weights, and context vectors. With causal masking, earlier queries cannot respond to a later changed token. Perturbing a masked value should leave the corresponding output unchanged.
Comparing heads. Repeat the controlled comparison for at least two heads, each with its own fixed \(W_Q,W_K,W_V\). Display their heatmaps on comparable scales, preserving token order. Explain any differences from the actual matrices and outputs.
Separate the single-head output from concatenated head outputs. Check masks before softmax and handle invalid all-masked rows explicitly. Answer whether the word replacement changed weights, whether heads differ, and what complementary information trained heads could provide. A heatmap alone does not establish that a head understands a semantic relation.

title: 24  Experiments and system integration
text:
24.6 Adapting answers to the reader
The adaptation assignment tests whether training changes the level and clarity of an answer. It uses the first part of From_Finetuning_to_Attention_Inside_LLMs.ipynb. Chapter 20 explains the QLoRA mechanism and alternatives such as prompting.
Preparing evidence. Select open question-answer examples from databricks-dolly-15k. For each training question, create child, student, and expert answers. Child answers should be simple and intuitive, student answers educational with moderate detail, and expert answers technically precise.
Before scaling up preparation, inspect a small batch. Validate generated JSON, require all three levels for each question, save JSONL, and reload it. Display the reloaded training data as a DataFrame so formatting and missing fields are visible.
Create a separate, manually reviewed test set of twenty question-answer examples spanning all three levels. Keep the underlying questions separate from training, not merely differently worded level instructions. Display the test table and review whether each expected answer fits its requested level.
Respecting model interfaces. Repeat adaptation for both source checkpoints, recording exact revisions:
Checkpoint | Input and target arrangement | |—|—| | HuggingFaceTB/SmolLM2-360M-Instruct | A causal text record containing question, expertise level, and answer, with the response-loss policy stated explicitly | | google/flan-t5-small | Encoder input containing question and expertise level, with the answer supplied as the separate decoder target |
The causal record uses explicit Question, Expertise level, and Answer fields. At inference, supply the question and level with an answer prompt, excluding the expected answer. For seq2seq training, do not append the target to encoder input. Chapter 18 explains these architectural differences.
Load each base model with the supported four-bit configuration, prepare it for quantized training, add compatible LoRA adapters, and optimize only the intended adapter parameters. Choose task type and target module paths for that architecture. The causal setup in Chapter 20 is a starting point, not an unchanged seq2seq recipe.
Record quantization settings, rank, scaling, dropout, target modules, trainable and total parameter counts, and training settings. Inspect which parameters enter the optimizer. A local arithmetic check preserves the earlier rank-one count and affine reconstruction example:

Code example: LoRA parameter count and affine dequantization checks

import torch

# A frozen 4 by 4 weight receives a rank-1 update.
d_in, d_out, rank = 4, 4, 1
torch.manual_seed(7)
A = torch.randn(rank, d_in, requires_grad=True)
B = torch.zeros(d_out, rank, requires_grad=True)
trainable = A.numel() + B.numel()
assert trainable == rank * (d_in + d_out)

# Affine quantization reconstructs a value from an integer code.
scale, q, zero_point = 0.1, 13, 3
x_hat = scale * (q - zero_point)
assert x_hat == 1.0
The \(4\times4\) rank-one update has eight adapter parameters, and \(0.1(13-3)=1.0\) verifies affine reconstruction. Neither calculation loads a model or verifies NF4 training. If hardware or package support prevents a required run, report that run as unexecuted rather than replacing it with this check.
Comparing answers. Generate base and adapted outputs for both models on the same twenty test examples. Keep prompting, decoding, and output limits comparable. Record one row per model and example using the source’s evidence fields:
Question | Level | Base output | Adapted output | Expected answer | Better after adaptation? | Notes | |—|—|—|—|—|—|—| | Record the held-out question | Child, student, or expert | Actual text | Actual text | Reviewed reference | Judgment supported by the rubric | Specific improvement or failure |
Use a common rubric covering requested expertise level, clarity, relevance, faithfulness to the question, and unsupported claims. A lower training loss alone cannot answer these questions. Show failures as well as improvements.
Compare which model followed the level and format more reliably, which was clearer, and which introduced more unsupported content. Explain observed differences with appropriate limits: architecture, checkpoint training, and capacity differ together.
Finally, discuss what changed after adaptation, how four-bit storage and adapters affect memory, and what increasing rank could change. Compare prompting with adaptation in terms of task evidence, data preparation, cost, and flexibility. The source does not supply a universal answer-quality threshold.

title: 24  Experiments and system integration
text:
24.7 Multimodal components and combined answers
The final experiment joins separate capabilities whose errors can propagate into one answer. It follows LLM_Architecture_HW4.ipynb, with the approved object or landmark case replacing its face-identification subject. Chapter 22 explains image representations and the distinction between retrieval and generation.
Captioning. Use at least five varied images, covering people, animals, an indoor scene, an outdoor scene, and multiple objects. Run a suitable pretrained captioning model with its matching processor. Record checkpoint revision, preprocessing, and decoding settings.
Display each image and its actual caption. Find at least two erroneous or incomplete captions. For each, record the prediction, a corrected description, and a plausible explanation grounded in visible evidence. Distinguish a missing detail from an invented object.
Question answering. Use at least three images and ask at least three questions per image: one object-recognition question, one counting question, and one color or attribute question. Display each image, question, and generated answer.
Find at least two failures and explain the expected answer and observed discrepancy. Caption quality does not establish counting ability, and a fluent answer can still contradict the image. Evaluate these tasks separately before combining components.
The original local patch example isolates only the first representation step:

Code example: Patch tokens as inputs to a vision-language pipeline

import torch

image = torch.arange(16.0).reshape(1, 1, 4, 4)
patches = image.unfold(2, 2, 2).unfold(3, 2, 2)
patches = patches.contiguous().reshape(1, 4, 4)
projection = torch.ones(4, 3)
patch_tokens = patches @ projection

assert patches.shape == (1, 4, 4)
assert patch_tokens.shape == (1, 4, 3)
print(patch_tokens)
It converts one \(4\times4\) grayscale image into four \(2\times2\) patches and projects each four-value patch to width three. Its output shape is \([1,4,3]\). A full model additionally requires its trained visual/text interface and output decoder.
Reference retrieval. Choose three to five object instances or landmarks, collecting at least eight images per category. Preserve the source’s quantitative split: five or six reference images and two or three distinct query images per category. Ensure the chosen counts total the collected images, and prevent duplicate photographs from crossing the split.
Use a matching pretrained image encoder and preprocessing for reference and query images. Normalize their embeddings and rank references by cosine similarity. State whether the category score uses a nearest reference or an explicit aggregation, and keep that rule fixed during evaluation.
Report the retrieved category, reference image, similarity score, and correct category for each query. Similarity is not a calibrated probability. If the system includes rejection for unknown categories, choose that rule using separate development evidence rather than the final query labels.
Combining components. A separate VQA or captioning component inspects the query image to answer an attribute or action question. Combine the retrieval result with that component’s answer, preserving uncertainty rather than turning a similarity score into certainty.
For example, retrieval might suggest a specific landmark while VQA describes its visible lighting. The combined response should retain both sources of evidence. Test the answer component with correct reference information as well as the retrieved result to distinguish its own failures from propagated retrieval errors.
Keep one complete record for each query:
Evidence field | What to retain | |—|—| | Input | Query image, question, and correct reference category | | Retrieval | Selected reference, predicted category, and similarity score | | Answer component | Actual caption or VQA answer with its settings | | Combined response | Final text and the evidence supplied to produce it | | Diagnosis | Retrieval error, answer error despite correct retrieval, propagated error, or successful result |
Explain several successful and failing cases using the stored component outputs. The original face task is deliberately omitted as a subject, while its reference/query comparison and combined-answer experiment are preserved in this substitution.
Book extension: resource measurements. Measure response time and peak memory separately for retrieval, answering, and the combined path. Follow Section 23.5 for synchronization and allocator interpretation. State whether loading, preprocessing, transfers, and cache reuse are included.
A faster retrieval stage does not necessarily make the full response faster if generation dominates. Likewise, a correct reference cannot compensate for an unsupported answer. These measurements and error records return to Chapter 1’s starting question: what output does the task require, and what evidence establishes that it is useful?

Final checkpoint
An AG News model has attractive word neighbors but poor test accuracy. What evidence is still needed before choosing a new embedding objective?
Feedback: Inspect validation comparisons, token coverage, pooling, classifier training, and concrete classification errors. Neighbor inspection alone does not isolate the cause of poor predictions.
A QLoRA run lowers training loss but produces equally technical answers at every requested level. Has it met the assignment’s main objective?
Feedback: No. Judge level adaptation on the reviewed held-out examples, using the same rubric before and after training for both required models.
A combined landmark answer identifies the wrong site but correctly describes a red door. How should the result be recorded?
Feedback: Preserve the retrieval error and the correct attribute result separately, then mark the final identification as a propagated error. One correct component does not make the combined answer correct.

title: Appendix A — Dictionary
text:
Expand abbreviations and direct readers to their substantive explanation.
Alphabetical expansions of the principal abbreviations used in the guide.

ALiBi: Attention with Linear Biases, a relative-position method.
BPE: Byte Pair Encoding, a greedy subword vocabulary-building algorithm.
BPTT: Backpropagation through time, gradient calculation through an unrolled recurrent computation.
CBOW: Continuous bag-of-words, an objective that predicts a center word from surrounding words.
CLIP: Contrastive Language-Image Pretraining.
CNN: Convolutional neural network.
DPO: Direct Preference Optimization.
FFN: Feed-forward network applied independently to each transformer token representation.
GELU: Gaussian Error Linear Unit activation.
KV cache: Key-value cache used to reuse attention projections during autoregressive decoding.
LLM: Large language model.
LoRA: Low-Rank Adaptation.
LSTM: Long short-term memory, a gated recurrent architecture.
MLM: Masked language modeling.
MLP: Multilayer perceptron, a feed-forward neural network built from affine layers and nonlinear activations.
MoE: Mixture of Experts, a model layer that routes each token to a subset of expert networks.
PEFT: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning.
QKV: Query, key, and value projections used by attention.
QLoRA: Quantized Low-Rank Adaptation.
RAG: Retrieval-augmented generation.
RLHF: Reinforcement learning from human feedback.
RMSNorm: Root mean square normalization.
RNN: Recurrent neural network.
RoPE: Rotary positional embedding.
SFT: Supervised fine-tuning.
STFT: Short-time Fourier transform.
TF-IDF: Term frequency-inverse document frequency, a document-feature weighting scheme.
TPOT: Time per output token.
TTFT: Time to first token.
UNK: Unknown-token marker used when a tokenizer cannot represent an input piece.
ViLT: Vision-and-Language Transformer.
ViT: Vision Transformer.
VQ-VAE: Vector-Quantized Variational Autoencoder.

Return to the notation reference for symbol dimensions and to the reading paths to locate the prerequisites for a chapter.
